Our experimental results show that the algorithm's security relies on the angle perturbation parameter which must be managed by the service provider without compromising security to protect users' privacy. Our experimental results show an improvement in the angle-based metric for sequences with  sequence with  locations that have been submitted by a user.

A crucial component for autonomous driving and robotics is place recognition, and an essential place recognition approach is learning-based topological mapping. However, topological mapping in environments with sparse landmarks poses a significant challenge. In this research, a novel topological mapping method is introduced that leverages both proximity and angular data within the feature space to effectively identify and connect locations. Experimental results indicate that the proposed approach surpasses existing methods by efficiently learning topological maps in under-connected graphs. Furthermore, the corresponding source code has been made available for public access on the link https://github.com/whdeng/topo_map.git.

Research on resting-state fMRI has led to numerous studies using statistical tests to compare single-time point studies or multi-site studies, often resulting in the collection of extensive data sets. When conducting single-site studies, larger sample sizes are necessary to yield reliable findings, whereas multi-site studies can generate significant statistical power with smaller groups, given that variability between sites far exceeds that within sites. Despite this, most recent meta-analysis studies have employed approaches suited for single-site data, not utilizing information about multiple sites to enhance results. To address this, we've developed an approach to simultaneously analyze data from multiple sites, leveraging group-level variability to boost sensitivity in functional connectivity measures. We've demonstrated this approach to be an extension of previous single-site procedures and an improvement over recent meta-analysis methods, resulting in significantly enhanced sensitivity in functional connectivity analysis. We've found that our approach has successfully recovered known functional connections while revealing novel, site-specific connections, uncovering patterns of variability associated with cognitive performance.

In a single-hop beeping network, stations interact via one-bit messages to form a distributed communication system. We explore the distributed computing domain's two core challenges, naming and counting issues, and our objective is to refine existing algorithms to reduce their energy usage and processing speed while ensuring optimal output. Our key contribution is the development of efficient, randomized algorithms that achieve optimal results (Optimal RAN and Optimal RC) for these problems, running in just $O(n \log n)$ time and using $O(\log n)$ energy and processing efficiency in the best-case scenario and $O(n \log n)$ time with high probability. Our algorithms are modelled after the recent state-of-the-art approaches by Moussaid et al. However, they utilize more energy-efficient and efficient message protocols.

Recent advancements in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, thanks to widespread use of language blending in personal communications. One significant challenge in processing code-mixed data arises from language labeling, which becomes difficult due to mixed languages sharing words. A related issue is building word embeddings for code-mixed languages, which presents an additional hurdle. A proposed solution is to create a graph-based framework for language modeling, which can be applied to CMLs, in contrast to existing approaches relying on solely n-gram models or word embeddings. This novel method employs graph convolutional networks to generate representations for mixed language words, which are then fed into a graph-based autoencoder to produce node embeddings. These node embeddings are used to predict the next word in a sequence within a code-mixed text.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyze how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 GPa and 300 GPa. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states leads to a more accurate description of the experimentally observed increase in critical temperature with pressure, and better agreement with the experimentally observed saturation of critical temperatures at high pressures. We find that this agreement is improved when considering the variable density of states at high pressures, and that the maximum critical temperature is reached when the electron-phonon coupling constant reaches a certain threshold.

This paper presents an innovative technique to create an adaptive framework for motion planning in dynamic environments. Unlike existing methods that utilize map-based global planning tools, our approach employs a dynamic global planner that responds to changing obstacles and bypasses the limitations of static map representation. A dynamic global planner is designed to generate routes based on the evolution of dynamic obstacles. However, a fault arises when a collision occurs due to a discrepancy between the estimated and actual positions of static obstacles. To mitigate this issue, a dynamic marker management system has been developed to eliminate redundant static obstacle markers and prevent collisions and route disruptions caused by dynamic obstacles. A dynamic filter is also incorporated to manage markers. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through successful navigation around moving agents and static obstacles in simulation environments.

This research introduces a visual relocalization technique using 3D surfel mapping that leverages passive observer capabilities with a single camera. Our proposed method combines effective depth estimation with online optimization to create and maintain a detailed 3D surfel map. A novel cost function and gradient descent-based optimizer are employed to address the complexity of integrating different modules, while an adaptive learning rate scheme enhances overall efficiency. Moreover, a detailed analysis of our design choices is provided along with comprehensive evaluations of our approach against competing baselines, as well as real-world experiments demonstrating its application in robotics.

In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as a sparse recovery challenge, where an underdetermined system of equations needs to be reconstructed from incomplete measurements. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel framework that draws on group sparsity and adaptive reconfiguration. A sparsity-promoting optimization is leveraged to identify key groups, along with their supporting load profiles, and an iterative adaptive protocol is developed accordingly. A critical analysis of the sparsity-promoting optimization is undertaken, along with an algorithmic implementation. Moreover, we investigate the feasibility of adaptive reconfiguration across different scenarios and provide a comparative evaluation of the proposed framework with traditional static precoding techniques.
We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve is seamlessly embedded within the rational function semifield of its constituent tree decomposition.

This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process under specific assumptions regarding its behavior over time. A key concept discussed here is the quasi-stationary distribution, which is particularly relevant in this context. Conditioned on a Markov process remaining within a specific subset, the future behavior of the process can, in certain instances, develop towards relative stability. One such example is provided by the conditioned random walk on a tree, where the process can be shown to converge towards a unique quasi-stationary distribution when restricted to the tree's trunks. A simple, explicit formula is derived to measure the speed at which the process converges towards its quasi-stationary distribution, relying on the specific characteristics of the tree and its associated Markov kernel. This result generalizes earlier work, specifically expanding upon the research conducted by Birkel [ark for Probab. Math. Sci. vol. 38, no. 2 (2010)], under more general conditions.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Igreja and Morton's 1-cohomology class, through a formal sequence, results in a Vassiliev invariant of order three. This finding reaffirms Morton and the first author's independent discovery.

The superconductor LiFeAs was found to transition from a non-superconducting, magnetically vulnerable state at 18.5 millikelvin. The impact of pressure on its magnetic and superconducting properties has been extensively studied in a wide range of conditions. The superconductor's behavior under high pressure has been found to be highly dependent on various factors, including temperature and the rate of pressure application. The diverse range of phase transitions that occur under high pressure in LiFeAs have been characterized by significant decreases in pressure required and increases in energy involved, as well as changes from first-order to second-order transitions. The behavior under high pressure in LiFeAs has been found to be highly complex and influenced by numerous factors. The superconductor's magnetic and superconducting properties under high pressure have been found to be highly variable and susceptible to multiple phase transitions that occur at different rates and temperatures. The maximum superconducting transition temperature under high pressure in LiFeAs has been found to be 28 GPa, as well as a broader pressure range than previously found. We examine a class of Type-II two Higgs doublet models where one of the doublets has CP-violation properties. Our analysis is based on a two-dimensional search space defined by the ratios of Yukawa couplings between the fermions and the Higgs fields. The model predictions are compared with the standard model outcomes in production rates, branching fractions, and decay topologies for the Higgs bosons decaying into fermion pairs. Our findings indicate that upcoming Higgs hunting efforts at future colliders will be able to probe a significant portion of the two Higgs doublet model's parameter space. The results also show that current LHC data has already set several limits on the model, however future searches are expected to be more stringent due to increased luminosity and energy.

We demonstrate through simulated molecular surface experiments that neuroevolutionary learning can independently design both the molecular structure of the self-assembling particles and their spatial organization, surpassing human-designed counterparts in temporally and spatially controlled self-assembly patterns. This achievement showcases the potential of using machine learning to address long-standing challenges in materials development and nanotechnology.

Chiral gauge theories are of great interest due to their potential to describe key components of quantum chromodynamics. These theories are challenging to analyze because their group theoretical properties ensure they cannot be in a dynamical Higgs phase, which is the desired outcome. However, recent studies of their core components have revealed an unexpected scenario. When the core component is a one-dimensional unitary matrix, the theory exhibits a dynamical Higgs phase even without an underlying symmetry. This research delves into the dynamics of this phase in theories with complex one-dimensional unitary matrices, representing higher-dimensional components. It finds that the transition between different behavior types occurs at specific critical points, determined by the fundamental coupling parameter. The study also explores how changing the constraints on the matrix components affects the theory's phase transition. The findings demonstrate that the dynamical Higgs phase can persist even under broader constraints, without relying on a underlying symmetry.

This study addresses the question of whether certain Navier-Stokes equations are well-suited for certain classes of functions that include smooth and critical Sobolev spaces. Specifically, it investigates the well-being of solutions to these equations under specific conditions. For 3-dimensional spaces and a certain range of values, the well-being is well understood. However, for higher dimensional spaces and a different range of values, the well-being is still an open question. It is known that if these equations do not do well, then certain predicted patterns will emerge. This research provides new results by showing that under specific conditions, these equations will not do well. These conditions are broader than what was previously known and are more likely to occur. They also provide insights into the behavior of specific functions that are critical in understanding the patterns mentioned above.

We investigate the polarization characteristics of magnon modes within collinear antiferromagnetic insulators that undergo a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya magnetic field variation. Considering the weak magnon scattering with electrons, we demonstrate that nonlinear magnon interactions have a significant impact on polarizing modes in an insulating antiferromagnet system. Notably, magnon polarization can be achieved through both the magnon gap and continuum without charge currents, utilizing either a local or non-local magnetic field. We design an antiferromagnetic thin film with a NNN exchange coupling much stronger than the other exchange interactions to separate the magnon gap from the other modes, making it feasible to polarize the magnon modes in the magnon gap with a magnetic field.

This research introduces two modifications for enhancing the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem, specifically incorporating quadratic forms and rank metric decoding to address potential parity bit attacks. We examine the parameters of the modified systems and carry out simulations to evaluate their resistance to state-of-the-art attacks.

Pre-trained language models have significantly advanced the pre-existing methods by effectively capturing the underlying patterns within written language, enabling tasks such as part-of-speech tagging, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. This research aims to revolutionize the pre-trained language models by incorporating the structural characteristics of hand-written text through the incorporation of graph convolutional networks. The proposed Handwritten Language Understanding Dataset enables the analysis of graph-based features like script, language, and part-of-speech tagging without needing explicit annotations. The experimental outcomes demonstrate the success of the proposed method in identifying handwritten text features like script, language, and part-of-speech tagging, often without explicit annotations, and on a par with state-of-the-art handwritten text classification models. Furthermore, the dataset provides opportunities for tasks such as handwritten script and language identification, as well as more intricate applications like handwritten text classification. The dataset and source code can be accessed at https://github.com/islake/haru-dataset and https://github.com/islake/haru-py.

The minimum weight spanning tree in graphs and its higher-dimensional equivalent, the minimum spanning acycle in simplicial complexes, were previously linked to a particular value by a zeta function. A recent study of these structures focused on the limits of a probability distribution based on this value. A related paper is now presenting a continuation of the research under the assumption that only partial information about the weights is available. The results show that the probability distribution still converges to a specific form in this case. The findings have been applied to a particular instance in dimensions three, leading to new limit theorems being established.

This paper presents a comprehensive overview of federated learning research, emphasizing the distinct variants of this approach - horizontal and vertical federated learning - and highlighting the key challenges associated with each. In the context of horizontal learning, participants contribute the same data type, whereas vertical learning involves participants contributing different data attributes of participants. Given the privacy concerns surrounding participant data, especially in the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, vertical learning is seen as a more suitable option for certain applications. The paper delves into the related literature, discussing the applications and challenges of vertical learning in tandem with the techniques for integrating multiple datasets. The paper also explores the primary issues of combining vertical learning participants at the server, including data alignment, communication, and computation costs. The paper concludes by identifying promising avenues for future research and presenting a framework for combining vertical learning participants.

A theoretical framework called B-Mesogenesis, which involves hypothetical dark matter components, predicts the occurrence of rare processes such as $B$-meson decays into a dark photon and a baryon, as well as the dark photon's subsequent decay into a lepton and a neutrino. In this study, we analyze the first time a dark photon is produced, focusing on decay modes featuring $B^+$, $B^0$, or $B_s^0$ mesons. Utilizing the GLW and ADS/MSSM models, we compute the relative frequencies of these decays and establish the current and future detection capabilities for the LHCb, Belle II, and Super-B 5 experiments.

In a Smart City environment with numerous entities interacting, our concern is the security implications of terrorist attacks on urban entities. This issue can be effectively managed by developing an adaptive multi-agent system that utilizes real-time entity data, including entity locations and operational statuses. By sharing this information among entities, an efficient protection mechanism can be implemented to prevent terrorist attacks or minimize their impact. Specifically, our proposed system allows entities to choose their communication partners securely. An entity can decide to share its information only when it is sure the potential partner has already been verified as safe. This approach can be achieved through the application of both a global authority and autonomous entities working together.

This study examines the behavior of Schwarzschild and charged black holes within a gravitational field with a time component distorted by $\sqrt{\frac{\Gamma}{3\pi}}$, where $\Gamma$ represents a positive constant. The investigation focuses on how the black hole's phase transition temperature and volume change in response to the distorted time component, and on determining the phase transition lines for both Schwarzschild and charged black holes. The results show a relationship between the distorted time component and these parameters. Additionally, the study explores connections between Hawking radiation, the distorted metric, and cosmic censorship, and discusses potential implications of a distorted metric on the late-time power law correction to Hubble's law.

Recent breakthroughs in reading comprehension were driven by large-scale models capable of understanding language. Pre-trained on extensive text datasets, these models excel in tasks like language modeling and sentence encoding. Their potential in task-specific training on reading comprehension datasets has been demonstrated, yet these datasets typically consist of short paragraphs. In contrast, real-world reading comprehension often involves retrieving and understanding longer documents. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces DocRet, a reading comprehension dataset centered around retrieving and processing longer documents to answer questions. DocRet comprises question-document pairs sourced from real-world scenarios, requiring the retrieval of longer documents. DocRet features diverse question types, document lengths, and domains, making it challenging for models to accurately retrieve and comprehend documents. DocRet supports multiple retrieval settings, including full-text retrieval and answer-span-based retrieval, as well as question-document and document-document retrieval. DocRet surpasses existing reading comprehension datasets in length, diversity, and practicality, providing a robust platform for the development of models capable of retrieving and understanding longer documents.

Despite the impressive performance of Graph Neural Networks on various real-world tasks, they require large-scale labeled graphs, which can be costly and resource-intensive to obtain, posing a significant challenge to their implementation. To address this issue, we have developed a pioneering pseudo-labeling framework that efficiently utilizes the information from partially labeled and unlabeled graphs to adaptively label each node, given the labels of a smaller source graph. This innovative approach is built upon two key components: a labeling classifier, optimized using both the labeled source and observed unlabeled graph, and a labeling propagator that transfers labeled information from established nodes to unlabeled ones. Our approach is then enhanced through label ranking and regularization, which ensures robust pseudo-labeling by discarding unreliable labels and enforcing consistency among neighboring nodes. Through comprehensive experiments on four benchmark datasets, we have demonstrated that our method consistently achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, especially in scenarios involving scarce labels.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a focused plasma column can serve as an efficient, non-destructive diagnostic tool for monitoring the dynamics of plasma wakefields and accelerating electrons. The radiation emitted by witness electrons in a focused beam can reveal important information about their initial conditions, including the plasma's phase at the time of emission. To enhance diagnostic capabilities and streamline data analysis, we present a new analytical approach and computational tool for extracting key parameters from radiation spectra. Our method is demonstrated using simulated data, generated based on realistic experimental conditions in an experiment conducted at the Accelerator Test Facility (ATF).

This paper addresses the challenge of the first fully-verifiable distributed learning application, allowing an algorithm to train an anonymous, verifiable tree-learning model in a completely public setting. However, when this model is used to train decision trees, it can compromise users' privacy due to the sensitive data involved. Therefore, the paper proposes an improved version of the model that incorporates differential privacy to protect users' privacy. Specifically, it introduces two new privacy-preserving algorithms for learning differentially private decision trees in a distributed setting. These algorithms utilize a novel concept called 'domain separation' to ensure the safety of these algorithms against malicious attacks. Furthermore, the paper conducts an extensive analysis, numerical experiments, and theoretical evaluations of the proposed algorithms to demonstrate their effectiveness and efficiency.

We establish a geometric relationship between various divergences, including those of Bregman and Kullback-Leibler, and develop an equivalent optimization problem with a single variable. This leads to an efficient Kullback-Leibler divergence calculation, based on the Riemannian gradient and Hessian, and resulting Riemannian Newton's algorithms. Our approach also enables the derivation of monotone optimization algorithms by generalizing the Fenchel-Moreau conjugate function.

This generalises the discrete Bayesian network class to the chain event graph class, retaining the Bayesian network's benefits for interrogation, propagation, and learning, but allowing for more organic modelling of unordered events and their sequential nature. This paper illustrates how product Dirichlet priors facilitate full model sampling with closed-form conjugate analysis, proving they characterise suitable homogeneity assumptions within this expanded model class. It showcases this capability with two educational illustrations.

In this study, a rapid and highly efficient finite-difference method is proposed for solving complex, globally convex optimization problems, even in high dimensions. The proposed algorithm is uniquely capable of handling inexact line searches, allowing it to converge at the optimal rate for a broad class of such problems. By incorporating an exact second-order derivative computation, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance in comparison to current state-of-the-art algorithms, as evidenced by our analytical convergence results and the results of various numerical experiments.

We study a basic model of two-headed cells navigating in a straight line, each time choosing between advancing, slowing down, turning left, and turning right. When close to walls, these cells exhibit oscillatory patterns reminiscent of circular motion, similar to a trajectory commonly observed in real-world bacteria called a "run-and-tumble" cycle. By introducing a simplified wall-following mechanism, we find that these cells can also consistently follow straight lines in the absence of obstacles, in contrast to a different model of bacteria that struggles to do so. As an extension, we examine the collective behavior of numerous two-headed cells implementing this wall-following strategy, resulting in coherent directional movement even in the presence of obstacles.

Within the framework of a theory proposing space-dependent densities of charge carriers,
we investigate the relationship between superconducting properties and the quasiconducting state in cuprate superconductors using an analogy with dipolar ferroelectrics.
This approach enables us to derive expressions for carrier interaction times and polarisation levels in cuprate compounds.
Results indicate that microwave conductivity varies inversely with temperature within the superconducting state,
and that energy gaps in the superconductor and ferroelectric states share a proportional relationship with the same control parameter.

This passage discusses an anisotropic curvature flow, referred to as a crystalline curvature flow, with specific examples where minimal and miminal crystalline extrinsic curvatures act as flow vectors. These include a planar curve with a unique flow and a Drosophila ocellar eye model, where the flow vectors are directed perpendicularly to both tangent vectors and a given curve. The flow vectors can also be directed towards nearest points on a surface, as seen in another example, where the points are chosen based on a specific distance threshold. The passage examines the level set formulation for these flows and proves that they are well-defined and time-consistent, with associated flow maps and normal vectors. Additionally, it demonstrates the existence of a weak solution for each time interval, with a specified convergence rate, and discusses an extension of these results to open sets.

Our survival relies heavily on plants, and they have remarkable adaptability, adjusting their rate of growth in response to changes in light and chemical signals. The complex interactions between these factors, such as light intensity and the presence of oxygen, can limit plant growth, leading to an intricate system of feedbacks. The development of new mathematical models based on this knowledge has allowed researchers to simulate how these factors interact and affect plant behavior, providing new insights into why certain environmental conditions, such as oxygen deficiency, can impede plant growth. The application of this understanding could lead to new methods for improving crop yields in challenging environmental contexts.

It has been established that the SLE loop measure arises as a natural consequence of combining two Liouville quantum gravity disks through conformal welding when the variable $\gamma^2$ equals $\kappa$ in the interval (0,4). To reach this conclusion, we built upon prior work involving conformal welding of LQG disks, utilizing the essential span tree technique. The resulting SLE loop measure shares key properties with the critical Gaussian integral foreign function. Furthermore, we explored how our findings relate to the concept of generalized conformal rigidity in the context of LQG.

The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative is a global partnership that strives for consistency in extracting biomarkers from imaging data to enable efficient quantitative analysis. One significant hurdle in this field is the lack of universally accepted guidelines and standards for translating imaging data into high-throughput biomarkers, contributing to issues with study reproducibility and interoperability. To address this problem, IBSI is working to develop and implement standardized guidelines for imaging biomarker development, including annotation, computational processing, and testing methods, and is promoting their widespread adoption across the industry.

We have analyzed the effects of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances on kaon photoproduction. Two isospin extension covariant models, describing both the production of kaon and lambda, were employed in our study. Our results indicate that these resonances significantly impact the resonant structure of kaon photoproduction. Notably, including the $N^{\ast}(1895)$ nucleon resonance and $D_{13}(1895)$ delta resonance helps align calculated differential cross sections and polarization observables with experimental data. Our findings also highlight the role of resonance contributions in distinct kinematic regions.

This research presents an advanced image processing protocol, developed to prepare images for the extraction of quantitative and qualitative data in biological studies. Comprising both automated and manual stages, the workflow is tailored for multi-color fluorescence microscopy, focal shift confocal microscopy, and super-resolution structured illumination microscopy imaging modes. Focused on labeling cell surface components with a specific protein in human cancer cells grown in two-dimensional culture dishes, the protocol is designed to identify and count individual cells as a byproduct of data extraction. Additionally, the paper includes a detailed description of the computational tools necessary for each step, encompassing open-source software for image processing and analysis, as well as guidance on data management, to facilitate the reproduction of our findings for the broader scientific community.

Building upon our previous research \cite{Liu:2019xhn}, we investigate how primordial black holes, which are now being considered as potential candidates for dark matter, may be simultaneously prevented from existing in our current universe while still having the potential to create gravitational waves in the early universe. We demonstrate that by applying the general principles of black hole formation across the entire spectrum of spacetime possibilities, the likelihood of these black holes not having formed can be restricted, thereby increasing the chances of those that do form decaying into radiation or collapsing into stable states. The restrictions we've introduced pertain to the mass of the black hole, $M$, and the duration of the early universe, characterized by the number of e-folds, $N$. Specifically, for black holes with masses of $10^{-16}\,{\rm g} < M < 10^{-14}\,{\rm g}$, formed when the universe was $N=1$ e-ford old, the likelihood of these black holes not having formed can be restricted to $Q_0(M) < 0.65$, with similar restrictions applying to the $Q_1(M)$ and $Q_2(M)$ cases. The restrictions we've introduced are particularly relevant for the range of black hole masses that are most strongly linked to the issue of dark matter, namely $10^{-14}\,{\rm g} < M < 10^{-12}\,{\rm g}$. The restrictions we've

University administrators and educational researchers are interested in understanding university course enrollment patterns. A model called the rank-choice process provides a grounded explanation for how students select courses based on preferences and availability. In this study, we develop an approach to infer the personal course preferences of students and the characteristics of university courses based on publicly available course enrollment data. A rank-choice model is employed to describe both individual and group course choices. To estimate individual and group parameters, we apply Bayesian inference. A criterion is established to determine optimal course parameter estimates. Simulation experiments confirm that our approach produces accurate estimates. We apply the method to analyze enrollment patterns at a large Chinese university from 2016 to 2017, revealing the underlying preferences of students and the characteristics of courses.

Within this investigation, the challenge of vehicle platooning with connected and automated vehicles is addressed using a control method for nonlinear systems via two network structures - the leader-following relative system and the leader-following leader-alongside system. An optimal control approach is employed for each of these configurations, where the control objective is to minimize the overall system distance between the leader and follower vehicles. This is achieved via two decentralized communication networks: the relative distance network and the alongside network. Using geometric control methods, the stability of the closed-loop system is demonstrated for both the relative system and the leader-alongside system, where the latter is considered an illustrative example of an underlying system. However, this concept can be broadly applied to various underlying system configurations.

One of the most widely used optimization method in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). When applying SGD to large models and distributed training setups, a significant amount of time is spent on data movement rather than computation or data preparation. Researchers have previously identified this issue and proposed an approach to reduce data movement by increasing the data batch size, however, this comes at the expense of increased per-iteration time and higher memory requirements due to the need to store larger gradients. A better solution to reduce data movement is a recent algorithm called Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD). This new approach achieves faster execution times than traditional SGD by optimizing the data exchange process. CA-SGD was initially evaluated on large models and has shown promising results, achieving up to a 2.5 times speedup over SGD. In this work, the effectiveness of CA-SGD is further tested on smaller models and various machine learning libraries, including TensorFlow, PyTorch and MXNet. Our results show that CA-SGD can significantly speed up training times on small models as well as large ones, and we provide practical tips for reducing data movement in machine learning training processes.

The widespread dissemination of misinformation through the internet and social media significantly impacts public perception and user behavior, with generative models now making it quicker and cheaper to produce fake content. To safeguard against misinformation, users must be able to rely on fact-checking. Our research focuses on whether fact-checking systems can accurately reject content that is obviously generated by machines, such as by analyzing computer-generated headlines. We evaluated six publicly accessible fact-checking systems using 1,000 manually created headlines that were generated using the GPT-2 model. Our results show that the majority of systems fail to detect machine-generated headlines in headlines, with only one system successfully identifying them in excess of chance. Our findings highlight the need for further improvements in detection capabilities, particularly since nearly all system scores significantly outperformed human scores in the same task.

In polycrystalline, amorphous, and ion-damaged Kitaev materials, a spontaneous
breakdown of inversion symmetry gives rise to a chiral structure. Utilizing
M\"{o}ssbauer spectroscopy and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) on a
single crystal and a high-quality thin film of $\alpha$-MnO$_2$, it was found
that the chiral structure spontaneously forms even at room temperature. The results
also demonstrate that inversion symmetry breaking leads to a time-reversal
symmetry breaking in a chiral spin liquid, with implications for the topological
properties of Kitaev materials.

Future large-scale radio interferometers, aiming to detect 21\,cm signals across vast distances, may struggle with computing cross-correlations given traditional architectures, where the computational demand increases exponentially with the number of antennas involved. Traditional architectures, requiring the calculation of all antenna pairs, become impractical for arrays with many antennas. The introduction of the FFT-correlator architecture reduces the computational complexity, but its results are valid only when input data from individual antennas have been calibrated to account for instrumental effects. Since calibrations are continually updated with changing instrumental characteristics, real-time re-calibration becomes necessary, leading to the need for frequent cross-correlations during the calibration process. We investigated the feasibility of using FFT-correlators by performing simultaneous 21\,cm and GMRT cross-correlations, demonstrating that the FFT-correlators can take advantage of the redundancy in large-scale arrays by efficiently computing cross-correlations of analogous time-series data from different antennas. Our analysis revealed that the distribution of spectral power across various frequencies allows for the identification of relevant antenna pairs, reducing the need for extensive computational resources.

For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been the go-to method for in-depth financial analysis, but it focuses solely on portfolio optimization, neglecting the vital task of time series analysis. Recent advancements in generative adversarial networks (GANs) have shown promise in generating pseudo data to aid machine learning model training, but the need for more realistic data generation has driven the development of novel generative models. This paper presents a novel generative model, called the Integrated Time Series Generator (ITSG), capable of accurately modeling the statistical properties of financial time series, thereby filling the gap between Markowitz's portfolio optimization and time series analysis techniques. By leveraging the strengths of variational autoencoders and score-based generative models, ITSG preserves the benefits of pseudo data generation while rectifying the limitations of previous generative models, such as conditional GANs, which were shown to compromise model performance. Comprehensive simulation results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed model over existing approaches, making it a valuable tool for time series analysis and potentially enhancing portfolio optimization.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$
analytically to three-loop order in QCD for arbitrary integer $N$,
utilizing an indefinite hypergeometric representation, and
furthermore, we have calculated the skewness dependence through
expansions in $\alpha_s$ and $x$, and matched it with the results obtained
by Schenke, Velkovska and Yuan at finite $x$ and $N$, and with the results
obtained by Borowka et al. in the limit $N \to \infty$, and
our results are available in a publicly accessible form.

Our research focuses on developing a classification tool for the largest sample of gamma-ray sources detected by the Fermi Large Area Telescope. A comprehensive dataset of several thousand radio-loud galaxies, which includes prominent categories of narrow-line Seyfert galaxies, blazars, and radio galaxies, serves as the input for our analysis. Based on the established identities of sources, we create training sets for machine learning algorithms to train the classifier. Using a year-long period of Fermi-LAT data, our tool identifies the source types as active galactic nuclei (AGN), including blazars and radio galaxies, with precise accuracy rates. A separate study is conducted on the AGES catalog to classify 700 sources, achieving a success rate of 90% for separating blazars and radio galaxies, and 85% for separating narrow-line Seyfert galaxies and blazars. A list of 188 blazars and 77 misidentified sources is generated, with the majority being previously unknown Fermi-LAT blazars. These newly identified sources are expected to contribute to future studies. Additionally, our tool's effectiveness in identifying the highly variable blazars that dominate the high-energy Skymap is evident, as it performs better on these sources compared to others.

Active participation and user engagement are key components of social networking, 
fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms. 
Traditionally, user-generated content was text-based, but with the rise of 
multi-media formats like images and videos, the definition has expanded. 
One area that is particularly interesting is micro-blogging, which is gaining 
popularity all over the world. This paper examines the characteristics of 
tweets, focusing on the language and user-related aspects, and investigates 
the patterns of user engagement through retweets and follow-backs. Using a large 
dataset from truefie08, we apply statistical methods to analyze the text and 
user-related data, and uncover some interesting trends in user behavior.

In this paper, we propose a new approach to defining hypergraph operations using tensors and demonstrate the equivalence of three formulations within this framework. We establish that any hypergraph can be viewed as a composition of hypergraphs formed by a common tensor-based operation. This operation allows us to identify and create novel hypergraph classes, enabling us to calculate various properties and spectra for hypergraphs constructed in this way. We also obtain results on the spectra of hypergraphs by applying our tensor-based method, and demonstrate its utility in constructing cospectral hypergraph pairs.

India achieved a groundbreaking success with the deployment and functioning of its initial space observatory, AstroSat, which marked a new era in space-based astronomical research in the country. Building upon this achievement, a cutting-edge next-generation space telescope called the Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST) is being developed to offer extended wavelength capabilities and enhanced observational capabilities. INSIST, which is a key component of ISRO's future large missions, is being designed to offer various cutting-edge features. These include the ability to conduct simultaneous uv and far uv spectroscopy, offer 10 times greater observing capacity than AstroSat, and stay in space for at least 10 years. INSRO is planning the launch of INSIST in 2023, which will be a collaborative effort with the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) as part of the eROSES program.

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data over time, the mixed model repeated measures approach often dominates. However, treating time as a categorical variable can introduce issues such as time warping, resulting in an inadequate fit. A novel method employing penalized splines with a Bayesian estimation process is proposed, allowing a smoother, continuous representation of time. Although initially presented in a purely Bayesian framework, the method is adapted to a semi Bayesian approach, similar to Julia's Difficult() function, to facilitate efficient maximum likelihood estimation. The developed approach is tested on data from two trials, showing improved fit and effectiveness when comparing treatment groups.

A novel computational strategy called ActionMol, grounded in the principles of transition path theory, has been developed to identify reaction pathways connecting target species via an intermediate transition state. By optimizing the Onsager-Machlup action along a path constrained to visit specific configurations and trajectory segments, ActionMol determines the most likely reaction pathway from an ensemble of simulated transition trajectories. Through extensive testing using challenging systems from organic chemistry and biology, ActionMol effectively extracts the optimal reaction pathway from an ensemble of transition paths, outperforming existing methods.

This paper focuses on a parabolic variant of complex Monge-Ampere equations and utilizes a PDE-based method akin to Phong et al to derive and establish L-infinity and Holder estimates. Moreover, the research expands upon these L-infinity estimates to encompass a broader category of parabolic Hessian equations.

Building on the established classes of polyregular functions and W-regular functions, we introduce a novel class of functions called (W, Star) -regular functions, defined as a composition of W-regular functions and star operations on this subset. We investigate the computational complexity properties of this new class by demonstrating its position relative to the complexity hierarchy, including a proof that it falls between E and NE, and another proof that it is within FL[rc], a level also containing polyregular functions and surpassing L. We further show that the addition of star operations to polyregular and W-regular functions creates distinct new complexity classes.

Conditional measure flow integrals, introduced in a prior paper, exhibit both expected and surprising properties. Like classical Ito integrals, they possess the 'hidden property'. However, they also exhibit an unusual property, evidenced by the equation $\mathrm{d}B^H$ equaling both $\mathrm{d}B^H$ and $\mathrm{d}B^{H+1}_{x|y}$ when conditional on $B^y$.

This research aims to investigate various types of normal subgroups using a specific topology derived from hull-kernel-type topological spaces. We have made significant advancements in this area, as our study demonstrates the applicability of the new topology to multiple subspaces, including convolution-type spaces, maximal ideal spaces of certain operator algebras, quasi-bounded function spaces, and other similar topological spaces. We have further established the relationship between the new topology and the associated topologies, as well as examined the properties of certain normal subgroups in a topological vector space. Our findings also show that every normal subgroup in a certain topological space contains a primitive subgroup, which is a subgroup that cannot be expressed as the union of two smaller subgroups. Additionally, the study highlights the differences between two types of normal subgroups in a topological vector space, with one type being strictly smaller than the other.

The Core77 dataset, released in 2019, is a key reference for text-to-SQL parsing for web applications. However, it differs from the primary target of semi-structured database retrieval (SSDBR) tasks, requiring additional components, including code generation and code search. To bridge this gap, we developed a comprehensive benchmark, WireCity-DB, to integrate the Core77 dataset with actual database schema. Furthermore, we established a new evaluation metric to measure code accuracy and developed new evaluation metrics to assess code search efficiency and effectiveness. Using this benchmark, we compared existing state-of-the-art models and found that they fall short in code search performance. To address this limitation, we proposed the WireCity-Search model, which not only produces accurate SQL queries but also efficiently retrieves relevant codes. Our model's performance was evaluated on the WireCity-DB benchmark and demonstrated superior performance compared to existing models.

In complex multi-robot systems, accurately navigating while avoiding potential collisions between robots is a significant challenge, largely due to the unpredictable movements of fellow robots. To tackle this, our study proposes a data-driven navigation method for collaborative robot systems, which leverages the concept of distributionally robust conditional value-at-risk to model and limit the likelihood of unexpected events, such as collisions. By developing an algorithm that iteratively refines the probabilities of these events, we ensure that the robots' planned path remains robust against various uncertain scenarios. Furthermore, our approach adapts to changes in the environment by leveraging the capabilities of probabilistic programming. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in reducing the frequency of unexpected events and reveal its potential to significantly accelerate convergence in large-scale collaborative robot systems, especially in scenarios with a high degree of uncertainty.

Recent data from the NOIRpops survey has significantly improved our understanding of Andromeda XXV by providing more precise velocity and metallicity information for its member stars. These updates support the claim that Andromeda XXV is a dwarf galaxy associated with the M31 halo, although further study is needed to determine the exact number of its member stars. The estimated metal composition of Andromeda XXV, denoted as [Fe/H], is significantly more negative than other dwarf galaxies linked to M31, with values comparable to the globular cluster M32. Notably, Andromeda XXV's velocity profile reveals a notable discrepancy between its radial velocity at its center and the combined movement of its stars, indicating a possible misalignment between the galaxy's spin and the surrounding space. The estimated total mass of Andromeda XXV's central region is around 2.64 million times the mass of our sun, with a radius of half this mass extending approximately 34 parsecs. The observed mass-to-light ratio of Andromeda XXV is relatively high among similar dwarf galaxies, possibly indicating a dense central core. The Andromeda XXV galaxy's properties suggest it may be a previously hidden satellite of M31.

In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-latency connections is made possible by non-orthogonal grant-free access with low signaling overhead. This research proposes a novel two-stage approach using a genetic algorithm (GA) to generate user-specific sequences for mMTC downlink transmissions. Initially, GA performs a multi-objective optimization of block-age and phase-tracking accuracy, and then an L1-Minimization algorithm refines these sequences via angle-of-arrival estimation. This two-stage method was found to outperform traditional sequences derived from existing protocols such as LTE, GMAC, and BLER, and even an optimized two-stage GA method, as recently proposed, under various random seed inputs.

A novel, simplified approach has been developed to model the thermodynamic behavior of moist air. This method utilizes thermodynamic potentials, specifically the chemical potential of water vapor, to establish a framework for understanding and analyzing thermodynamic processes. By considering the properties of closed water bodies, an empirical relationship was formulated to replicate the behavior of real systems, such as those encountered in clouds. This new approach is capable of being implemented in large-scale numerical models, providing a reliable and efficient method for studying the thermodynamic behavior of moist air.

Algebras defined over the field F1, also known as "neutral elements," are explored in depth, specifically those defined as algebraic series expansions and infinitesimal algebraic series expansions, also relating to algebraic infinitesimal expansions. The concept of limit in these algebras is discussed, focusing on the role of element epsilon, also denoted as eps. The paper also discusses the relationship between these algebras and Rota-Baxter algebras, specifically illustrating examples of Rota-Baxter algebras within the context of algebraic series expansions.

Research on spoken dialogue systems has traditionally relied on a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses for interpreting meaning and monitoring the dialogue flow.  Recent studies, however, have shown the potential benefits of using confusion networks as an alternative.  Confusion networks, which retain time-normalized arcs and probabilities from N-best lists, have been proposed as a representation of ASR uncertainty.  This paper challenges the assumption that confusion networks provide more uncertainty information than the top-N list itself, and offers an alternative: a set of expanded N-best lists.  This paper presents theoretical evidence that the top-N list and expanded N-best lists contain equivalent amounts of uncertainty information, and suggests that either representation could be used.  Furthermore, the study shows that the optimal size of the top-N list can be determined rather than a fixed N, and that the size of the top-N list and the quality of the ASR system affect the similarity in information content between the top-N list and an expanded N-best list.

We calculate Joyce's enumerative invariants for semistable coherent sheaves of specific ranks and degrees on complex projective curves, which are mathematically isomorphic to moduli spaces of sheaves. This is then applied to two particular instances: when the sheaves are holomorphic with torsion, and when they are part of an extended Fujiki decomposition of a K3 surface, with a K3 surface being equivalent to a 2-dimensional projective space minus 9 points. This outcome results in an alternative proof for a particular case of a theorem by Borrelli, with the added feature that enumerative invariants can be expressed using a polynomial that characterizes the Hilbert scheme of points on a K3 surface, which is known to be irreducible.

A critical factor in secret sharing schemes is the count of minimal qualified subsets, as knowing this value results in the richest possible access structure. Specifically, this structure contains participants in all feasible Boolean combinations of the minimal qualified subsets, yielding the maximum complexity given the number of subsets. Every access structure can be considered a subset of this universal structure when having the same number of minimal qualified subsets, thereby the universal access structure possesses the highest complexity given the subset count. It is demonstrated that the complexity of the universal access structure, consisting of $n$, with $n\geq 2$, is at least $n$ and at most $2^n-2$.

To determine entanglement in polarization qubit experiments, we employ an adjusted form of the quantum state discrimination optimality criterion proposed by Buisson et al., which we refer to as the EB criterion. We apply this criterion to optimize measurements made by the PJN device, a quantum photon tripleter used in experiments measuring entanglement. By using the EB criterion, we find optimal settings for measurements made by PJN device and compare them to previous experiments. We demonstrate that optimal settings can lead to precision that is not achievable through other methods, such as the Q metric or QBT, which were previously used. Notably, measurements based on the EB criterion achieve precision comparable to that of optimal measurements allowed by quantum mechanics, while experiments using the PJN device previously yielded lower results using the Q metric or QBT. We attribute this difference to the EB criterion's ability to adjust the prior probabilities of input states, which is not the case for the Q metric or QBT.

The long-lived solitary vortices in plasma turbulence, known as magnetic island instabilities, continue to be a focus of study in plasma turbulence. These structures, formed through the mesoscale evolution of microinstabilities, develop along with macroscopic gradients and drive currents that impact the overall plasma dynamics. These solitary vortices exhibit complex behavior, including the formation of smaller vortices within their structure, and their evolution is influenced by their size and surrounding turbulence level. These conditions result in various growth rates and timescales, and a detailed understanding of their formation requires a multi-scale approach. These formation processes are typically characterized by the formation of coherent structures, and in the case of magnetic island instivities, these coherent structures are known as Hads. These structures are formed through the evolution of currents along magnetic field lines, and their development results in the formation of small vortices that grow over time.
