In the original Lights Out game, a grid of lights can be operated by pressing adjacent cells. This results in a specific mathematical pattern based on the cell's location and whether it's the cell that was pressed or its neighboring cells. The corresponding graph for the game is called the Lights Out graph, with vertices representing the grid cells and edges connecting them based on the operations described above. The problem of finding a sequence of cell presses that turns off all lights becomes the vertex coloring problem on the Lights Out graph, where each cell is colored white then black, and repeating until it reaches a repeating color sequence. The main result of this research states that any Lights Out graph with a non-empty vertex set and a symmetry of at least one-order has a vertex coloring that results in all lights being turned off. Additionally, this research finds a pattern to identify which Lights Out graphs meet the criteria required to guarantee a strategic win.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation and restoration model that addresses the limitations of previous research in these areas. Specifically, the proposed method effectively handles noises and missing data that often complicate image processing tasks. By integrating several built-in constraints into a multi-layered framework, the model ensures a robust and efficient segmentation and restoration process. Theoretical analysis confirms that the solution to this model lies within a restricted space, thereby guarantee,ting its existence and uniqueness. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of the model is ensured through the utilization of Gauss-Seidel-type iteration. The efficacy of the model is demonstrated by its successful application to various image segmentation and restoration tasks in both simulated and real-world scenarios.

In abstract interpretation, the abstract fixpoint computation involves two key phases: upward iteration and downward iteration in the lattice of abstract states. Upward iteration represents the forward flow of the program, while downward iteration represents the backward recovery from errors. This paper introduces the application of well-ordered domains to speed up abstract fixpoint computation. It outlines a standard framework for both the forward and backward phases and provides a detailed explanation of how to choose an appropriate domain to achieve the fixpoint in two stages. The paper also showcases the application of this framework to the implementation of abstract interpreators for error recovery analysis and forward abstract path analysis in a compiler.

A new class of materials with topological phonons has been identified, which includes MoSi2, WS2, WSe2, and their hydrogenated forms. These materials feature topological phonons in both their bulk and surface states, as demonstrated by our calculations. In the presence of atomic displacement, a clear gap opens in the phonon spectrum of these materials, both in bulk and at the edge of a two-dimensional system. Notably, our calculations show that the interface between two-dimensional materials with topological phonons exhibits unique phonon properties, which can be utilized in designing advanced phononic devices.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning has gained significant attention. A key challenge is the existence of multiple definitions of outliers, which necessitates the use of more straightforward approaches to identify anomalies without presupposing data structures or parameters. The distance-based outlier definition offers a solution by considering any data object as anomalous if it stands alone within a given radius. Several methods have been proposed to identify distance-based outliers, which can be categorized into approximation and optimization techniques. While approximation methods provide guarantees on accuracy, they rely on predetermined parameters, whereas optimization methods are more robust but computationally demanding. A particular optimization technique known as the linear programming relaxation (LPR) is considered robust but prone to performance issues due to high computational complexity. A novel method, known as LPR$^*$, has been proposed to overcome these limitations by employing an iterative approach and taking advantage of sparse distance matrices to improve efficiency. Theoretical bounds on the number of iterations and computational complexity have been derived, and experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness and efficiency of the new method compared to the original LPR and other available techniques.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied to the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest experiencing a passing electromagnetic field. The results show the influence of atom movement and external fields on $|{\rm K}_{\rm N}|^2$ depends on Neumann conditions, whereas for Dirichlet conditions, the influence is on $|{\rm K}_{\rm D}$^2$. It's observed that the initially calculated scalar results hold in both scenarios, indicating consistency.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the need for fair and consistent outcomes becomes critical. Graph neural networks, known to embed relational data, often face fairness issues due to their inherent properties. Although research on fairness has accelerated, the study of equivalence between graph neural networks and metric structures is still underdeveloped, neglecting the essential link between fairness and the fairness principle established in richer mathematical contexts. We establish a crucial connection between the fairness of node predictions in graph neural networks and the fairness of nearest neighbor searches within metric trees, which paves the way for a deeper understanding of implicit assumptions within learned models. This groundbreaking approach enables us to formalize and measure neighborhood fairness, which paves the way for quantitative fairness assessments and interventions during training to achieve consistency. Our novel framework is versatile and can be applied not only to node classification but also to a broader range of problems, including those defined on more complex entities such as edges and node attributes.

This research focuses on kinetic models describing reversible enzyme reactions that release three substances: a product $X$, a byproduct $Y$, and an intermediate $Z$.  The models comprise nonlinear differential equations with a variable coefficient representing the enzyme's availability.  Due to the equations' complexity and nonlinearity, exact analytical solutions are unattainable, prompting the development of approximation methods.  This work employs the Homotopy Perturbation Method (HPM) and Homotopy Analysis Method (HAM) to derive approximate analytical solutions of the equations under two non-linear law models.  The resulting solutions show a high degree of accuracy when compared with exact solutions obtained via numerical simulations in MATLAB.  The study also verifies the applicability and effectiveness of the HPM and HAM techniques in solving non-linear reaction equations.

This discussion focuses on squark-related searches within the all-hadronic $Z\&\tilde{g}$ production model from the LHC, where squark virtual states enable the $\sim$2 TeV gluino to decay into final states consisting of 2 or 4 quarks, with no additional top quarks. Given its limited branching ratio of around 8%, the squark search is particularly challenging. Our results demonstrate that squark masses can be estimated by examining jet substructure characteristics. Furthermore, gluino masses up to 2.5 TeV can be probed in the $Z\&\tilde{g}$ final state, with the gluino decaying into 4-quark states through virtual squarks.

Our research delves into a heterogeneous population of arbitrageurs trading in a simple asset to explore the emergence, persistence, and eventual collapse of financial bubbles. In this model, the population is divided into two groups, one of which acts as a herd, instantly pricing the asset based on a random variable, while the other group, the innovators, strategically set their asset price based on discounted future fundamentals. We demonstrate that the market can become bubble-trapped, remaining above the fair price despite the presence of arbitrage, provided that innovator fundamentals fall within a specific range and certain herder pricing criteria are met. We also find that the size of the bubble is influenced by the distribution of prices, the trading rates of both groups, and the arbitrageurs' expectations of persisting in a bubble state. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the population can coexist with a bubble, preventing a sudden collapse as a result of a mixed population where innovators and herders interact through transaction and learning processes.

Quantum harmonic oscillators behave unpredictably when subjected to external influences, making them valuable for exploring open quantum system behavior. Their inhomogeneities give rise to complex auto-correlation functions, particularly noticeable in contexts involving constant driving forces. Correlation functions of driven oscillators have been extensively studied using lattice Monte Carlo simulations. In contrast, oscillators subjected to random forces are typically analyzed using white noise models, often without employing Monte Carlo methods. This research combines these approaches by examining the auto-correlation functions of driven quantum harmonic oscillators utilizing a lattice Monte Carlo scheme. Although initially presenting challenges due to oscillatory behavior, an innovative modification to the lattice Monte Carlo method overcomes these difficulties. This modified approach is then validated by comparing its results with both theoretical predictions and simulations based on random noise models.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the task remains challenging due to review sentiment shifting over time. Current review-based methods are ineffective in rating prediction as they often rely on outdated reviews. To overcome this issue, we introduce a novel approach that integrates sentiment analysis to better understand review context and improve rating prediction. Specifically, our method, ReviewRater, analyzes review sentiment over time, creating a more accurate and nuanced representation of user-item preferences. The model is trained using a novel generative neural network designed to predict ratings based on both historical interactions and sentiment patterns. The evaluation of ReviewRater on three real-world datasets shows substantial improvement over state-of-the-art methods in rating prediction, with a notable increase in performance on long-term datasets.

Developing CS NLP systems is hindered by the scarcity of CS datasets. Creating these datasets is an expensive process due to requirements such as data collection from multiple languages and careful annotation. Recently, advancements in models like BERT have made it feasible to create large datasets from parallel corpora without manual annotation, given that the CS variety has existing translations. However, this method is impractical as it necessitates the availability of numerous translators for rare CS varieties. This research investigates the use of monolingual data and self-training to create datasets for uncommon CS varieties. We also explore the limits of self-training in CS NLP. For L2D experiments, we find that using L1 fine-tuning improves results. We also demonstrate that having a related low-resource L1 language as target improves results. We present a new dataset created for the CS variety Kinyarwanda-English and report state-of-the-art results for L2D tasks. We further show that self-training significantly enhances model performance for both L2D and L2Z tasks. However, for tasks requiring more complex CS awareness, such as CS parsing, self-training remains ineffective.

A subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface, which fix the boundary of a open set, or are free, is demonstrated to be Roelcke precompact if it possesses a bounded subordained left basis. This property is also applied to establish the bounded Galois theorem for a subgroup of surface homeomorphisms, which fix the boundary of an open set, or are free, within a specific compact surface. A subgroup of surface homeomorphisms, which fix the boundary of an open set, or are free, is shown to be Roelcke precompact if it contains a bounded subordained left basis. This property is also utilized to establish the bounded Galois theorem for a subgroup of surface homeomorphisms, which fix the boundary of an open set, or are free, within a specific compact surface.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models based on products of group and coset spaces, which are generalized versions of lambda deformations. We're focusing on two distinct scenarios: one involving Wess-Zumino terms related to afibrational modules and another involving those related to fibration modules. The branes in these cases correspond to certain types of G2-Brane, Kazama-Sen-Witten Brane, and Rozansky-Witten Brane.

As tasks increasingly rely on computer execution, the demand for reliable solutions is rising across domains, including engineering and computer graphics. A fundamental component of addressing these issues is the mesh, a composite of basic elements where hexahedral elements offer superior properties for numerical computations. However, their creation often requires manual input, which can be time-consuming and error-prone. To streamline this process, the development of an inverse mesh generator based on the Level Set Method is presented. This tool efficiently generates near-exact hexahedral meshes from point cloud data, eliminating the need for manually defined surface descriptions. By leveraging advancements in Advanced Mesh Generation, the newly developed approach offers rapid, high-precision hexahedral mesh creation.

The task of relation extraction aims to identify and extract significant connections between entities within text, which is a crucial component in understanding semantic networks. As the demand for relation extraction continues to rise, particularly for extracting relevant information from large text corpora quickly, inexact matching between queries and answers becomes increasingly impractical. Therefore, a more efficient approach has been developed that enables the use of partial entity and relation instances as search queries and retrieves relevant data, even with partial matches. This approach leverages an innovative technique to incorporate relation instances as search queries and retrieves relevant data, in particular cases where entity and relation classes are insufficient to isolate desired data. Experimentation on two benchmark datasets reveals the proposed method's performance and efficiency in retrieving relevant data under various degrees of entity and relation partial matching.

This paper presents a delay prediction model for deep submicron CMOS inverters based on the 65nm CMOS technology from IBM. Inverters' delay is significantly influenced by the dimensions of transistors, which this model can take into account by considering various device sizes. The model also includes other important parameters like bias current, voltage, and load capacitance. To develop this model, a large dataset of 65nm CMOS inverters was generated with different parameters, and then delay values were calculated and collected. The dataset was divided into two parts, and the first part was used to train the model, which was then verified using the second part of the dataset. The results show that the model can accurately predict the delay of CMOS inverters with an average error of less than 0.05 ns.

We've developed a new method of learning within the framework of the minimax reinforcement learning model, where the goal is to obtain the most robust $Q$-function that remains consistent with the return's Lipschitz continuity across all policies. This approach, which we call "Lip-Q-learning," can be formulated as an optimization problem that utilizes variational learning. We then derive an iterative algorithm to solve for the most robust $Q$-function and provide theoretical guarantees for its convergence. Moreover, our results show that Lip-Q-learning offers enhanced stability and flexibility, allowing for the easy extension of various constraints and considerations, such as temperature parameter adjustments and risk-averse design. We showcase the effectiveness of our method through several scenarios, including the learning of optimal return strategies in both Markov decision processes and Markov games.

Research has shown that the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) processes objects and living things differently, but how animals and in-between cases, like fish and dinosaurs, are processed, is less understood. To explore this, researchers studied brain activity in response to pictures of real and imaginary humans, birds, fish, and insects, as well as images of these groups with imaginary fish and human traits. They found that VTC responded strongly to real animals and inanimate objects, but less to imaginary examples of these groups. Importantly, they found that this response varied continuously from real humans to fish to insects, but was weaker for imaginary combinations of these groups. These results support the idea that animacy, or the sense of something being alive, is on a scale and that the brain is organized accordingly. This organization is thought to be due to either how similar things are to each other, or how similar they are to a common ancestor.

In scientific simulations, higher-order finite element methods are commonly used to approximate characteristics of problems like concentration profiles and temperature distributions. However, achieving optimal performance often requires a delicate balance between the approximate solution and mesh configuration. This paper demonstrates how an adaptive refinement technique, based on an error estimation formula derived from the Petrov-Galerkin method, can be employed to optimize the pairing of approximations and meshes. This error estimator formula assesses errors in approximation relative to a weighted average of the approximate solution and its projected counterpart. By locally re-mesh based on approximations that are robust to local perturbations, the proposed approach enables optimal pairing of approximations and meshes. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique in reducing errors in approximation and improving solution efficiency.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low hard states of black hole X-ray transients, have been analyzed using VELA data for the source MAXI J1535-571. Observations with the eXtreme Universe Spectroscopic Investigator instrument detected high-quality type-C QPOs spectra. A soft black body component model was applied to the XIS data, revealing the hard X-ray component's origin. Analysis using the Fourier power spectrum tool revealed the presence of two type-C QPOs. A joint fit using the relativistic corona reflection model Hotman and the Maxwell distribution model was applied to the XIS and HXD cross-calibration data. Results suggest that the QPOs could be either the upper or lower boundary of the outer disk edge. Additionally, parameter values indicate that the disk edge could be close to the photon axis, while the source of the hard X-ray component above 10 keV could be either the baryonic jet or the comptonized component.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning for cooperative tasks, previous research found that MARL agents are vulnerable to adversarial attacks where minor alterations result in significantly decreased performance or even instability. To address this concern, our study focuses on developing robust cooperative MARL agents against such attacks, aiming to limit the impact to no more than a predetermined threshold. We introduce a novel attack method with specific features: the ability to be executed locally on each agent without needing global information, the ability to be deterministic with limited influence, and the goal of decreasing the agents' cooperative rewards. Our proposed robust learning framework for defending against MARL attacks consists of two main parts: a baseline strategy for identifying the most critical parameters for the actions taken by MARL agents and a method of regularizing the parameters to minimize the impact of potential attacks. Through experiments on the multi-agent grid world and the Chesser scenario, we found that the learned agents developed strategies that are resilient to various types of distributed and local adversarial attacks that aim to lower their cooperative rewards.

The increasing use of smartphones and wearable devices has led to everyday visual data collection on a massive scale, which can be drawn upon by various applications, including location-free identification of materials using real-world images. This study focuses on material recognition in images, and a key challenge in this area is achieving high levels of accuracy without the need for lab-scale conditions. To address this issue, we first develop a novel material representation, known as a material signature, based on a collection of images. This signature serves as a compromise between performance and memory efficiency. Next, we propose an approach for creating a database of material signatures, and then leverage existing image classification libraries to expand our approach to work with video inputs. Finally, we demonstrate the practical applications of our approach in real-world scenarios using a case study of identifying types of coffee based on images.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The paper proceeds by describing four different types of Lie 2-algebras derived from 2-plectic manifolds, semi-simple Lie algebras, semi-simple 3-Lie algebras and 3-dimensional 1-coleman algebras respectively. The objective is to establish an exact sequence of functors that links the categories of these Lie 2-algebras to the corresponding homotopy types of 2-term L∞-algebras.

We introduce a novel method for matching local image features, incorporating the strengths of both hand-crafted and learned features. Our approach relies on a single column transformer architecture, which allows the exchange of information between pixel positions, feature channels, and spatial locations. By doing so, we can tackle the limitations of dense descriptor interpolation. Additionally, our method features a relative orientation regression that outperves existing geodesic and neural approaches. Evaluation on existing datasets reveals that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art performance, especially in challenging low-texture scenes. Furthermore, we leverage our method to develop a novel global image descriptor, achieving exceptional results on visual correspondence and image retrieval benchmarks.

The article discusses the challenges associated with the ground-based identification of Faraday rotation angles due to ionospheric influence and presents a new approach for calculating the Zeeman splitting without relying on inaccurate magnetic field measurements. A method is proposed for combining the effects of the interstellar and ionospheric magnetic fields on the linear polarization of discrete spectral lines. The article also outlines the necessary observations and calculations for characterizing the magnetic field perpendicular to the line of sight and determining the Zeeman splitting, with a focus on improving our understanding of the magnetic field structure.

This research paper presents a real-world implementation of a pioneering predictive pricing strategy aimed at influencing consumers to shift their energy usage away from peak hours and load management via smart appliances. The goal is to create an energy pricing plan that optimizes the dynamics between consumer energy behavior, electricity distribution, and generator revenue. To achieve this, we utilize an advanced predictive model, coupled with a bio-inspired algorithm for generating real-time optimal pricing profiles. The effectiveness of our pricing plan is evaluated through a comprehensive analysis of social welfare, consumer surplus, and harmonic distortion. Our findings indicate that this pricing plan successfully prompts consumers to adjust their energy consumption behavior. The paper also explores the impact of various pricing protocols on generator revenue, harmonic distortion, and network performance, providing valuable insights into these aspects.

This paper examines the thermodynamic characteristics of the Bennett process acting on (d-2) dimensional black strings in anti-de Sitter space. The investigations into accretion models, Hawking temperature, and energy and entropy analysis confirm that black strings in anti-de Sitter space adhere to the first law of thermodynamics. Additionally, we verified that the Ising model's critical temperature is immune to external magnetic field influence, in line with current understanding. Assuming that the cosmological constant and string tension are regulated parameters, we determined their respective values. Further, we applied the Bennett process to a system of thermally charged black strings in anti-de Sitter space, thereby assessing its stability under such transformation. The results show that the black string's stability is not affected by the process; however, its thermodynamic characteristics do undergo alteration.

The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, the limiting spectral measure enables the identification of subspaces within the full space, each corresponding to a specific eigenvalue. Building upon these findings, the results extend von Neumann's theorem by expressing the rate of convergence in terms of a spectral measure, while also generalizing a previous study on $C^r$-summability.

Our research team has identified and studied 14 extremely distant metal-poor stars located approximately 200 thousand light-years away in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Third Data Release. Through spectroscopic analysis, we verified the low metal content of these stars, further verified their luminosity classifications using spectroscopic methods, and found them to be very old based on their chemical signatures. Additionally, by analyzing their movement within space, we determined that these stars are not connected to each other through space movement patterns, indicating that they are most likely part of the original building blocks of the Galaxy. Our findings suggest that these stars, being very old and having very low metal content, must have masses below 0.1 times the mass of the sun to survive for such a long time.

This research investigates the trends in fire seasons across various global regions from 1996 to 2016, using nighttime imagery from satellite sensors VIIRS/DNB and MODIS. An analysis of 21 billion fire sub-observations yielded around 1.8 million distinct fires, showing widespread seasonality. The length of fire seasons generally varies between five to twenty-one consecutive observations, resulting in most regions having seasons lasting between five to thirteen weeks. Long fire seasons are notably observed in South America and Southeast Asia. While some regions, like sub-Saharan Africa, have consistently recurring fire seasons, others, like those in Europe and the former Soviet Union, often lack them. Changes in fire season lengths and frequencies have been analyzed using statistical time-series methods, revealing significant trends. Fire frequencies have increased in nearly all regions, with seasonal lengths extending in around 75% of areas and shortening in nearly 20%. This research provides insights into the complex relationships between climate change, land use, and wildfires.

We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different underlying assumptions regarding how various morphological characteristics like inflectional patterns and word length interrelate. We compared these measures using a set of 106 languages from the Standard Language Index dataset, creating a multivariate analysis with principal component analysis. Surprisingly, our results indicate that first principal component accounts for over 40% of variance, suggesting significant correlations between different morphological complexity measures. This finding implies that many of these measures capture similar aspects of morphological complexity. We verified this by performing dimensionality reduction and classifying measures into clusters based on their similarities. Our analysis also reveals that certain measures primarily capture unique aspects of inflectional patterns or word length, highlighting their distinct contributions to morphological complexity.

Researchers who study galaxy formation are trying to find an alternative to the standard cold dark matter model due to its difficult predictions.  One theoretical replacement, self-interacting dark matter, has been linked to lower interaction rates and still agrees with observed galaxy halo shapes.  A different approach, fuzzy dark matter, adds probabilistic phase uncertainty, resulting in substructure profiles that differ from standard predictions.  Our study combines these two concepts into a single theoretical framework by incorporating scattering and phase uncertainty into the substructure equation.  Our results show that a combination of these two factors generally leads to less dense profiles at the center, but the effect depends on specific assumptions about the phase uncertainty and standard physical processes.  Our model, however, still struggles to fully explain the observed characteristics of Milky Way galaxy substructures.

We introduce an approach for efficiently reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an optimal approximation space. This method leverages two primary sources of information: a precomputed solution for a particular parameter value and a snapshot collection obtained at various parameter settings. Our algorithm iteratively constructs an enhanced approximation space based on these inputs, ultimately yielding a highly accurate solution for the PPDE. The key innovation lies in the integration of harmonic analysis techniques, which enable the development of a precise error estimate that guides the algorithm's decision-making process. The proposed method is theoretically grounded and provides a guarantee of convergence, while its iterative and adaptive nature allows it to effectively mitigate computational waste. Several numerical case studies illustrate the effectiveness of our approach for reduction of order in the context of PPDEs.

This research introduces several novel approaches to extracting features from random data, grounded in statistical principles.  Three distinct methods, derived from independent component analysis, are proposed:  m-arithmetic K-times FastICA, using either Frobenius norm or umbral norm, and a variant of entropy-based criteria.  The umbral norm is particularly well-suited for data sets featuring umbral (or sparse with umbral noise) mixtures.  The effectiveness of these techniques is validated through various simulations, including those involving high-dimensional data.  Notably, m-ar-K-FastICA umbral FastICA and m-ar-K-FastICA Frobenius FastICA methods exhibit improved extraction accuracy and stability when data is random, particularly in high-dimensional scenarios.

Identifying trending social media data streams in real-time has become a crucial task for monitoring various events, from natural disasters and riots to sports competitions and television shows. Researchers have developed complex systems using multiple sensors to process these streams. This study proposes an event detection framework utilizing social media data streams. It employs a distributed architecture with seven modules to first filter the data and then gather relevant information. Subsequently, the framework combines the data with Wikipedia's knowledge base to identify trending topics. Finally, the system uses NLP techniques to analyze the content of the social media data and detect events occurring simultaneously. Our approach was tested on real-world social media data streams and demonstrated successful event detection.

We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity of very weak solutions for the measure-valued elliptic PDE $-\divergence A(x,\nabla u) = Q$. Our analysis also yields a regularity result for very weak solutions of the nonlinear elliptic equation $|\D u|^{p-2}|\divergence \D u|^{p-2}\divergence \D u = f$.

To address the scarcity of cobalt and address applications for hydrogen storage, we've explored cobalt-rich compounds with a high HfP structure, which we've theoretically analyzed to determine their phase diagrams and phase stability. Our results show that $\beta$-Mn phases have a wider HfP stability range than previously thought, extending from 40% to 66.7% cobalt content. A hydrogen pressure of 10 MPa enhances the stability of cobalt-rich compounds at higher temperatures. At 10 MPa hydrogen pressure, the phase boundary between Hf$_{12}$Co$_{88}$ and Hf$_{12}$Co$_{82}$ HfP transitions to Hf$_{12}$Co$_{78}$, whereas on the hydrogen-rich side, the HfP structure remains stable from Hf$_{88}$H$_{12}$ to Hf$_{82}$H$_{18}$. A hydrogen absorption capacity of 4.2 wt% is achieved in Hf$_{12}$Co$_{88}$ at 10 MPa and 500 K.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the primary approach. Each ad impression is auctioned off with a bid, where the goal is to maximize revenue per impression. However, due to the vast number of requests and limited information available for each, bidding processes face significant challenges. This study presents a new learning-based real-time bidding system, incorporating the user's risk tolerance to guide bidding decisions. A robust algorithm is proposed to quickly learn and adapt the user's risk tolerance from online feedback signals. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed system's ability to overcome uncertainty common in initial stages, achieve stable outcomes, and maximize revenue by considering the user's risk tolerance. Comparisons show the proposed approach surpasses traditional strategies, securing higher revenue.

Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study demonstrates that in a specific scenario, Wigner negativity can be generated without nonclassical correlations, provided non-local interactions exist. It is proposed that this phenomenon is rooted in quantum steering, which enables remote disturbance of one party's state, effectively disrupting local positivity, thereby yielding Wigner negativity. Utilizing an optical interferometer and coupled cavity cavities, this phenomenon was successfully observed and observed. Our research reveals a novel method for detecting non-local interactions and highlights the importance of these interactions in Wigner negativity, presenting an opportunity for the development of more precise quantum key distribution protocols.

In practical quantum key distribution (QKD) systems, the random number seeds used for privacy protection are often chosen from external sources, such as global random number generators, without being uniformly distributed. Consequently, the secure bound of QKD systems is limited by the largest value of conditional min-entropy in their corresponding phase spaces, which is determined by the non-uniformity of these seeds. We have developed a method to quantify this non-uniformity by transforming it into a quadratic form, which allows for easier computation and interpretation. We have also proposed a series of seed quality metrics based on this formulation and have analyzed the relationship between these metrics and the secure bound. Furthermore, our research has identified the optimal metric for assessing random number seeds and has found that, in QKD systems using fast entanglement verification methods, the secure bound can be approximated by the number of random samples used, provided that this number exceeds the seed non-uniformity's quadratic root.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

We demonstrate under mild conditions that the solution to the martingale problem given by Feller's diffusion equation, which describes a multiplicative population growth model with varying growth rates and a finite number of types, converges to a unique deterministic limit. This outcome surpasses the existing results, which rely on more stringent conditions, and also resolves an open question from the 1998 paper by Pardhanani and McKean.

In this work, we introduce a new method to analyze multi-phonic complex phenomena in waveguide QED systems by employing effective vertex functions combined with perturbation theory. By utilizing renormalized coupling constants and counting parameters, we can organize terms in the Liouville space and identify the most dominant effects. The use of vertex functions allows us to incorporate the effects of finite bandwidth and nontrivial transmission functions in resonator systems. We demonstrate this approach by comparing it with a wave equation simulation of a specific system, and observe that incorporating the vertex function's structure leads to a more accurate description of the interaction process. Specifically, this method produces results consistent within 10% of the numerical simulations at a low-N count, while significantly simplifying the problem to finite-dimensional systems, thus opening up new possibilities for diagnostically tractable systems.

A potential way to study low-mass dark matter is by utilizing boosted dark matter interactions with protons via off-axis events at neutrino experiments such as DUNE. In light of this, we have thoroughly examined the relativistic proton structure factor for a dark matter fermion. Our analysis reveals that for boosted dark matter, its behavior is predominantly influenced by the time component, rather than the traditional framework provided by quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, we have calculated various spin-dependent cross-sections for a dark matter fermion interacting with a proton. These calculations can serve as a reference point for upcoming DUNE dark matter research.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to variations in channel delay and amplitude. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by the requirement for accurate phase and amplitude matching of reference and received signals. This constraint can be mitigated by utilizing a reconfigurable analog phase shifter, but such a device would significantly increase the complexity of the receiver. An alternative solution is a digital replacement based on the maximum likelihood (ML) criterion, but the ML algorithm is computationally demanding. In this research, a novel, efficient method based on the fast Fourier transform (FFT) has been developed to overcome these challenges. The new algorithm first aligns the phase of the received CPM signal, then employs an FFT-based search to find the closest match in a codebook of pre-generated, phase-aligned CPM signals. By using the ML criterion after the FFT-based search, the proposed ML-FFT ML algorithm has been shown to outperform conventional detection methods, even when the receiver is subject to significant phase shifts.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of comparative feedback. To overcome this limitation, we investigate the potential of leveraging human preferences expressed through ratings rather than comparisons. While comparing any two options is challenging, soliciting ratings for multiple options might be more feasible. However, this rated feedback is inherently ambiguous due to the multiple possible ordering of options it implies. To circumvent this ambiguity, we present a MaLPo algorithm that learns preferences from rated feedback, allowing multiple options without necessitating comparisons. We establish theoretical bounds on MaLPo's regret and observe that it generalizes well across different preference types, including those with inherent patterns and those that are uniformly distributed. Experimental results on both synthetic and real datasets corroborate our theory and demonstrate that MaLPo outperforms comparison-based methods.

We utilize lattice QCD and QED calculations to investigate the nucleon structure revealed by electron scattering. Our study involves combining lattice QCD and QED calculations with semi-restricted electroweak form factors, and we analyze our results in both dimensionless and physical units. Additionally, we use unitary transformations to decouple flavor charges from nucleon charges, allowing us to explore various combinations of flavor nucleon form factors. Our study provides a precise calculation at an electroweak scale prototype of mass, and our results are compatible with experimental data from modern high-precision electroweak experiments.

A novel adjustable variation of the Toric code has been proposed that effectively models a frustrated lattice of qubits found in topological orders, where specific modifications mimic quantum paramagnets characterized by intricate free energy landscapes separated by sharp phase transitions. In this work, a more streamlined approach to encoding qudits as products of Clifford gates and CZ gates is presented, one where each site utilizes a single qudit rather than an encoded particle-antiparticle pair. This adjustable quantum code is realized on a square lattice using superconducting qubits and investigated numerically, where simulations confirm the presence of sharp phase transitions in line with the predicted ground state properties. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that these adjustable variations of the Toric code can facilitate quantum computations within the ground state, where measurements are free from systematic errors. In light of these properties, it has been proposed that these codes could serve as an ideal testing ground for investigating the intricate dynamics of quantum matter out of thermal equilibrium.

We investigate the eigenspectra of large, randomly constructed Hermitian block matrices, whose structure is perturbed by a finite rank complex correction term. Given that the band's width expands faster than the square root of the matrix's size, our analysis demonstrates that the statistical distribution of the imaginary components of the eigenvectors aligns with the results obtained from the complex Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This finding is achieved through the application of a novel variant of the Stochastic Matryoshka Method.

Recent advancements in Deep Learning have led to notable improvements in the accuracy of dialogue systems, yet the processes require substantial labor and resources due to the need for annotated dialogue data. The majority of current dialogue datasets are insufficient in quantity and poorly aligned with respect to language models they are intended for. The primary reason for these limitations is the high complexity involved in parsing dialogue content into a meaningful representation. The use of Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) as a layer has shown potential in mitigating these limitations, as it effectively captures the core meaning of spoken language while being relatively simpler to parse. Consequently, we develop DialAMR, a large-scale dialogue dataset comprising over 216K conversational sequences, each paired with a paragraph-level representation in AMR format. The dataset is made available via a public repository at: https://github.com/danielwu95/DialAMR. We also present baseline models that operate directly on the AMR layer, demonstrating the effectiveness of this representation in generating dialogue sequences in response to varied prompts.

To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, algorithmic interpretability must be measured. This study draws on principles from the fields of programming languages and artificial intelligence to establish a comprehensive framework for assessing interpretability. This proposed method meets five critical criteria: it must be applicable to a broad range of algorithms, effective in real-world scenarios, easy to understand and analyze, relevant to the specific context, and adaptable to change. Additionally, the development of interpretability measurements must respect the principles of fairness and avoid perpetuating harmful biases. Utilizing functional programming concepts, the proposed framework demonstrates the importance of modular and reusable code in achieving interpretability.

Anomaly detection without labeled data is an underexplored area of study. Most research applications lack the resources or costs associated with annotating data. We propose an efficient anomaly detection method that utilizes weak supervision signals, such as timestamps, to identify irregular data samples. These weak supervision signals are readily available in many research domains and can be utilized to develop effective anomaly detection methods. We introduce an innovative approach that combines clustering with a regularity constraint, ensuring that cluster representatives adhere to the provided supervision signal. This method is computationally efficient and can be easily scaled up for high-dimensional data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on real-world datasets, highlighting its strengths and weaknesses in the process.

Recent advances in computing have made it possible to obtain accurate, data-driven estimates of threshold-invariant extreme value parameters by analysing sequences of block maxima or minima. This has improved modelling of extreme events based on these parameters, but it's worth noting that modelling of extremes traditionally focuses on identifying a single, optimal parameter value. When working with sequences of block maxima or minima, it's clear that a single parameter doesn't exist - instead, it's more accurate to describe a parameter that varies little as the sample size increases. A new approach has been developed to model such processes, involving a random field that remains nearly constant as the sample size grows. This random field is constrained by a mean extremal index and an extremal index that describes variability in the process over both time and space. The model accounts for both long-range and short-range dependencies, with the latter influencing the process on larger scales. A nonparametric approach has been implemented to estimate this model from time series data, with the method first identifying a self-similar random field that describes homogeneity in the process and then allowing for modelling of both dependencies and irregular patterns. A case study has been conducted to demonstrate the method's effectiveness using 15 years of daily maximum temperatures in Toronto. The model has been used to create an ensemble of future projections of extreme temperature events under different climate scenarios, with the results indicating a clear increase in the frequency of such events on both annual and decadal scales.

This analysis addresses the task of identifying the shape with the largest area given a specific perimeter in a two-dimensional space. We have formulated a general solution for shapes defined by polynomial functions and demonstrated it specifically for shapes composed of quadratic and linear segments. We have also found the optimal shape with the largest area given a fixed perimeter in the cases where the shape is able to encompass points within the unit circle and where the shape is restricted to points outside the unit circle.

This paper presents the current state of a widely used commonsense knowledge graph (CSKG) known as ConceptNet, in the context of the Semantics of Benchmarks workshop. ConceptNet is a crowdsourced, open-source knowledge graph that records a wide range of natural language reasoning capabilities. We demonstrate the challenges of maintaining and evaluating a distributed knowledge base like ConceptNet, and how the development of benchmark tasks has contributed to our understanding of the issues.

The Herschel-GAL plane survey, a key component of the Hi-GAL project, utilizes the Herschel satellite to survey the Milky Way's Galactic plane, leveraging SPIRE and PACS instruments to utilize 3 different frequency ranges. The survey's extensive dataset necessitates the development of automated tools to efficiently extract source information. Our study utilizes the HI-GAL dataset to evaluate the performance of the ROMA source extraction tool on mock and actual Hi-GAL datasets using various observation conditions. The source count function and confusion noise level are analyzed to optimize the source extraction process for the Hi-GAL data. Our results indicate that ROMA, a robust source extraction tool, is well-suited for various astronomical surveys, and its performance parameters can serve as benchmarks for other similar studies.

The study of multiple-population structures in globular clusters offers valuable insights into their formation and evolution. We analyzed several key clusters, including NGC1851, NGC1904, NGC5281, and NGC6397, using spectroscopic data to investigate their multiple-star populations. The data revealed a multiple-component distribution for iron content, as well as variations in helium abundance according to [Fe/H] values. In the chromosome maps of these clusters, we observed a shift in iron content and multiple-star populations' positions. The data from NGC6397 show a positive relationship between [Fe/H] and UVJ color-magnitude diagrams' brightness, supporting the different population hypothesis. The data from NGC5281 reveal multiple stars' positions aligning with iron content, rather than luminosity, in the UBVRI diagrams. The analysis of NGC1904's multiple-star populations shows a correlation between [Fe/H] and UVJ color-magnitude diagrams' brightness. The positions of multiple-star populations in the UBVRI diagrams correspond to iron content, with brighter stars on the blue half of the Turnoff having higher [Fe/H] values. The positions of multiple-star populations in the UBVRI diagrams correspond to iron content, with multiple-star populations in the upper blue half of the diagram having higher [Fe/H] values. The data from NGC1851 show a positive relationship between [Fe/H] and UVJ color-magnitude diagrams' brightness, with multiple-star populations in the upper blue

To facilitate a deeper understanding of one-dimensional physical systems, we consider a simplified single file model, focusing on its largest particle as it interacts with a specific type of boundary. The boundary is characterised as being highly absorptive, but also exhibits random behaviour in its absorption properties. The file's dynamics are modelled using a combination of Brownian motion and a telegraph process, both governed by the same time scale. By examining the large N limit, where N represents the number of particles in the file, we establish a Fokker-Planck equation for the boundary condition's process. The complexity of this problem necessitates a novel approach to solving this equation, which we accomplish by first simplifying the equation and then applying absorbing boundary conditions to a related system. The resulting solutions allow us to derive mean first passage times for both absorbing and reflecting boundary conditions, which can be generalised to any initial conditions.

Quantum mechanics contradicts the universally assumed, classical cause-and-effect relationship established by Bayes' rule in physics. While believed to hold for all processes, Bayes' rule leads to logical inconsistencies when applied to quantum mechanics. We demonstrate the failure of Bayes' rule in quantum mechanics by examining its use of conditional probabilities for two independent events. This failure is often resolved by using a quantum version of Bayes' rule, but its employment raises further inconsistencies in conjunction with quantum mechanics. To resolve these inconsistencies, we suggest an alternative formulation of Bayes' rule that avoids nonphysical operations such as negative probabilities and entanglement.

We initially report findings regarding corrections to system size for the state equation, trace anomaly, and speed of sound, using two specific theoretical frameworks: a model for massless scalar fields and another based on quenched QCD, both applying periodic boundary conditions. Additionally, we share ongoing results applying Dirichlet boundary conditions to quenched QCD.

We developed a far ultraviolet spectrometer for the Hubble Space Telescope's Cosmic Origins Spectrograph by creating two new detectors capable of observing beyond 1200 Angstroms, effectively doubling the observable range to 1000-2000 Angstroms. To eliminate solar radiation, a hydrogen absorption cell was used. Our laboratory testing of the novel detectors and filters utilized flight-like conditions to assess their performance. To validate the new detector's functionality on the spacecraft, initial observations were carried out, including reproducible spectra of Capella and Procyon, whose spectra were compared to those acquired with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrometer and the Goddard High Energy Spectroscopic Imager.

This study explores whether systems with Graph Symmetric Properties can implement effective distributed control strategies. A new definition for optimal distributed control is presented as a multi-objective problem, balancing control costs and tracking performance. To improve system responsiveness and reduce costs, an adaptive algorithm is developed that consistently leads to optimal distributed control, even in systems with uncertain system parameters, through continuous learning and adaptation of local control strategies. In finite-time, both cooperative and non-cooperative optimal distributed control policies can be derived using Lyapunov-based stability analysis, which ensures stability and improved performance with continuous adaptation. To verify the effectiveness of this learning-based approach, numerical simulations are conducted to demonstrate its ability to adapt to changing system parameters.

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm. This paper introduces active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components, reducing a database's image representation burden and streamlining image search. It achieves this through a dynamic process where the search algorithm identifies key images and assigns them to the database, both maintaining their original sizes and being actively updated as needed. This allows the search algorithm to be independently optimized for performance, a task the paper addresses using active learning with a custom loss function. Experimental results demonstrate that active indexing significantly accelerates image search, achieving up to a 70-fold speed increase for given neural networks, while allowing them to be trained from scratch with no pre-existing model required.

This study verifies that physical layer-based authentication is achievable in a specific scenario - when an adversary is not present. However, when an adversary is considered part of the channel model, it becomes clear that no authentication is possible under certain conditions. Specifically, this is true in a scenario where an arbitrary number of attackers are present in an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel. One potential solution to this issue is to implement a form of authentication that involves a shared secret, but these methods are vulnerable to eavesdropping. Therefore, an alternative approach is proposed here, using a type of channel coding that incorporates authentication, but this time authentication is only guaranteed in a scenario with no attackers. To address this limitation, a modified version of the DMC is proposed, incorporating an attacker, and referred to as the authenticated multiple-access DMC. It is shown that, under certain conditions, it is possible to achieve physical layer-based authentication in this modified DMC, using a specific method that involves a two-stage transmission process. This study also identifies the conditions under which this method is possible, and develops a mathematical framework to calculate the required level of cooperation from the transmitters.

Reevaluating the study of Brownian particles in a solvent might be necessary, 
considering recent findings that the running state of these particles could
be a transient phenomenon. Data from experiments and simulations indicate
that immediately entering the running state likely results in localised,
oscillatory motion rather than being purely diffusive in nature. A simple
model, grounded in nonlinear dynamics theory, effectively captures the main
features observed in both theoretical and experimental analyses, in addition
to accurately predicting the duration of the oscillatory phase and subsequently
settling into steady-state running motion.

This paper presents an adaptable, data-driven approach to creating personalized economic models.
Utilizing the framework of dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models, the method enables economists to craft tailored models with adjustable variables and circumstances.
Through an enhanced version of the particle stockholder algorithm, the methodology efficiently samples model parameters, thereby simulating diverse model outcomes.
To verify the method's effectiveness, the paper applies it to a simplified monetary policy transmission model and examines the efficacy of this approach in understanding monetary policy implementation.
Furthermore, the paper investigates the variability of the fiscal multiplier under different economic conditions and with varying fiscal stimuli, ultimately simulating the impacts of fiscal policy shocks across distinct business cycle phases.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to photons in the vacuum that emit an energy back to the charge in proportion to n^2, a greater increase than that of the Landau levels, a phenomenon that occurs even in the limit of no scattering.

Evaluating the effectiveness of hyperbolic space in modeling fine-tuned NER data, we discovered that previous assessments were overly cautious due to the limited data set, which does not accurately represent the full range of English language entities. A more thorough examination is now conducted using the expanded GRACE dataset within the NER domain, leading to the creation of new HyperGLUE benchmarks. These benchmarks compare the performance of cutting-edge NER models with and without hyperbolic space, revealing that current models have not yet taken full advantage of the benefits that hyperbolic space can provide. Consequently, the proposed HyperGLUE dataset is designed to help NER systems reach their full potential by leveraging the structural benefits of hyperbolic space.

This paper establishes upper limits on the Hankel determinants for the $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ special types, specifically within the univalent function class and the $\mathcal{U}$ class defined by a specific condition involving functions that are analytic in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, with normalization where $f(z)=z+a_2z^2+\cdots$.

Achieving efficient and sustainable operation in cloud data centers largely depends on load balancing, which has become increasingly challenging due to the surge in online services and mobile applications that access resources on-demand, creating unpredictable patterns of resource usage. To address this issue, data center operators use a method of proactive load balancing that temporarily allocates resources to customers to maintain desired levels of performance, based on predicted resource demands and agreed-upon service levels. While this approach allows for more effective management, it requires accurate predictions that are often hampered by the resource's non-linear and time-varying nature. To mitigate this issue, we have developed the Prepartition method of proactive load balancing that dynamically adjusts to changing conditions and can accommodate both linear and non-linear resource characteristics, ensuring optimal balance between resource utilization and customer service requirements. Furthermore, our approach can adapt to changes in resource demands in real-time, while providing automatic compensation for discrepancies between predicted and actual resource demands. We have compared our method with traditional reactive load balancing in terms of scalability, responsiveness, and energy efficiency, using real-world data to demonstrate its advantages and showcase its potential benefits in terms of cost savings and improved scalability.

In modeling systems of rival agents as games, assuming each party makes rational decisions, the probable outcomes can be identified using equilibrium concepts like the Nash equilibrium. In various real-world scenarios, factors like weather, traffic or fiscal policy, beyond the agents' control, can impact game payoffs. Traditional Nash equilibrium solutions may not always accurately reflect actual system behavior, especially when agent decisions are heavily influenced by external factors. In this study, the authors propose a framework to extend game modeling, allowing for multiple variables influencing game decisions. The proposed method is then demonstrated by applying it to a traffic routing game. The authors show that by incorporating factors like road conditions and demand, the model can capture more realistic routing patterns and approximate equilibrium traffic patterns more accurately than single-origin Nash equilibria. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential trade-offs between computational requirements and the level of model detail needed.

This study presents a new identification result for causal effects in the presence of unobserved confounding variables, using instrumental variables and adjustments for these variables through moment conditions. We demonstrate that using only partial data on adjustment variables or using multiple variables does not lead to a convergent estimator for the causal effect. In the case of weak confounding variables, utilizing partial adjustment variable data converges to the true causal effect, whereas including multiple adjustment variables may not. Based on these findings, we develop a novel approach to adjusting for confounding variables and establish its finite-sample convergence rate. This method can be applied in practice and is empirically verified to yield superior results.

Significant physical harm can result from cyber assaults on Industrial Control Systems, and the rising necessity for ensuring the security of these systems led to the development of Standard 998 by the American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE). Although this standard provides guidelines, it is essential to conduct risk assessments to identify and address potential hazards. In this research, we adapt an existing method for automated general vulnerability assessment and attack detection from Industrial Control Systems, and apply it to verify that Stuxnet, a notable malware, does not contradict the guidelines outlined in Standard 998.

A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents via deep learning models, but these models are typically trained on English data, leaving other languages, such as the Indian language Hindi, under-represented. Consequently, applications built on top of these English-based models fail to accurately translate or summarize Hindi texts, often producing subpar results. To bridge this gap, we introduce mHindiSumm, a Hindi summarization model trained solely on Hindi data, thereby eliminating the need for cross-language support. Our model relies on a multi-task approach that combines abstractive and extractive summarization to produce more coherent and well-formed summaries. Extensive evaluations validate the superiority of our model over state-of-the-art English-based Hindi summarizers.

We establish the definition and attributes of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to providing characteristics for such structures, along with examining the relationship between an S-ring of Krull type $R$ and its completion with respect to an admissible ideal, which results in another S-ring of Krull type. Moreover, we define the graded version of an S-ring of Krull type and examine how it can be obtained from the previous concept. We also introduce the concept of a quasi-affine S-ring of Krull type, derived from the previous two, and investigate its connection to the property of being a valuation ring.

Our objective is to identify and characterize potential planetary systems by detecting close-in distant companions of early-type stars. Utilizing the VLT/SPHERE ZIMPOL imager, we conducted extensive observations of two such candidates, HIP 1481 and HIP 88399, under non-redundant imaging and angular differential imaging schemes, including polarimetry to identify potential exoplanets. Following thorough observations, our results indicate that neither target hosts a detectable companion within the 0.1 to 100 AU radius range. Upper mass limits for any potential companion were established at approximately $<2.5 M_J$ for HIP 1481 and $<5 M_J$ for HIP 88399, within the close-in zone. However, for a companion with a semi-major axis similar to that of our Solar System, our team's current data do not allow us to rule out the presence of a giant planet, as upper mass limits for such a companion would be around 1 $M_J$ for HIP 1481 and 2 $M_J$ for HIP 88399.

Variational autoencoders have become the new standard for working with complex, high-dimensional data in state-of-the-art generative modeling. Researchers and engineers prioritize them over traditional autoencoders due to their superior reconstructive capabilities. A key benefit of vae's in latent space exploration lies in their compact and structured representation of input data. However, this compactness comes with the drawback of losing valuable information in the input data, resulting in a potentially biased analysis. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages vae's compactness without relying on the potentially distorted latent space. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of this method across multiple real-world scenarios.

Smart home technology is gaining momentum, driven by IoT, yet it also invites cyber threats that necessitate robust and cost-effective security measures. This research contributes to filling this need by designing an affordable, network security system utilizing a private blockchain and a location tracking technique based on wireless signal strength. Our investigation focuses on the feasibility of private blockchain due to its lower energy consumption and faster transaction finalization compared to public ones. Additionally, we assessed the accuracy of location tracking, finding that the method can determine a device's location within a 2-meter margin of error, while demonstrating that device location can be securely shared across the network using the blockchain-based system.

A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio values is presented, employing a deep learning based method to implicitly map a continuous LLR range to a 1-bit representation. Through this technique, we achieve significant reductions in memory usage, allowing for the representation of any real-valued vector as a binary vector. Our method was inspired by related work in neural process models and is compared to alternative quantization schemes under two performance metrics: representation efficiency and classification accuracy. Our results demonstrate that this method outperforms recent research in both aspects, while also exhibiting adaptability to various probability distributions.

We have devised two new parameterized algorithms to solve two distinct problems related to directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Firstly, we have developed an algorithm to test whether a DAG can be drawn as an upward planar drawing, considering external nodes, and to identify the minimum number of external nodes required for such a drawing. This problem is parameterized by the number of external nodes. Secondly, we have developed an algorithm to test whether a DAG can be drawn as an external upward planar drawing, considering a constraint on the position of external nodes, and to identify the minimum number of external nodes required for such a drawing. This problem is parameterized by the sum of the position constraints applied to external nodes. Both algorithms run in $O(T) \times k^3$ time, where $T$ denotes the number of pairs of external nodes, and $k$ denotes the parameter under examination. This enables us to efficiently solve two open problems proposed in recent studies.

Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. This difficulty stems from the class overlap inherent in these datasets, exacerbated by the diversity of images within each class. State-of-the-art methods inevitably produce noisy predictions, likely due to class ambiguity. Our approach addresses this problem by leveraging crowd-sourced noise labels and ensemble learning to create more reliable image classifications. By forming an ensemble of classifiers from multiple neural networks, we achieve improved robustness against label noise. Our method also incorporates the use of clean labels from human experts for minority classes, thereby augmenting the dataset with additional information. Through the application of active learning, we selectively update the labels of noisy instances, thereby purging noise from the dataset. Our approach is empirically validated on several crowdsourced image datasets, demonstrating superior performance to existing state-of-the-art methods.

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we can prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables.

A particular matrix known as a covering array has specific characteristics. It is made up of different symbols and certain sub-matrices must include each combination of those symbols a set number of times. The best, or smallest, such matrices are known as optimal, and if they have equal rows they are referred to as monotone. Previous research had established a lower limit for the size of these optimal matrices. This paper verifies the size of these optimal matrices and further, the size of the smallest possible monotone matrices.

This paper investigates the noisy maximally entangled states |0;1FN$ \rangle$ and investigates the two-party quantum verifier's ability to consistently detect these states despite interference from a finite number of incorrect states, using the quantum Cosimer method. It demonstrates the development of precise thresholds for four-dimensional noisy maximally entangled states and near maximally entangled states, as well as a novel QCCM formula for the latter, in contrast to previous noisy maximally entangled states research. Notably, this research reveals that noisy maximally entangled states can be efficiently identified even with the presence of noise, a phenomenon not previously observed in near maximally entangled states.
