Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. We've developed a new method to regularize the parameters of a categorical Bernoulli model used in text analysis, which involves using a Lasso-type approach. We've combined this with a novel regularization technique that utilizes a generalized P\'{o}lya-Guraa (GP) distribution, enabling us to correlate the lengths of different word sequences within a document. This method allows us to create a sparse model by treating the GP distribution's parameters as a single block and applying a Lasso-type approach, which we've tested and proven effective using the Berkeley Segmentation Inventory Task dataset.

In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have become increasingly diverse and complex, driving the demand for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems to coexist with general-purpose systems. The integration of hypervisors has emerged as a potential solution to achieve this requirement, although existing hypervisors tend to introduce significant overhead, making them unsuitable for high-performance embedded applications. To address this challenge, T-Visor, a lightweight type-1 hypervisor, has been designed to enable the coexistence of real-time and general-purpose systems, while providing hard real-time guarantees and achieving efficiency through per-OS-Device virtualized device management. The evaluation results demonstrate T-Visor's capacity to provide hard real-time hard real-time hard real-time guarantees and device virtualization benefits, all within 11% of the execution time compared to the bare-metal performance of Linux.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals align their cameras parallel to the vertical axis.  Lately, the subject has garnered considerable interest due to the proliferation of single-lens mirrorless and compact cameras, often used by hikers and tourists to capture scenes.  Notwithstanding the proliferation of related studies, the issue remains understudied.  This research presents a novel approach to panoramic image processing, incorporating both alignment and stitching modules.  The proposed system boasts a reduced parameter set, enabling an algorithm with lower computational demands to be developed.  The efficacy of the proposed method was validated using real-world datasets.

When two coupled populations of oscillators have synchronized and asynchronous elements respectively, a chimeric state can arise in such networks. We've analyzed chimeras in systems where one parameter influences an oscillator's behavior, drawn randomly from a uniform distribution, for oscillators in two-dimensional spaces. Our study follows earlier research outlined in Schoeller et al. 2010 and 2011, and we've explored how robust these chimeras are in response to changes in the distribution of the coupling strength probability. Our findings show a strong correlation between the robustness of the chimeric state and the width of this distribution, and we've used numerical methods to determine the points at which the chimeras would break or form, investigating the effects of different uniform distributions on these transition points.

We investigate the effectiveness of model-based reinforcement learning algorithms in non-stationary environments. On average, model-based approaches typically offer significant performance gains over model-free methods. However, the available model-based algorithms in non-stationary environments is limited. To bridge this gap, we develop RegMBRL, a regression-based model-based reinforcement learning technique designed for Markov decision processes with piece-wise affine reward and transition functions. These functions are characteristic of many real-world environments with non-stationary behavior. To optimize performance, RegMBRL uses a deep neural network to update both the transition and reward models and leverages these models to determine the optimal policy. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that RegMBLR achieves nearly optimal regret, with a rate of logarithmic scaling. To substantiate our findings, we conduct experiments on simple reinforcement learning benchmarks, demonstrating that RegMBLR surpasses model-free baselines.

We present a multi-layer quiver in this paper, using which we can build a higher dimension (n+1) algebras with $n$ layers as a quotient of the product of quivers. We show that the resulting algebra has properties such that any bicritical minimal resolution is a n-slice algebra. Furthermore, under certain conditions, the fundamental group of this algebra is topologically non-trivial.

We develop reflected entropy in the context of random tensor networks, addressing the potential issue of a reflected entropy spike during the page phase transition by introducing a refined boundary condition. The gluing entropy is redefined with improved properties and our findings align with the entanglement structure of the underlying state. The refined boundary condition leads to a specific limit that maintains reflection positivity, giving rise to a reduced entropy spike in our model. The discrepancy between our results and theoretical predictions is least prominent in the limit of large tensor dimensions.

We suggest that the organizational process in living systems can be modeled as a continuous struggle to minimize the local rate of entropy within those systems. This model connects the underlying physics of life to the study of systems in critical conditions, where small variations result in significantly varied outcomes. We propose that criticality contributes to the formation and longevity of long-lasting patterns within and across generations. This concept is supported by studies in various biological systems, such as the branching of arteries, the arrangement of leaves on stems, and the formation of long-lasting ice crystals within frost flowers. These patterns are not only aesthetically pleasing but also play a crucial role in understanding and predicting their behavior. For example, the branching of arteries influences the distribution of blood flow, while the arrangement of leaves affects both the structure and function of these systems. By modeling these patterns as near-critical systems, we can gain valuable insights into their behavior and how they adapt to changes over time. This understanding can be applied to a wide range of systems, including those studied in physics, biology, and even social sciences.

We investigate the dynamics of a basic 3D version of the H\'{e}non map, specifically focusing on its dissipative and orientation-preserving variants. Within this system, stable sets like the omega-limit sets of attractors and invariant circles are identified. Attractors in this system are found to possess chaotic characteristics, marked by approaches to specific invariant circles at a constant rate, accompanied by a diverse set of omega-limit sets. The system's phase space is characterized by a mix of these stable sets, with the attractors themselves displaying approaches to these sets at varying rates. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the system's behavior can be tailored to achieve the desired movements between these stable sets.

The gravitational-gauge theory relationship known as the double copy is a well established concept that links both scattering amplitudes and classical solutions, as well as suggesting its application to more complex, non-perturbative data. This study investigates the characteristics of manifolds in the gravitational field by proposing an alternative version of the double copy theory with a singular approach to gravitational properties, specifically focusing on the impact it has on multipoles and monopoles under this new framework.

This paper examines the statistical behavior of hooks divisible by a fixed integer $t$ within the partitions of $n$. We derive the probability distribution of hooks divisible by $t$, both exactly and asymptotically, and discuss similar results for $t$-cores and other $t$-related combinatorial properties in partitions. Additionally, we discuss how these findings can be applied to the study of random partitions. We compare our analytical methods with existing approaches and explore the asymptotic cases in more detail. We also investigate the statistical behavior of specific $t$-related properties such as the longest $t$-core and hooks within the partitions of $n$, and derive the probability distribution of $t$-cores in partitions of $n$.

Quantum particles experiencing tunneling can be studied by analyzing the interferograms produced when they pass through a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, where one of the arms contains a barrier that causes the particles to tunnel.  The effect of the barrier on the particles' phase during the tunneling process can be compared to their phase advancement based on their group velocity, a concept related to the Larmor precession of associated magnetic dipoles.  By equating these phase advancements with one another, a mathematical formula expressing the ratio of the barrier's width to the quantum wave function's decay length describes the tunneling process.  The wave function's decay length is calculated as being twice as long as the Larmor precession time multiplied by the group velocity.  The phase advancement due to the barrier corresponds with the part of the Thomas-Fermi model that considers the barrier's classical width, rather than its quantum properties.  The phase can also be studied using the Heisenberg group's curvature, where this phase can be seen as resulting from a particle moving along a geodesic on the two-dimensional complex plane, where the curvature is seen as contributing to the particle's tunneling time.  The relationship between the Thomas-Fermi model and the Heisenberg group's formalism is also explored.

This research investigates the leading twist distribution amplitudes of P-wave non-relativistic mesons, demonstrating that at a leading order approximation, these amplitudes can be represented by a single, universal function, irrespective of specific meson types. Empirical evidence suggests that leading twist distribution amplitudes of 1^3P0 and 1^3P2 mesons are linked by a linear relationship. Our findings support the concept that lattice-gauge-theory can be used to determine the universal function, thereby providing a connection between amplitudes of relativistic and non-relativistic mesons.

Researchers have long believed that quantum mechanics is strictly linear, with linear evolution and unitary observables. However, recent findings in three-level systems suggest that this is not the case, especially when contextuality is considered. It has also been found that leveraging non-linear quantum mechanics holds promise for quantum computing, interferometry, and information processing. Our work presents a complete set of two-qubit non-local observables capable of detecting any arbitrary quantum state, similar to the Bell inequalities. Notably, previous studies have proposed an all-linear Bell inequality, known as the Clauser-Horne-Shor-Simmons inequality, to demonstrate quantum mechanics nonlocality. In contrast, we identify certain non-local observables unable to distinguish classical and quantum states, while others do so uniquely. Our research offers insights into the characteristics of non-local observables and provides insights into the potential applications of non-linear quantum mechanics.

The extended BMS algebra generated by supertranslation and superrotation vector fields at null infinity is predicted to be the symmetry algebra of the quantum gravity S-matrix. However, determining the algebra of quantized extended BMS charges has proven challenging. Recent advancements in celestial holography indicate a connection between impact parameters of graviton scattering and celestial leading photons. Leveraging this insight, we successfully quantize the extended BMS charges and find them expressed in terms of differential forms on the space of impact parameters. Notably, the resulting quantization does not introduce any algebraic complications, and the extended BMS algebra retains its simple form.

Learning with an ever-growing number of categories poses significant challenges, particularly when models encounter new classes after being fully trained, at which point adding new training data may be impractical. The solution to this issue is continual learning, especially effective when using online settings where examples are presented one by one. The idea of reusing previously seen data to aid in learning subsequent categories dates back to 1969, with Marshall Marshall Cresswell and Alan Rosen proposing this approach in his seminal work. The authors discovered that reusing the initial set of examples while learning subsequent categories leads to improved results. The experiments presented in the article demonstrate the effectiveness of this method and compare it to other online algorithms for continual learning.

In metric geometry, a discussion revolves around generalized Riemannian manifolds, and Einstein's vacuum field equations can be expressed as a specific gradient-like vector field. This discussion will focus on metric geometries from both a Riemannian and Finslerian perspective.

In the wake of several recently constructed permutation polynomials over finite fields with square orders, our focus shifts to analyzing permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders through a detailed examination of their coefficients. Utilizing the multivariate method and resultant elimination techniques, we establish novel categories of sparse permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders, with various degrees of completeness, for any $q=p^{k}$ where the prime $p$ exceeds $2$.

Approximately $4$ billion individuals worldwide are affected by intestinal
parasites. The health risks associated with these infections encompass a broad
range of serious health issues such as malnutrition, anemia and various types
of disease in individuals from birth to adulthood. This research aims to develop
a model to identify intestinal parasite infections in children by collecting and
analyzing data from the Bayan-Ovoo sum of Gobi-Altai province, which includes
taking stool samples for each child and recording relevant symptoms and signs.
The study employs a machine learning technique known as a Random Forest algorithm
to train the model and achieve high accuracy in predicting intestinal parasite
infections using the data collected.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. To calculate the Nash equilibrium, a Markov chain approximation approach and a dynamic programming technique are used to solve nonlinear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. Numerical examples demonstrate the efficacy and accuracy of the proposed method.

This research presents a novel approach to developing a Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) controller for stabilizing a quadcopter's roll and pitch angles in real-time. We have successfully designed a roll-pitch PIDA control system, integrated it with a stabilizing flight control system, and tested its effectiveness using a quadcopter equipped with a Raspberry Pi 4 computer. We have evaluated the control algorithm's performance, determining its optimal gains through accelerated learning methods and subsequent trial flights. The results demonstrate the control system's capability to rapidly stabilize the quadcopter's roll and pitch angles at an average rate of 1.03 seconds.

A comprehensive examination of low-energy interactions between pions and nucleons is provided,
with discussions of key processes and theories, such as pion-nucleon scattering, pion production,
and the pion-deuteron reaction. Chiral effective field theory serves as a theoretical framework.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking interactions left by high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector, with its four layers, helps to pinpoint the origin of these interactions. Upgrade work on the detector's front-end readout system and on-detweet signal processing has been completed, along with off-detetent data analysis tools and infrastructure. Development of a dedicated readout board, called Fine Mechanical System, continues.

This study centers around Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) within the local volume to better understand how black holes influence galaxy evolution across various sizes and morphological types. By employing the 2MASS All-Sky Near-infrared Source Catalog to identify near-infrared sources and the Hyperleda Catalog of galaxies to match these sources with their host galaxies, a complete catalog of 1848 galaxies containing 1847 black holes across 14 different subtypes was compiled within a specific luminosity range. This comprehensive catalog includes morphological information on the host galaxies, enabling an analysis of their diverse shapes and sizes. The findings reveal a higher prevalence of blue and bulge-dominated galaxies among less luminous AGNs and a stronger presence of spiral and pseudobulge galaxies. Conversely, luminous AGNs are more often associated with elliptical galaxies. The study's focus on the local volume ensures highly accurate measurements, and the comprehensive nature of the catalog allows for the first time a detailed look at the relationship between AGNs and their host galaxies across various morphological types.

High-energy heavy-ion collisions involve various Nucleon-Nucleon (NN) scattering processes. To gain a better understanding of these processes, it is essential to consider the influence of nuclear short-range correlations (SRC) that affect large-scale NN scattering parameters and scale-dependent cross-sections. This study examines how SRC modify the kinematic enhancement factor for a particular NN channel and determine their effect on the overall kinetic energy and specific NN collision rate within a nucleus. Utilizing a theoretical model, it was found that for a particular NN channel, the correlation due to $d_{05}$ can result in a significant increase in the associated cross-section of approximately 20%, 30%, and 40% at proton energies of 100 MeV, 200 MeV, and 300 MeV respectively. Furthermore, incorporating SRC into calculations of the nucleus' kinetic energy and total NN collision rate resulted in increased values of 9% and 25% respectively, when using a $d_{05}$ correlation parameter. This study also reveals that the effect of SRC on the total NN collision rate is highly energy-dependent.

Our research focuses on the application of complex scaling in neural networks, an innovative technique that allows complex numbers as scaling layers without compromising its representational capabilities.  We evaluated the value of complex scaling within the context of robustness and expressiveness, two critical aspects of neural networks, through a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical testing. The results indicate that complex scaling retains full flexibility while significantly enhancing robustness, outperforming traditional real-valued methods. Furthermore, our findings suggest that complex scaling can be used to achieve precise control over expressiveness, offering a more subtle and accurate tuning compared to existing methods.  We validated the efficacy of complex scaling on CIFAR10/100 and ImageNet datasets, and the associated code is available on GitHub.

The concept of saturation momentum plays a crucial role in large-$x$ QCD, particularly when considering processes at high energies. Although the saturation momentum is essential for understanding certain high-energy processes, specifically those at large $x$, its value remains poorly defined. In this work, we establish an expression for the gluon density that incorporates a saturation momentum, $Q_S(n)$, as a function of rapidity $n$. We then determine the uncertainty ranges for this saturation momentum. We utilize these findings to evaluate the $x$-dependent gluon density and calculate the probability distribution of $x$ at small $x$, comparing our results with available data and other theoretical predictions.

Using high-resolution spectra collected by the Subaru-Subaru Prime Focus Spectrograph, we analyzed the abundance of twelve chemical elements in 407 metal-poor stars with a magnitude range of 8.8 < i < 9.0 and a specific range of spectral characteristics. These stars have a wide range of metallicities spanning from -3 to -2.3, and our analysis focused on determining the abundance ratios of twelve chemical elements, including iron, in these stars. Additionally, we studied the variability of these abundance ratios, known as [X/Fe] scatter, in these stars. Our analysis revealed a significant [X/Fe] scatter among dwarf and subgiant stars with a mean intrinsic scatter of 0.04 to 0.11 depending on the elements. Our results also show a strong metallicity dependence in the [alpha]-elements, suggesting a significant increase in the [alpha]-elements at low metallicities compared to the iron-peak and s-process elements. Our analysis of the [r/a] abundance ratios in these stars also indicates a significant mean excess, approximately 0.12 dex, and a positive correlation with metallicity. Our results are consistent with an external galaxy merger explanation for the observed [r/a] abundance ratios in these stars. Our analysis of the [C/Fe] abundance ratios in these stars also shows a significant mean excess, approximately 0.12 to 0.20 dex, and a positive correlation with metallicity. Our results

A novel machine learning approach has been developed that identifies and measures the potential impact of omitted significant predictors on predictive models. The algorithm extends the capabilities of machine learning, enabling not only predictive tasks but also robust inference and sensitivity analysis. An empirical example demonstrates its practicality, showcasing its ability to be applied in data sets containing inherent uncertainty, such as educational assessment results. Through a case study, the method's value is illustrated in the field of large-scale computer-based testing for educational assessments, where the focus is on developing machine learning models for predicting general estimation formulas (GEFs) from a large data set of item response theory (IRT) variables. The results show that the predictive performance of machine learning models can be improved by considering the potential impact of influential predictors, thereby enhancing trust in their use for making decisions in real-world applications.

This study presents SQUID, an open-source tool for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. It utilizes PyTorch for the classical components, allowing for the creation of multiple quantum models that can be optimized with back-propagation. We demonstrate SQUID's capabilities by showcasing its implementation in two well-known classification tasks, where we compare its performance with the original classifiers. Furthermore, we provide a tutorial on utilizing SQUICAL in these tasks, highlighting its potential applications and future research directions.

Researchers have studied pointwise slant submanifolds in almost Hermitian manifolds. Specifically, they've focused on novel types of pointwise slant submanifolds in complex space forms. By doing so, they've resolved several key issues. To be precise, they've addressed the following: existence, classification, and findings related to a novel type of pointwise slant submanifold called non-Tzitzeica slant submanifolds in complex space forms.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop sensitive and efficient low-energy detectors that can operate at room temperature and are minimally maintained. Such detectors could range in weight from grams to kilograms and could detect nuclear recoil events triggered by various factors including neutron scattering, CEvNS, or interactions with dark matter. Ongoing research, including existing and planned studies, is being conducted to explore the practicality of this technique for multiple applications.

Our study delves into the behavior of active colloidal dimers in response to varying gradients of activity. The dimers can exhibit chemotaxis, where they're attracted to areas of higher activity, or chemorepulsion, where they're repelled from areas of higher activity. We've observed that the direction of this response is influenced by the relative rates at which the dimer's ends interact with their respective environments. Additionally, we've observed a non-intuitive behavior where dimerars can exhibit stable, long-lasting equilibrium positions at distances from these actin gradients. This equilibrium is caused by the dimer's response to the gradient being balanced due to its finite response speed. This research offers insights into understanding and predicting the behavior of active colloidal particles in various biological and chemical systems.

The researchers conducted a low temperature specific heat study on samples of $\delta$-doped MoSi$_2$Se four-layer structures with holes per sublayer being at a density of $e^2/h$ ($\approx$ 0.043, 0.030, and 0.011 meV/K) per Co atom per sublayer. Their findings matched those found via low-energy inelastic neutron scattering, a more advanced technique. Using angular resolved spectroscopy, they identified specific heat peaks at almost the expected Majorana mode locations. Combining these findings with computational modeling via exact diagonalization, they discovered that these peaks originated from the slow decay of magnetrorotons - bound states formed from the pairing of quasiparticles and collective magnetization fluctuations - at low energy and temperature. Notably, their data showed that these magnetrorotons have a significantly longer decay length at densities of $e^2/h$ ($\approx$ 0.043, 0.030, and 0.011 meV/K) per Co atom per sublayer, contrasting with earlier findings at these same densities.

Epidemics on massive contact networks pose significant challenges for analysis due to their intricate nature. This study creates a natural epidemic model on a network by dividing individuals into groups, allowing for a more manageable study within the confines of each cluster's dynamics. When clusters vary in size, the model yields diverse outcomes, depending on the larger cluster's activity and connection to smaller ones. By distinguishing and examining individual characteristics, the model successfully explains the varied patterns of outbreaks observed in previous studies. This framework offers a new approach for understanding complex epidemic trends on massive contact networks.

The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results as long as the underlying data model is accurate, but inaccuracies often arise due to instrumental, observational, and data processing issues.  To rectify model errors, CMB data are often processed through a simulation-based correction scheme known as optimal map-making.  This paper presents an alternative, iterative method for correcting the noise structure in CMB maps, distinct from the traditional maximum likelihood approach.  Our new technique transforms the data to match an updated, corrected data model learned from simulations at each iteration, an approach influenced by machine learning concepts like adversarial training.  When applied to realistic simulations of the Planck scanning strategy using an idealized detector model, our method demonstrates comparable performance to optimal map-making methods, but with significantly reduced computational costs.  Our implementation of this technique is available as the MAPMSI package through Python.

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be complicated by the context in which terms are taught, leading to misunderstandings between the teacher and the learner about the objects being referred to. We investigate the idea that referential ambiguity - situations where the teacher is unclear about which object they're pointing to - can hinder learning. We explore a simple scenario where the teacher uses a pre-trained visual model to identify the qualities of an object, then describes it as part of the teaching process. We compare two training methods for the learner: one where the learner uses the same visual model, and another with a smaller capacity that's trained alongside the teacher using self-supervised learning. We test the efficacy of these methods on the popular ZEST [1] dataset, extending it to three new tasks. Our results show that the learner with the smaller capacity performs similarly, and sometimes better, than the larger capacity learner. We discuss how this approach aligns with theories of effective teaching, such as explaining away to resolve referential ambiguity.

Quantum process tomography is crucial for building quantum computers, establishing quantum networks, and developing quantum sensors. Like state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel necessitates a massive number of measurements, exponentially increasing with the number of quantum bits in the channel. This work presents a new method to efficiently map the quantum channel without this exponential constraint, allowing it to be applied in multi-qubit channels. This method leverages a set of specially constructed quantum states called stabilizer states, whose matrix representations can be efficiently computed. This method has the potential to significantly decrease the number of measurements needed to characterize multi-qubit channels, making it more computationally feasible.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, along with formulating new conjectures that stem from numerical experiments.

The advent of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) holds great potential for transforming communications systems. By harnessing their adaptability and swift deployment capabilities, it becomes feasible to supply content in densely populated areas or regions lacking essential infrastructure. In this study, we explore a UAV model that serves a maximum number of users at various locations within a set time frame. To optimize content delivery, we develop a mixed-integer optimization model. However, this problem proves to be an NP-hard problem. Consequently, we propose a two-layer bi-level optimization framework to address it. In the first instance, we reduce the original problem to a two-layer quadratic program and introduce a surrogate function as an approximation. In the second instance, we extract linear key components from the surrogate function to create a convex optimization program. In this study, we utilize convex optimization to approximate the original problem. Simulation results show that our proposed solution yields superior performance compared to existing models.

The low-energy electronic structure of an unbiased bilayer graphene, characterized by quadratic dispersions at points K and K' and crossing of Fermi levels at points M and M', is investigated. It is shown that short-range interactions can trigger a density wave transition by breaking the glide symmetry, with resulting point group symmetry $D_{3h}/\mathbb{Z}_6$. The analysis, based on the functional renormalization group approach, reveals that the density wave transition is controlled by a non-Fermi liquid scaling near the critical density and that the effective Hamiltonian can be transformed into a fermionic form with a six-fold symmetry. The spectrum can be categorized into three distinct types: a six-fold degenerate state, a non-degenerate state with a gap, and a six-fold degenerate state with oppositely directed wavevectors. Additionally, it is found that the density wave transition can be accompanied by a symmetry-breaking phase, characterized by a non-trivial topological structure, in which the system's boundary can be transformed into a solenoid and all wavevectors along the edge are parallel to the edge's normal vector.

The molecular structure of a spherical Sc2TbN @ C80 fullerene was computed using Density Functional Theory with the Generalized Gradient Approximation method to obtain its electronic band structure. The study found that high-energy molecular orbitals made up by Sc and Tb impurities have a significant impact on the system's electronic band structure. The researchers observed a change in the system's electronic band structure with temperature, caused by a gradual increase in the energy of these impurity-made molecular orbitals. The movement of the Fermi level towards the higher energy side as the temperature rises also indicates a rise in the system's work function. The system's electronic band structure exhibits a symmetry that matches its high-spin five-magnetization state. The study found that the system's magnetic properties are maintained even at high temperatures, but the impurity-made molecular orbitals start to rise in energy at around 800 K, indicating a change in their hybridization pattern with the surrounding C80 cage electrons. The system's electronic band structure exhibits a mirror image symmetry that matches its high-spin five-magnetization state. The study concludes that the system exhibits a unique temperature-dependent behavior in its electronic band structure.

The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various non-IT objects, at its core. A key aspect in its functioning is secure data transmission, facilitated by encryption. Due to low-powered devices' limited processing capabilities, conventional encryption algorithms are impractical. A suitable alternative is elliptic curve cryptography, which, despite its relatively recent introduction, has become a preferred choice for secure data exchange. This paper assesses the current state of elliptic curve cryptography and presents an innovative implementation of the ecdh key exchange protocol on a raspberry pi 4 model. Additionally, it discusses the practical challenges and potential applications of this implementation within smart home settings.

The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum beating and has been effectively utilized in both atomic and spin qubit research. Conducting these measurements under the most efficient use of measurements possible is crucial, especially for large ensembles of qubits. In this study, we introduce a model-based approach for optimizing the efficiency of Ramsey measurements. The method we present is universally applicable and can be applied to various types of spin systems. We also examine the specific case of spin qubits found in silicon, providing detailed mathematical derivations and numerical simulations of the results. A key finding of our research is that the optimal measurement configuration often lies outside of the traditional set of measurements commonly used in laboratories, namely the x-y plane. By applying our method to a hypothetical qubit and incorporating the effects of decoherence, we find that the most efficient measurements tend to be those along the x-z plane. Furthermore, we show that the optimal measurement configuration can be robust against variations in the coherence times of these qubits and even the presence of noise. The research presented here provides a valuable framework for laboratory settings, offering a practical strategy for enhancing the overall performance of Ramsey measurements.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various spatial metrics, but they often have different theoretical underpinnings, leading to confusion in their applications. We propose the Gromov centrality family, derived from the excess of the triangle inequality within a geometric network embedding, and demonstrate its broad applicability across various metric-based centrality metrics. The Gromov centrality family seamlessly unifies different centrality metrics while accounting for their unique characteristics. Its calculation is straightforward, employing standard network embedding techniques, along with a triadic neighborhood examination, making it computationally efficient. The Gromov centrality family effectively addresses limitations in several prominent centrality metrics, and its applications to well-studied networks highlight its practical value in enhancing our understanding and management of complex networks.

The phenomenon of a spinning body in motion can be simplified by considering an azimuthally symmetric gravitational field, which averted the issue of equatorial plane alignment in motion. This led Newton to believe that a spinning body's gravitational effect increases with increasing distance and approach, much like a force proportional to the square of the radius. However, this misconception was corrected by considering an object's shadow, which falls short of reaching a second-order approximation as predicted by Newton's original model. The corrected model was then compared against the findings of Newton's model and the work of other mathematicians, including Lagrange and Maclaurin.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in the 1990s, the theory initially relied on a computationally difficult method for structure determination. This paper showcases the application of a more efficient algorithm, initially used for classification, as a standalone tool for identifying bundles. Due to its computational advancements, this algorithm allows for handling larger systems. Real-world problems, such as signal processing, have been successfully analyzed using the method.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg has the potential to offer new insights into string compactifications. By using T-duality on torus bundles, known as almost abelian solvmanifolds, it can be demonstrated that this framework captures the target space geometry, even for non-flat connections. A specific 3d and 4d string compactifications case study was conducted, and the $C^*$-algebra T-dual of the local geometry was calculated. The resulting T-duals were identified as noncommutative toroidal orbifolds, characterized by specific algebraic $C^*$-subalgebras. This work lays the groundwork for a comprehensive mathematical examination of string compactifications via $C^*$-algebra T-duality.

We have developed a novel embedding technique that translates any tetrahedral graph T1 into another tetrahedral graph T2 with a certain structural characteristic. Specifically, T2 can be constructed such that it contains an essentially identical copy of T1 along with an added set of edges connecting all its vertices. The time complexity of this embedding algorithm is directly proportional to the number of vertices in T1. A significant consequence of this technique is that it provides an alternative proof for a well-established result in graph theory, namely that graphs with a certain degree of connectivity and a limited tree width can be efficiently embedded in a three-dimensional space while preserving their original connections. In particular, this technique allows us to achieve an exponential improvement in time complexity over existing methods for a specific class of graphs with a limited tree width. The underlying idea of our technique is that it allows us to efficiently generate an order of vertices for a specific type of three-dimensional graph structure such that when the vertices are ordered from smallest to largest, the distances between any two vertices are essentially linearly related to their positional difference.

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing theory states that asymptotic behavior is dictated by the slowest-converging center manifold. In this study, we present counterexamples that challenge this notion by introducing scenarios where the asymptotic behavior is determined by an arbitrary, specifically chosen subset of converging centers. We further illustrate the smoothness sensitivity of these dynamical systems with regard to their parameters.

We have developed a novel approach to apply the density matrix renormalization group method efficiently within the parquet renormalized equation of motion, which describes the dynamics of interacting many-body systems in the flat band Kyoto model. This advancement enables the DMRG method to handle systems with thousands of sites by switching from fermionic to qubit-based excitation modes, which significantly reduces computational costs associated with the latter. Our research showcases the effectiveness of this approach through successful simulations of the interplay between electron-electron interactions and topological ordering in the Kyodo model, where we compute time-dependent correlation functions with high precision. This case study highlights the significant potential of the PR-EoM method in understanding the effects of weak electron-electron interactions on topological ordering at the level of quantum fluctuations.

Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are a leading approach for learning probabilistic models, but often face challenges due to the conflicting objectives of balancing inference and representation quality. We propose a novel framework called the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD), an autoencoder variant that reverses the optimization order to refine the decoder while fixing the encoder. This results in DGD being optimized solely for the decoder, similar to generative models, with the added benefit of improved inference through the learned encoder. Our experiments demonstrate that DGD outperforms VAEs in both representation and inference capabilities, with the added benefit of requiring no additional hyperparameter tuning for inference optimization. Furthermore, DGD can be used as a versatile tool for identifying suitable priors for VAEs.

The detection of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background could significantly impact the cosmological expansion timeline. To account for this, researchers have modified the cosmological model to incorporate a primordial gravitational-wave background with an unknown amplitude. They then used data from the Planck satellite and BAO measurements, as well as the Hubble constant's currently accepted value, while imposing constraints on dark energy properties using ADAMANT. This setup allowed for a first-order approximation of the background's amplitude. They found that incorporating this variation resulted in a slight change to the base cosmological parameters, with the added constraint of the background's amplitude at approximately 1.0 times the expected value. They further determined that including this variation would result in a small change to the predicted matter density, with the added constraint of the background's amplitude weakening this effect. However, this alteration did not substantially impact the predicted uncertainty ranges for the model's other parameters.

Our study presents the initial findings from a survey of molecular emissions 
originating from the inner coma of comet C/2015 ER61 (PANSTARRS), a highly active
tailless comet observed by the ALMA millimeter continuum camera at 346 GHz. 
Our observations, conducted between April 6-8, 2017 when the comet was approximately
300 million kilometers from Earth, revealed the presence of H$_2$O and CO in its jet
emissions, as well as HCN, CS, and CH$_3$OH in their thermal continuum emissions. 
Our data, combined with the observations of H$_2$O and CO, suggest a water release
rate of 2 x 10$^{28}$ molecules per second and a gas production profile featuring
extremely high and variable emission rates for H$_2$O and CO. Our analysis of the
gas morphology and line fluxes indicates that the detected species have similar
directions of motion and distribution patterns, pointing to a source of gas located
near the nucleus's surface and a gas outflow velocity of approximately 0.5 km/s.
Our results also imply that the detected species have similar and extremely low
escape velocities, suggesting a shared mechanical explanation. Our data further
suggest that the detected species have similar and extremely low abundance ratios
with respect to H$_2$O, indicating a shared chemical origin. Our observations of
