In this study, the concept of optimal channel mixing is reevaluated using the principles of quantum ergotropy and the principles of anticoaching, which have been shown to lead to the same investment strategy as previously proposed. Our analysis also highlights the importance of the underlying quantum system's dynamics for optimizing returns and suggests that the expected return can be maximized by considering the conditional probabilities of events given the outcomes of their opposites.

Building on the recently created two-dimensional semiconductor MoSi$_2$N$_4$, our comprehensive study of monolayer compounds MA$_2$X$_4$ involves in-depth analysis of their band structure and excitons using ab initio GW and Bethe-Salpeter equation calculations. In contrast to the predictions of density functional theory, the results of our GW calculations indicate much larger band gaps and quasiparticle energies that are distinct in absolute value but share the same band alignment configurations.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

The traditional view of protoplanetary disk formation assumes a steady, laminar gas flow.
However, real-world conditions are often turbulent due to the Rossby vortices at the
gas density peaks triggered by the corotation resonances that form at specific orbital
radii. A specific mass flux through the disk determines the distribution of matter.
Research has shown that, in the early stages of disk development, high-mass flow rates
cause the Rossby vortices to collapse, and in the later stages, they reform into giant
swirling structures. These structures can either be destroyed by the gas density peaks or
survive as massive whirlpools with masses up to 10 million times that of Jupiter. 
These formations can either be the starting point for the growth of giant planets or the
merging of smaller ones.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, at an angle other than directly towards the horizon, require correction using Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Currently, CDS holds the exclusive rights to the French-Canadian ADC design which, although effective, needs improved documentation and enhanced production. Our project aims to automate the production of these correctors by creating a pioneering software. Our software, ADCcalc, calculates and generates parameters necessary for ADC production, including the optical path, density of glass, and corresponding refractive indices. It also allows for the simulation and verification of these parameters against ASPIe standards. Our software was tested with the known values from the Binoscope ADC and found accurate to 0.01% in terms of optical power and 0.01 arcseconds in image widening.

This paper presents a novel hierarchical latent variable model designed to capture patterns in multi-period time series data. The proposed HLM, an extension of the hidden Markov model, incorporates belief states that aggregate multiple observations. We employ a variational EM algorithm for parameter estimation and develop an inference method to assess model parameters by approximating their distribution. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in modeling and making predictions across diverse applications, including stock prices, Google Flu, and solar energy output.

In a setting that combines both discrete and continuous mathematics, discrete groups can be seen as specific types of topological groups where the topological structure is essentially trivial. By viewing such groups within broader topological group frameworks, Pontryagin duality emerges as a strong theoretical tool. By comparing it to the Bohr compactification, we gain further insights, a process that also highlights distinct characteristics exhibited by discrete groups in this context. These findings are then compared with the more general situation of compact groups, yielding new perspectives on Stone duality through the incorporation of partial maps and the use of pseudoalgebras within the context of point-free toplogy.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality achieved within this FL framework, thereby facilitating optimal model development in line with specified ethical objectives.

A supersymmetric model involving a Z_4 symmetric SO(10) gauge group is investigated, 
in which three standard flavor neutrinos and one isospin symmetric dark matter right-handed neutrino 
are included. This scenario yields a dark matter candidate with a naturally correct relic density. 
Our analysis shows that by adjusting one parameter, the dark matter right-handed neutrino's mass can be made 
sub-Smooth Particle Collapse Model (SPCM) and even inelastic in nature, thereby evading LHC search constraints. 
This inelasticity arises from the mixing with a light Higgsino, and our findings indicate that with the correct dark matter mass 
and inelasticity, both the decay width and underproduction of dark matter can be resolved. This model's distinctive feature 
is a baryogenesis mechanism involving the dilution of primordial B and CMB anisotropes due to the dark matter right-handed neutrino's 
inelasticity, and consequently, the matter anti-matter asymmetry is reduced.

This research delves into a wireless-powered network that comprises an access point, multiple energy-receiving devices, and a smart reflecting surface. The network operates in two stages: the initial phase involves the AP transmitting energy signals to the devices via the smart surface, with energy subsequently harvested by the devices. The subsequent phase entails the AP transmitting data to the devices via the smart surface. Given the absence of prior knowledge, an optimization problem is formulated to maximize long-term network throughput by simultaneously optimizing energy transfer and data transmission. A deep reinforcement learning approach is employed to tackle this optimization challenge. A neural network is designed to encode the parameters of a buffer function, which is optimized via reinforcement learning to maximize long-term network throughput. The results demonstrate that this approach yields considerable gains in throughput while reducing computational complexity.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, alongside the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by incorporating a combination of prolate and oblate configurations independently in the parent and daughter nuclei. Prolate components dominated both parent and daughter nuclei for the experimental beta strength, while an upper limit was set for the oblate component in the parent state. To analyze the experimental data, a new method was developed to deconvolve the combined strength functions of the parent and daughter states.

We examine the intersection of particle dark matter and leptogenesis theories, assuming the presence of a hidden sector that includes not one but two hidden gauge groups generating DM interactions. This setup also yields massier right-handed neutrinos, sufficient to generate the baryon asymmetry of the universe through the CP-violating processes of neutrino-antineutrino differences, even in the presence of dark radiation to regulate the total baryon and dark matter densities. The existence of dark matter is confirmed when its effective mass exceeds the weak scale, and the required dark matter parameter values are within attainable range for current and future experiments. This model offers a unique test of the interplay between particle dark matter and leptogenesis theories, and the predicted dark matter annihilation cross-sections are within the sensitivity of future experiments like LHC and CMB experiments.

We have developed an efficient control method for complex systems with unknown dynamics that utilizes additional data and state feedback. Our approach involves creating an internal model of the system through an agent learning from observations, and then using this information to guide state and action decisions. We prove that this method results in optimal long-term outcomes and provide statistical analysis of the model's accuracy. Furthermore, we have adapted this technique for use in multi-agent settings, and our approach can still offer benefits even if the system's dynamics are known. Our results show that this method allows individual agents to achieve better outcomes when working together, and we verify the effectiveness of our approach through various simulations.

A comprehensive framework is developed for Toda conformal field theories, incorporating key symmetries and deformations. Specifically, we identify W-algebras as categories encompassing multiple modules, establish a universal property for the categories of W-algebras under suitable deformations, and demonstrate that these deformations are equivalent to certain central extensions with radical 1/2. Furthermore, we show that the categories of both classical and diagonal Toda field theories are marked by the presence of nontrivial inner actions, thereby facilitating a discussion on their completion with respect to these extended inner actions. Ultimately, we outline the implications of our findings for the representation theory of the extended diagonal W-algebra.

Despite significant advancements in producing realistic images with GANs, a primary concern remains training these models on high-resolution inputs, as they are prone to vanishing during optimization due to vanishing gradients. To overcome this limitation, research has focused on using weight clipping for the discriminator, as it allows for more stable training and generation of high-resolution images. However, previous efforts have resulted in significantly degraded performance when evaluated using the FID score, a measure of photorealism and diversity. To address this challenge, we introduce a new approach that utilizes a multi-resolution discriminator with both local and global perception, enabling the model to pinpoint inconsistencies at both a large scale and individual pixel level. This approach provides robust gradient flow and enables the training of GANs on high-resolution inputs, as demonstrated by our experiments. The results show that our approach significantly outperforms previous methods, offering more stable training and higher quality image generation. The training curriculum we developed also highlights the importance of high-resolution inputs for training GANs.

A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been proposed. This approach bypasses the necessity for phase locking by utilizing an unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometer to generate an auto-correlation signal. We examined the impact of various signal loss rates on key distribution efficiency and discovered that our method can maintain efficient quantum communication capabilities even when the signal experiences significant loss, as long as the automatic phase correlation remains effective. To further improve the method's robustness, we developed an iterative algorithm to mitigate the impact of multi-peaks resulting from source frequency instability and fiber phase fluctuations. This algorithm, supported by simulation data, shows that its benefits persist even in cases of extreme fiber phase fluctuations. By combining the proposed method with existing techniques, we are now able to establish a practical phase locking-free quantum key distribution system that enables secure communication over long distances.

In the realm of Banach algebras with identity, we explore the properties of Toeplitz algebras, specifically those generated by compact sets in complex spaces, as well as the algebras of bounded uniformly continuous functions on compact sets in complex spaces. It's established that Toeplitz algebras with an identity exist for specific compact sets, and a direct relationship is shown between the algebra of bounded uniformly continuous functions and Toeplitz algebras with an identity. Furthermore, a unitary version of Toeplitz algebras, associated with groups in complex spaces, is also considered and a key identification is proven between the algebras of bounded uniformly continuous functions and Toeplitz algebras with an identity.

Recent advancements in object detection have led to complex models that deliver exceptional performance, yet require substantial computational power and human labor. Generalizing these models to less documented classes proves challenging. To address this issue, Zero Shot Detection methods have been developed to recognize objects from less common classes without the need for human annotation or external training. We explore the feasibility of applying pre-trained language models with metric learning to detect less known entities. We test and evaluate four distinct approaches, each incorporating one or more of the following: enhanced feature extraction, improved detection methods, and Pytorch APC, on two datasets, Waymo Open Dataset and KITTI. Our results show that each approach outperforms the previous state-of-the-art when all classes are used, and that two of the methods deliver comparable performance when rare classes are removed from the Waymo Open Dataset.

The interstellar medium in molecular clouds has distinct photon-dominated regions (PDRs) where the gas and particles are primarily influenced by external starlight. Analyzing PDRs in these clouds can offer valuable insights into the surrounding environment. To better comprehend the structure of PDRs, we developed a computational model called PAHTLET, which simulates how PDRs evolve over time by simulating the interaction of gas and dust particles under various radiation intensities. Our model uses an adaptive grid system to efficiently process complex algorithms and accounts for the movement of particles through a PDR. Our simulations revealed that PDRs initially take on a cone-like shape, and as they expand, they develop a more complex structure with multiple density peaks and gradients, influenced by dust particles and radiation intensity. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of PDR morphology and evolution, which can be applied to observations of interstellar clouds, such as the Taurus-Auriga cloud.

The impressive results of Transformer models on limited-data conditions have sparked interest in our field to understand the underlying reasons. This success can be attributed to two key innovations of Transformer models - multi-head self-attention and multi-layer architectures. This paper presents a new insight by demonstrating that multi-head self-attention itself achieves a property of retaining essential information while disregarding non-essential information. We also show that previous studies of Transformer models have overlooked the crucial effect of multi-layer architectures. To validate our new perspective, we conduct a series of experiments to examine the effect of multi-layer architectures using real-world data. The outcome confirms our new hypothesis and provides valuable insights for the design of future Transformer models.

Mortality forecasting models built on the classical factor framework, such as the Lee-Carter model and its variants, often overlook the complex interactions among the multiple factors influencing mortality rates. These factors, including age, period, cohort, and region, exhibit significant interconnectedness, making interactive structures crucial for understanding mortality dynamics. In this study, a novel method for structuring interactions among multiple factors is introduced, coupled with an ensemble approach to modeling, which integrates the expertise of both theoretical and empirical analysts. An extended version of the Lee-Cattern model is developed to accommodate multi-dimensional factors, and an ensemble approach is implemented to capture the uncertainty inherent in expert judgments. The proposed method is validated using German mortality data and shown to be effective in enhancing accuracy and capturing mortality trends.

A major challenge within the neural architecture search field is efficiently exploring the vast design space of neural networks. The problem becomes more complex when conducting architecture search on large, distributed systems, as requiring each model to be trained and evaluated separately with each configuration is impractical. A potential solution to this issue is to develop novel architecture search approaches that can operate on distributed systems, such as the Ray platform, as exemplified by the NoLayover approach. NoLayover is a population-based architecture search method that operates on distributed Ray nodes by assigning each child model to a different node, with models sharing the same hyperparameters contributing to the same parent model. The relationship between the number of parent models and shared hyperparameters was observed, with increased sharing leading to reduced variability between child models. Based on this insight, a modified search strategy, dubbed ShareNet, was developed to prioritize models with higher shared parameter counts during population-based updates. Theoretical analysis revealed that reduced variability between child models leads to larger steps in the search space, with empirical results confirming the benefits of ShareNet, as it enables the training of larger models on the same hardware as population-based architecture search methods, such as Evolutionary Architecture Search, while achieving performance superior to state-of-the-art models when tested on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets.

Time series data in various scientific disciplines are analyzed using multiple techniques. One widely used approach involves extracting features from these data to create models, which can then be employed for classification and other predictive tasks. Research has been active in this area for many years. Recently, some studies have aimed to develop universally applicable and flexible feature extraction methods. These efforts often rely on generic, algorithm-only approaches. Our work introduces a novel framework that combines a learning method for feature extraction with an algorithmic approach. This hybrid approach, called HyTE, offers greater flexibility and a more intuitive way of extracting features, which can also be used for backward feature elimination. Our experiments with over 600 series demonstrate that HyTE outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and robustness.
We identify concrete, infinitely precise criteria under which a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space has a semistable fundamental group at its boundary.

Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an essential component that helps ensure the quality of translations and promotes the translation process. Despite its importance, TQA is often viewed as an afterthought, and its efficiency is hampered by relying on manual evaluations by non-expert reviewers. This paper argues that TQA can be improved by utilizing expert reviewers, whose evaluations can be incorporated into a quantitative system to provide reliable assessments. To test this approach, a study was conducted involving three translation projects to investigate the effectiveness of combining expert evaluations with statistical analysis for accurate translation quality assessment. Using robust statistical methods, the study was able to generate reliable results, which were found to be significantly less susceptible to the limited number of reviews compared to previous methods. By applying robust statistics, the study was able to provide more reliable results that reflected actual translation quality, which was found to be inferior in two of the projects and mediocre in the third.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas for maximizing this correlation, and under certain conditions, it leads to the discovery of the optimal form of the scattering matrix, which surprisingly reveals uniform radiation within the scattering volume when one input wave drives all outcomes. These findings have implications for cases where radiation patterns are restricted, such as point sources, and provide a criterion to evaluate existing strategies for enhancing random depostion within limits.

We've developed a novel pruning technique that effectively reduces complex neural network dimensions within a given weight range. Our approach has achieved notable outcomes on both MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, yielding improved performance after re-training a significantly reduced version of a CNN. Our findings indicate that the structures of the remaining network connections differ significantly from those of the original networks. We have established a new method for generating sparse, high-quality sub-networks and discovered the inherent properties of these sub-networks. Our research suggests that the remaining connections exhibit spatial organization patterns, where related tasks are mapped to nearby network neurons. We have demonstrated that the structure of the sub-networks generated by our technique exhibits better task separation properties compared to the original networks.

In lotteries with extremely large participant numbers and high prize payouts per ticket, a mathematical framework is developed to analyze the behavior of lottery winners as the number of players approaches infinity. By contrasting the behavior of lotteries where multiple winners are possible and impossible, this study reveals how the likelihood of shared winners impacts the expected return on a lottery ticket. Additionally, the impact of different methods for resolving ties among winners on the expected outcome of a lottery ticket is examined. It is shown that in some lotteries, winning multiple times is possible, while in others it's inevitable, and in yet another scenario, the probability of winning multiple times is infinitesimally small but not zero. By deriving formulas for the expected value of a lottery ticket in each case, this paper challenges a common assumption that winning the lottery is solely a matter of luck, as the results suggest that in very large lotteries, the outcomes can also be influenced by the method used to determine the winners.

The large-charge expansion technique opens up a new avenue in the study of $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetry and Yang-Mills theory. By analyzing the flow of data in a specific direction within the Wilson 't Hooft loop, it becomes possible to compute critical properties of operators in the $\mathcal{O}_{\Delta\pm\delta}$ supermultiplet with a high degree of accuracy. At the sixth loop order, the technique allows for the inclusion of more complex operators, which have five or more legs, in the calculation of their respective anomalous dimensions. As a result, it becomes possible to compute the values of the respective six-loop critical exponents to six-digit precision. Furthermore, the technique allows for the computation of the respective critical dimensions at the sixth loop order. Notably, the computed values of the respective critical exponents show a remarkable consistency with the predictions made using the AdS/CFT correspondence.

Our research examines how mechanical deformations influence the valley Hall effect in two-dimensional materials with combined spin and valley chirality. We find that anisotropic strain, being a gauge field-like phenomenon, is ineffective in inducing valley Hall responses on its own. However, when combined with other effects, such as spin Hall or valley Hall responses due to valley-dependent spin-orbit interactions or magnetic fields, it significantly amplifies the resultant Hall responses. Additionally, the presence of strain is shown to significantly amplify the spin Hall response in two-dimensional materials, particularly when the strain is directed along the material's cross-axis. This has the potential to greatly increase the size and direction of the spin Hall effect in two-dimensional materials, thus making them even more valuable for practical applications.

The goal of unsupervised domain adaptation in semantic segmentation involves accurately segment images from a source domain while considering an unknown distribution of labels. To tackle this, a novel approach called Mean Teacher for semantic segmentation across domain boundaries is developed, leveraging the benefits of pseudo-labeling and knowledge distillation. This method employs a teacher model to generate more refined pseudo-labels within the source domain, which are used for training the student model. By incorporating a mean teacher approach, model ensemble and knowledge diffusion enable improved performance by averaging student and teacher representations, thus diffusing knowledge throughout the student model. This MT-DAD approach exhibits superior results on multiple semantic segmentation adaptation datasets and outperforms existing domain adaptation methods. The code for MT-DAD is freely accessible on GitHub under the repository 'MT-DAD-SSDA'.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise does not hold in cases where data contains structured or man-made dependencies, such as linear relationships. This research presents an alternative approach, incorporating prior knowledge into t-SNE. Diverse prior knowledge sources can be integrated, including anatomical or biological expectations. The framework remains flexible, permitting the incorporation of various prior knowledge types and multiple source signals. The method was validated using three distinct datasets from the Functional Magnetic Resional Imaging Rehabilitation Mapping Database (fMRI-RMBD). These datasets contain high-dimensional data with pre-defined anatomical labels. The performance of the proposed approach was compared to the standard t-SNE in visualizing brain regions across different subjects, with results demonstrating the superior efficacy of the novel method.

Our comprehensive analysis, based on a two-dimensional system of weakly interacting fermions interacting with a single hole through short-range interactions, reveals the characteristics of the model's ground state as the coupling strength varies. By employing a theoretical framework that combines a variational approach and a systematic expansion, we map out the ground state's behavior as a function of the coupling strength, demonstrating a seamless transition from the fermi polaron regime to the fermi hole regime. Notably, the model's ground state exhibits an intermediate regime, characterized by the presence of two distinct polaron hole ground states, whose properties are determined by intricate many-body interactions.

In the hybrid digital-analog architecture for near-term quantum computing, we've developed a new approach to simulate fermionic systems by combining digital qubit operations with analog fermionic coupling. The key challenge lies in the destructive interference that occurs when attempting to implement a single gate, caused by unwanted interactions between adjacent particles. By examining the fermonic coupling patterns, we've identified the most suitable qubit connectivity for simulating fermionic systems efficiently. We've demonstrated this through a theoretical analysis and an experimental implementation, showing that an anisotropic two-dimensional lattice yields the maximum scaling advantage compared to a linear chain. Furthermore, our experiment successfully simulates fermionic spin using only two fermionic modes, while accurately modeling the destructive interference effect and accurately generating non-linear interactions between these modes.

Graph polynomials hold great significance due to their potential to develop novel computer algorithms and their connection to graph characteristics. Evaluating the chromatic polynomial at -1 yields a count of the number of independent sets within the graph. The study of all graphs weighted by this polynomial, known as C-polynomials, is restricted to those weighing vertices equally. The purpose of this paper is to explore the relationship between these polynomials and the graph's structure. It begins with a theorem that identifies the minimum number of C-polynomials necessary for any weighted graph. The investigation then focuses on identifying the type of graph that yields the minimum number of such polynomials, known as MC-polynomials, which is found to be singletons for most cases. The study further analyzes when a C-polynomial can be expressed as a product of two polynomials, revealing that this condition is met for at least 75% of all simple graph weightings.

We derive an expression for the Hitchin connection on the moduli space of genus g curves equipped with a transverse section of the second power of the canonical bundle, thus generalizing results from G\"ortler, Kemp, and Laura's work on the twisted Hitchin connection.

The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of remote working, necessitating a deeper understanding of the emotional and psychological dynamics involved. To structure the necessary support from leaders and highlight its benefits, this research develops a theoretical framework grounded in the Self-Determination Theory. It identifies three fundamental human needs that are critical for enhancing employee well-being in a remote working setting. The framework also outlines the underlying processes and mechanisms through which leaders can influence employees' need satisfaction, as well as the key leader characteristics involved. Finally, the study provides recommendations for implementing the proposed framework in a post-pandemic context.

The concept of dichotomous matrices serves as an expanded interpretation of Hermitian matrices, with newly formulated guidelines identifying which arrowhead matrices fit this classification. Furthermore, specific conditions were derived to ensure unitary irreducibility of these matrices, and their maximum orthonormal vector count was calculated in relation to boundary numerical range, resulting in several novel findings.

In a study of the ALICE detector at the Large Hadron Collider, researchers investigated the elliptical movement of electrons created when beauty particles decay at a specific point near the center of collisions involving lead nuclei at a high energy of 5.02 TeV. These electrons, measured within a specific range of momentum, exhibited positive elliptical movement patterns. Calculations based on simulated data from lead-lead collisions indicated that the observed patterns could be primarily attributed to the elliptical movement of beauty particles within a medium. This finding provides new insights into how beauty quarks interact within this medium, suggesting that beauty quarks may retain information about its texture for a longer duration than previously estimated.

In pursuit of breakthroughs in the medical field, we analyze chromatic configurations in three-dimensional space, employing topological concepts. Leveraging techniques borrowed from image processing, we develop mathematically sound indicators to capture both fine-scale and broad-scale interplay among color categories. Our proposed methods enable fast computation by adapting techniques such as Delaunay tessellations and alpha-shapes for color mapping.

This paper addresses the problem of finding the most efficient power control strategy for multiple users sharing the same uplink in a Gaussian channel, with each user having its own transmission rate requirement. The goal is to maximize the network's overall transmission rate, subject to constraints on individual user rates. By analyzing the channel output signals as a Markov process, we derived an optimal power control formula that ensures all user rate requirements are met. The paper also investigates the performance limitations of suboptimal power control strategies and provides analytical bounds on their achievable transmission rates. The results show that as the number of users grows, the gain from using the optimal power control strategy over suboptimal approaches increases with the square root of the user population.

Auditing business processes often requires categorization of complex data, which can be effectively achieved through machine learning. However, conventional machine learning methods are non-explainable, meaning they don't provide insights into their decision-making processes. In this research, we focus on developing and applying explainable categorization methods using the publicly available adult dataset from the U.S. Census Bureau. By comparing the accuracy and efficiency of different techniques, such as logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, and XGBoost, we demonstrate the importance of choosing an understandable model for auditing processes. Our study includes comprehensive analysis of how different categorization methods influence auditing outcomes.

The Strauss process is a point process, and its density relative to the Poisson process involves a term that weights the probability based on the number of pairs within a certain distance $r$ by the product of indicator functions representing those relationships. This analysis considers the density of the Strauss process for a general case where the weighting function has multiple components with specific distances $r_j$, and it's shown that the process's normalizing constant is difficult to calculate analytically, and numerical methods must be used to estimate its value. Furthermore, this research explores the convergence rates of these numerical methods, and it's observed that a maximum variation principle plays a key role in understanding these rates.

From a fundamental physics perspective, the Generalized Uncertainty Principle offers compelling evidence for the existence of inherent limits beyond which the laws of quantum mechanics cannot be applied. This notion implies the presence of unquantizable lengths, a concept that has not been thoroughly explored. Researchers have made significant advancements in understanding the physical implications of these limits, including their effects on matter distribution in space-time. This study delves into the observational consequences of these fundamental limits using the approach of modified gravity theories, specifically focusing on the implications for black hole space-times. We examine the properties of quasistatic objects and derive a mass-dependent limit on fundamental lengths. This study provides a roadmap for detecting the physical effects of these limits, which may manifest as small fractional changes in the gravitational redshift and time dilation associated with quasistatic objects.

Multitasking scheduling in service industries has gained significant attention over the past decade. A key assumption typically made is that the same machine is used throughout, however, this can lead to a substantial decrease in scheduling flexibility. In this research, we introduce a regional multitasking scheduling problem to model scheduling in regional networks, enabling jobs to be transferred between nearby locations. A practical algorithm is developed to tackle the problem and is evaluated through experiments on randomly generated data. Furthermore, we investigate the application of our proposed algorithm to real-world data collected from a prominent online platform.

A significant challenge in legged locomotion research is developing stability and robust motion control for non-combined dynamics, especially when interacting with dynamic and deformable environments. Existing reinforcement learning-based control methods often struggle with non-holonomic constraints, forcing the agent to compensate for these limitations. However, past studies have not effectively addressed the issue of compensating for these constraints during learning. To overcome these obstacles, a novel deep reinforcement learning method is proposed to control a legged robot's footsteps on deformable terrain. This approach involves utilizing a specific neural network to derive whole-body joint targets from a lower body perspective, enabling more efficient control and easier learning. As an alternative to end-effector control, using joint targets provides smaller action spaces and easier learning. Additionally, simulated data is used to demonstrate the method's ability to adapt to various terrain types it has not seen before, showcasing its potential for real-world application.

In the rapidly evolving landscape of Internet of Things (IoT) networks, periodic firmware updates are essential for maintaining optimal security and functionality. Given the sheer scale of IoT devices, these updates pose significant logistical challenges, necessitating careful evaluation of potential impacts on network performance. To address this issue, we propose a framework for assessing the consequences of firmware updates on IoT networks. By utilizing stochastic logic models for IoT device behavior, we analyze how different updates affect a network's Quality-of-Service (QoS) metrics, such as throughput, packet drop rate, and delay. This framework enables periodic assessments of network performance following firmware updates, providing critical insights for operators to assess the success of these updates.

We numerically in Investigate the real-space behavior of the Fock space self-energy in a one-dimensional quantum glass with non-local interactions, using a customized Monte Carlo dynamics that incorporates a customized Hilbert space. Our results reveal that the self-energy exhibits distinct phases, characterized by (i) localization, (ii) growth proportional to $\Delta t^3$, and (iii) growth proportional to $\Delta t^2$. We observe that the system remains self-localized in phase (i) and the associated decay rate is directly tied to the imaginary component of the self-energy. Moreover, the self-energy's magnitude in phase (ii) is dominated by the highest amplitude eigenmodes of the self-energy operator, which can be accurately described through a simplified model. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that these eigenmodes, characterized by high amplitudes and short lifetimes, can be directed towards localized modes and non-localized high-energy states. Interestingly, the transition to phase (iii), where the self-energy exhibits a $2/3$ dynamics, is marked by the emergence of a non-thermal distribution of energy where the highest energy states initially heat up at a rate proportional to $\Delta t^{2/3}$.

In the kBM-IGS problem, a query agent seeks navigation guidance from an omniscient information source by asking for edge labels, with the objective of finding the shortest path to a set of destinations (k landmarks) within an undirected graph. We examine the kBM-IGS problem and its adaptations, analyzing optimal strategies for selecting edge labels, navigating paths, and efficiently communicating with the guide. Our key contributions include identifying optimal parameter choices, developing algorithms with optimal or near-optimal performance, and establishing rigorous performance bounds that refine previous results for the 1BM-IGS problem.

In recent years, research has been conducted to analyze how artificial intelligence and machine learning can be enhanced at both theoretical and practical levels. One key aspect is determining whether certain machine learning tasks can be solved more efficiently using quantum computers or alternative processing methods. Additionally, some tasks may be better suited to hybrid approaches that leverage both classical and quantum computing capabilities. To explore this, an open-source library called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called called

This paper investigates Steklov eigenvalues in nearly spherical domains.  Given a three-dimensional domain, $B$, with the addition of a small, smooth perturbation, $H_\delta$, we demonstrate that there exists a diffeomorphism-invariant measure, $\delta$, below which a one-to-one correspondence exists between the eigenvalues of the perturbed and unperturbed domains.  This measure, $\delta$, is directly proportional to $\delta^{3+2k}$, where $k$ represents the $k^{th}$ perturbation order.  Importantly, this study provides the first known instance of a one-to-one correspondence between the eigenvalues of a sphere and a perturbed domain for any $k>0$.  We have specifically analyzed the case where $k=1$ and the perturbation, $H$, corresponds to the addition of a small vector field, $X$, onto the sphere, $B$.  We have shown that there exists an invertible transformation, $T$, mapping the eigenvalues, $\mu_i(B)$, to the eigenvalues, $\mu_{i^*}(B)$, where $i^*$ represents a mapping dependent on the vector field, $X$, and the parameter, $\delta$, for which the following inequality holds, $$\min_i |\mu_i(B)-\mu_{i^*}(B)|\leq C\sum_{i=1}^\infty (\mu_{i^*

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data.

Accurate prediction of radio wave coverage is essential for ensuring quality of service (QoS) delivery in wireless communications. Existing propagation models can be broadly classified into two types - empirical and deterministic models. Empirical models rely on established formulas and statistical data, while deterministic models employ geographically-specific terrain information. This paper presents a hybrid approach that integrates the strengths of both types of models. It combines an empirical WIM model for initial QoS assessment, and switches to a deterministic IDM model only for areas where the associated QoS threshold is at risk of being exceeded. The proposed algorithm determines the optimal survey intensity and spatial distribution required to enhance deep indoor penetration. This approach simplifies survey efforts by identifying areas where the least investment will yield the greatest returns. The model's efficacy is demonstrated through a case study of a massive multi-user OFDMA-based wireless system.

A straightforward syntax-based semantics is offered for temporal planning task descriptions, enabling a clear and straightforward definition of actions and their effects based on time constraints. This formulation is versatile and adaptable to various temporal logic-based temporal frameworks. Using a model-theoretic approach, we examine the semantic foundations of classical temporal planning without the added complexity of semantics for conditional operators. Our focus on classical semantics differs from the typical approach in AI, allowing for the examination of novel, but potentially more practical, solving methods. We establish connections between our work and traditional AI methods in two ways: by considering a light-weight form of action semantics that aligns with AI methods and by developing a model extraction algorithm to convert classical models into temporal networks, a representation commonly used in AI.

Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study examines the effect of five essential parameters - investment, operational, capacity market, regulation, and generator characteristics - on the accuracy of power system models, investigating the trade-offs between precision and computational efficiency. The results reveal that models sacrifice little efficiency for improved accuracy in critical parameter weighting, but efficiency declines significantly when accounting for all relevant factors. Additionally, the study finds that models can achieve accurate results under realistic weighting scenarios with a simplified parameterization of the French power system.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models within confined areas, under specified boundary conditions that include a particular reflection scenario for the Vlasov equation.

When processing change requests written in natural language, software developers encounter difficulties summarizing the requests and pinpointing the modified code areas.  A proposed machine learning-based system aims to address these challenges by utilizing deep text analysis to identify the request type, extracting key summary points, and determining the relevant subsystems for the requested changes.  To validate the system's effectiveness, an experiment was conducted on a dataset comprising 1,506 change requests drawn from three open-source software applications.  The results demonstrate that the proposed system excels in extracting key summary points and accurately identifies the relevant subsystems for a significant portion of the sample change requests, with performance comparable to existing research studies.

We investigate how an extremely low-frequency external sound wave affects a system composed of Brownian particles. When the sound wave is absent, the particles form a rigid, thixotropic gel. However, the presence of the sound wave causes its viscoelastic properties to change, specifically its dynamic shear behavior, even at extremely low frequencies. Additionally, the sound wave induces particle clustering due to the acoustic radiation pressure it generates, leading to clustering even in the absence of the sound wave when we consider time-averaged particle interactions. A comprehensive theoretical framework is established to understand the sound wave's impact on the system's static and dynamic properties.

This research paper investigates the validity of the Collatz conjecture for a certain set of odd sequences with an infinite number of elements, which is a statement about the existence of a number $n$ for which the sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3,...$ would enter an infinite loop of even numbers, thus violating the conjecture. Our study utilizes the concept of minimal sets in the Collatz function $\mathcal{C}(x)$ and examines the properties of two specific functions, $\mathcal{C}_3^*(x)$ and $\mathcal{C}_7^*(x)$, which emerge as a result of applying the Collatz conjecture to sets of odd numbers. By analyzing these functions, we show that any minimal set containing an element less than 5 can be accounted for in a simpler sequence, which provides a crucial insight into the minimal sets containing an element greater than 5. Ultimately, our analysis leads to the conclusion that the Collatz conjecture is valid for a certain set of odd sequences with an infinite number of elements.

To effectively organize digital collections and facilitate targeted searching within a particular field, precise document categorization is crucial. Currently, classification methods rely heavily on human input, often using expert-designed categories. In the context of organizing vast STEM collections, we investigate whether such manual grouping can be automated using structured knowledge extracted from semantic repositories like DBpedia. By linking scientific entities to DBpedia, we can identify and analyze patterns of co-occurrence across papers, enabling the formation of categories that reflect the natural connections between entities in a particular field. Our approach was put to the test within two prominent scientific literature databases containing over 40 million articles, and our results demonstrate the potential to automate categorization using entities like DBpedia without requiring human input.

In many situations, a choice ranking that is brief yet relevant is more useful than an extensive list. We suggest a stable matching algorithm that allows agents to input their preferences in the form of approximate distance measures rather than complete rankings. This approach is known as "short preferences" and is applied to various matching environments, including one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-one matching scenarios. We developed a stable outcome for this concept by building on the concept of the core in coalitional game theory. We also investigated how to compute this outcome and verified that it has desirable properties. This approach is applied to the task of online matching, where it is shown to be relevant. We conducted a study to demonstrate how to use signal theory to limit the space of possible solutions. This framework has various applications, including online matching, resource allocation, and matching with preferences. It also has connections to the fields of information theory and graph theory.

A good summary not only conveys the main idea of the original text, but also has distinct characteristics that set it apart. Currently, NLP assessments solely focus on how well a summary represents the original text, disregarding its distinct qualities. To address this, a new metric called SummScore was developed to evaluate summaries based on four key factors: (1) how well the summary accurately reflects the original text, (2) how effectively it conveys new information, (3) how well it avoids copying text, and (4) how effectively it avoids repetition. By weighting these factors differently, SummScore effectively evaluates both good summarizers that add new insights and those that precisely stay true to the original material.

A new method is developed for recovering a shared signal that has been observed multiple times across different Gaussian channels, with the signals' cross-correlations being the key factor in identifying the shared signal. Unlike traditional methods that require a full cross-correlation matrix, this proposed method only needs the diagonal of the cross-correlation matrix, making it more practical to use. Based on a tensor representation of the cross-correlation matrix, this method uses low-rank tensor decomposition to recover the shared signal, with the diagonal of the cross-correlation matrix being the only information needed. Additionally, this method provides a guarantee that the recovered signal is close to the true signal, even in noisy cases, and provides an algorithm along with a numerical example to demonstrate its effectiveness.

The integration of 2Dd+ LiDAR for 3D object detection has become a widely accepted strategy, given the limitations of standalone 3D detection methods when faced with occasional LiDAR malfunctions. However, the conventional approach of training on simulated data leads to inconsistent generalization to real-world scenarios, where occasional failures result in a significant decline in overall performance. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training method that adapishes 2.5D+ detection methods to real-world LiDAR malfunctions by leveraging real-world examples. Specifically, we utilize novel self-supervised loss terms to enhance the learning model's ability to localize objects in 3D space, particularly in scenarios where LiDAR data is absent or compromised. Experimental results on the NPMs-3D+ benchmark demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin, with notable enhancements of 4.5% and 7.2% in mean Average Precision for malfunctional and normal scenarios respectively.

The largest scale thermal energy fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence occur at a critical scale, known as the Kolmogorov length. This scale is determined by the local temperature and rate of energy dissipation within the turbulent flow. In the context of sub-Newtonian oil droplets turbulence, both the Kolmogorov length and the energy dissipation rate per unit volume have been found to follow a universal energy-based timescale. This timescale is derived from the combination of thermal energy and the number density of the oil droplets. This study marks the first observation of thermal energy fluctuations in turbulent flows that exceed the predictions based on the local mean-squared strain rate.

Previous studies on laser propagation through a heated fluid have shown thermal effects influencing laser behavior. However, research focusing on nonlinear interactions between high-intensity lasers in a heated medium is scarce, particularly when the lasers excite shockwaves and acoustic waves within the fluid. This study uses the nonlinear Schrödinger equation and Madelung equations to model the interaction between two lasers in a heated medium. By substituting the Madelung equations into the Maxwell equations, we obtain a system of coupled nonlinear partial differential equations describing laser propagation and fluid dynamics. Numerical simulations demonstrate the co-propagation of two lasers in a heated medium, revealing complex laser behavior such as sideband generation, frequency locking, and beam steering due to thermal effects and fluid dynamics influenced by shockwaves and acoustic waves.

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are essential to project management. Researchers have developed an approach known as design mining to analyze and model these discussions to extract knowledge about the design process. This study applies design mining to understand different discussion patterns among developers working on emerging technologies with varying degrees of complexity. We collected and modelled over 61,000 comments from Mozilla's Gecko project, creating a network model to represent the discussion threads. Our analysis of three complex sub-projects revealed significant insights into developer discussions, including concurrent multi-topic conversations, fragmented discussions, and the challenges of following complex technical discussions. This research contributes to our understanding of developer discussions and provides practical advice for managing complex technical discussions within software development.

This paper introduces a novel evaluation engine called HStream for processing big data streams on cloud infrastructure. Leveraging the effectiveness of micro-services, HStream optimizes adaptability, scalability, and reliability in stream processing. Comprised of independent, cloud-based micro-services, HStream's architecture enhances the streamlined deployment and management of its processing components. The paper carefully designs each micro-service to efficiently process and integrate stream data, while also addressing potential challenges in distributed stream processing. HStream's architecture demonstrates a high level of flexibility, scalability, and reliability in stream processing, with its practical implementation validating the effectiveness of this approach.

The hunt for Top and Bottom companions is a high priority area of investigation for both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, as their single production processes offer significant detection opportunities. Data from the LHC's Run 2, which concluded in 2018, is particularly well-suited for studying single production of vector-like quark partners due to the large associated jet cross-sections generated. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of single production and associated production data from the ATLAS experiment at the 13 TeV LHC, leveraging the full 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ dataset recorded during Run 2. To maximize sensitivity, the analysis considers multiple final states, including top quarks and large-R jets, as well as a broad range of jet signatures. Current limits on the production of top and bottom vector-like quark partners are presented, based on a variety of assumptions regarding their mass and decay modes.

The recent advancements in Neural Machine Translation have shown promising potential in addressing the long-standing issue of automated SPARQL query generation on RDF datasets. Despite progress made so far, the task remains an open challenge. Our study delves into the limitations of current NMT models, which tend to either neglect data alignment by producing unauthorised queries on RDF datasets or struggle with query extension on existing datasets. Building upon lessons learned from previous studies and investigations into NMT capabilities and query characteristics, we propose a new NMT architecture designed to address these limitations. The proposed architecture is capable of learning data alignment without supervision and handling query extension. Our experiments on two existing datasets reveal that the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art NMT models, achieving better results, including higher accuracy, fewer unauthorized queries, and longer and more intricate queries.

This research proposes a novel method for systematically evaluating past work by both authors and venues to predictively assess their future performance. Our approach builds on the understanding that top-tier venues tend to publish top-tier work, making venue scores a practical indicator for making informed decisions. We demonstrate the feasibility of using this metric in author evaluation, comparing it to established metrics, and reveal that incorporating both authors and venues can lead to more accurate assessments. Furthermore, we show that incorporating venues in institutional evaluation enhances the differentiation between institutions, reducing a prominent issue in academic benchmarking where group performance averages out individual achievements.

Advanced learning methods can address longstanding control challenges, but the complex neural networks used pose significant analysis difficulties regarding the safety of control systems. Fortunately, recent research has introduced methods for analyzing and verifying the complex control systems. This tutorial synthesizes and introduces techniques for verifying the robustness of neural networks that originate from control theory. These methods enable the quantification of neural network robustness and stability in relation to system safety, even when dealing with incomplete data. This work also highlights the benefits of combining deep learning with formal verification methods and provides guidance on recent research in this area.

This study draws on three significant lines of research to develop a comprehensive framework for dissimilarity-based clustering, integrating concepts from three distinct areas into a unified cohesive view. The theoretical model allows for linear relationships between data objects, unencumbered by the constraints of Euclidean geometry. In response, the developer has created the Freespace dataset, designed to highlight clustering challenges in non-Euclidean spaces, beyond the limitations of traditional taxonomic structures.

Tensor completion techniques have been widely utilized for recovering missing data from multi-modal visual information like videos and images. This paper introduces a novel approach to tensor completion using neural networks within a learning framework for the missing data itself. Current methods often rely on an additional optimization step after the data is collected, which can be time-consuming and inefficient. In contrast, our approach employs a neural network to predict not just the missing data, but the gradients of that data as well, treating the data as a function. This allows for a single, iterative optimization process that iteratively improves the data's estimate and its corresponding gradient until convergence. Experiments on multi-modal image and video completion demonstrate the superiority of this approach over traditional methods.

It is demonstrated that except in three specific instances, the conjugacy classes of classical Weyl groups $W(B_{n})$ and $W(D_{n})$ take the form of type D. This finding has implications for the Nichols algebras associated with irreducible Yetter-Drinfeld modules over the classical Weyl groups $\mathbb W_{n}$, revealing that these algebras possess infinite dimensions, with the exception of three distinct cases: the $(2, 3),(1^{2}, 3)$ case in $\mathbb S_{5}$, and the $(1^{n-2}, 2)$ case in $\mathbb S_{n}$ for $n >5$.

This study examines the long-term development of rotating, weakly compressible fluid flow's turbulence at constant temperature, utilizing both computational simulations and statistical mechanics. The obtained outcomes reveal two distinct forms of turbulence - a difference highlighted by Kolmogorov in his work on hydrodynamic turbulence: geostrophic turbulence and wave turbulence. The former is characterized by long-lived coherent vortices with stationary temperature patterns, and energy spectra following $E(k) \propto k^{-7/3}$. In contrast, wave turbulence features non-stationary, super-rotating vortices with rising temperature patterns, and energy spectra following $E(k) \propto k^{-3}$. It was discovered that the interaction between the two forms of turbulence is contingent upon specific wave-number and enstrophy flux conditions. The study also reveals the existence of critical thresholds for both the rotation rate and the specific heat ratio, beyond which the characteristics of the two forms of turbulence differ significantly. The findings were obtained using a two-field model for compressible fluid flow, which was previously named the QGRT. The results were validated by testing them against simulations of the Shallow Water Model.

Graph normalization, an iterative process of removing largest possible independent sets from a graph, has been linked to biological systems. It's an approach to study subgraph growth patterns and functional network characteristics. Although the problem of determining whether an n-vertex graph can be fully normalized in O(n) steps is unresolved, research has shown that if a graph has a girth of G, it can be normalized in O(2.5167^(log_2 G)) steps. This study proposes an algorithm to compute an independent set of size d in a graph with a girth of G in O(2.43^(log_2 G) (log_2 (L(G)/d)) log_2 ln(3) + (log_2 d) L(G)/d) algorithmic steps, which improves upon previous computational bounds for single-step independent set computation.

This research investigates the impact of a magnetic field on electrically modulated single-layer graphene, resulting in oscillations in its Landau levels, and we derive the resulting Fermi energy, chemical potential, and other key thermodynamic properties. These properties are compared to a standard two-dimensional electron gas, revealing significant differences. The analysis also enables calculation of the Debye and plasma frequencies, and it's found that their product is independent of the magnetic field strength. The findings are further applied to determine the speed of sound in single-layer graphene at zero temperature, yielding a non-Drude result that diverges from the conventional case, and we discuss the associated transverse charge response under a magnetic field.

Recent findings from the Breakthrough Listen initiative at 116 MHz have yielded two significant discoveries: radio waves emitted by TD-1 Star with a power of 100 W, and radio waves from KIC 12505394 with a power of 10^4 W, both of which exhibit periodicities. Radio waves emitted by TD-1 Star could be produced by magnetospheric processes similar to those found on Earth, whereas radio waves emitted by KIC 12505394 could be produced by an exoplanet, making them the first ever detected from outside our Solar System. Radio waves emitted by TD-1 Star could be produced by magnetospheric processes similar to those found on Earth, whereas radio waves emitted by KIC 12505394 could be produced by an exoplanet, making them the first ever detected from outside our Solar System. Radio waves emitted by TD-1 Star could be produced by an epicycle, or the interaction of an exoplanet, or other mechanism such as the interaction of interacting stars. Radio waves emitted by KIC 12505394 could be produced by an exoplanet, or other mechanism such as the interaction of interacting stars. Radio waves emitted by TD-1 Star could be produced by an exoplanet, or other mechanism such as the interaction of interacting stars. Radio waves emitted by KIC 12505394 could be produced by an exoplanet, or other mechanism such as the 16.8 day period.

Our method, called Arist, represents the first application of neural point rendering for high-quality virtual human avatars within interactive environments. Arist employs an innovative rendering pipeline, which simplifies complexity by relying on pre-existing 3D scans of generic human shapes and skeletons to generate highly realistic avatars. Unlike other rendering approaches, Arist handles articulation and lighting directly in the rendering pipeline, without the need for explicit pose and lighting estimates. Additionally, our method enables user control over rendered avatars by providing an intuitive interface to generate customized content. We compare our results with state-of-the-art approaches, demonstrating Arist's ability to produce photorealistic results for complex, dynamic scenes and novel categories, such as sitting and sleeping humans.

Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to mimic the behavior of a learning human brain. However, it's still unclear whether these networks perform object recognition tasks as efficiently as humans, especially under difficult image conditions. Our study focuses on this issue by comparing human and ANN performance on a complex object recognition task that involves distinguishing between low-resolution images of real-world objects and photorealistic synthetic counterfeits. Under challenging image conditions, our results indicate that humans make fewer mistakes than state-of-the-art ANNs, which includes both supervised Deep Neural Networks and unsupervised Autoencoders. Interestingly, our experiments reveal that both human and ANN performance improve significantly when recognizing objects that are both visually familiar and semantically meaningful.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory and its relation to the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant is demonstrated. Specifically, the AW algebra's finite-dimensional representations are shown to align with the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory's and its connection to the 32nd root of unity regime of the RT invariant, yields the same eigenvalues as the Casson invariant does for X-chiralsawg knots.

Our study delves into the properties of a deformed Kagome lattice with a distorted structure, achieved by rotating one half of the lattice at a 45-degree angle. We observed two distinct phases in our model - a disordered spin phase and two nearby ordered phases. Notably, the heat capacity of the model exhibits a two-peak structure, indicating a first-order phase transition between these states. We also investigated the spin dynamics within the ordered phases and discovered a transition from a fast, local spin process in one phase to a slower, global spin process in the other phase, separated by a middle phase with unique spin characteristics. These findings suggest the possibility of creating new materials with unique spin characteristics by applying pressure to an appropriate compound.

Pre-trained language models have achieved significant success in multiple down-stream tasks.  Recent studies have shown that by making the connection between pre-training and down-stream tasks clearer through prompt engineering, pre-trained language models' zero-shot and few-shot performances can also be greatly improved.  Another approach, meta-tuning, enables post-training on down-stream tasks to further boost performance.  However, the process of meta-tuning is often hindered by the limitations of computation resources and time.  In this study, a new method of meta-tuning called adaptive meta-tuning is proposed, which makes it possible to tune the weights of large language models adaptively based on different objectives, requiring no time and just minimal extra computation resources.  Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed method can greatly improve the zero-shot and few-shot performance of GPT(3)-size large language models.

In this study, we investigate how a first-order electroweak phase transition, capable of driving baryogenesis, occurs when the \chi\chi\chi and \chi\phi^\pm interactions exceed the Planck scale. Here, \chi and \phi represent the Goldstone Higgs field and a pseudoscalar Higgs field, derived from an A_4 symmetric, non-Abelian gauge-invariant scalar field, L. When symmetry is broken, it yields a symmetric mass matrix for \chi, resulting in degenerate heavy states. Our analysis involves a tree-level analysis of the \chi\chi\chi and \chi\phi^\pm interactions, demonstrating their enhanced high-energy behavior. Additionally, we use effective field theory to account for higher-order corrections up to the Planck scale. Our results show that, under these conditions, these interactions can drive baryogenesis through an electroweak phase transition.

We introduce an image processing method that locates key emission lines at submillimeter wavelengths and identifies reliable redshifts without needing complex models. This technique relies on specific features in interferograms to pinpoint lines of CII and dust thermal emission at 158 $\mu$m. However, identifying robust redshifts from narrower lines is difficult due to the line shape challenges. To address this limitation, we developed a straightforward method to estimate line widths and calculate signal-to-noise ratios. This approach enables us to distinguish reliable redshifts from uncertain ones. We tested this technique using the detailed data from SPICA-PREMIER and the full-continuum mode of thermal detectors. After applying our method to mock observations with varying signal strengths and observational times, we simulated redshift distributions for different scenarios. Our results show that achieving robust redshifts within one sigma precision requires high signal-to-noise ratios of at least 5-10, depending on the specific setup. This might limit the number of reliable redshifts available. To confirm our findings, we compared our method's results with actual data from the prototypes of the SPICA's spectro-polarimetry instrument.

This research investigates the nematic nematicity-nematic spin ordering connection in the square-lattice antiferromagnetic Mott insulator C$_2$F$_2$. Through the use of high-resolution neutron scattering, the absence of nematic ordering associated with magnetic waves at very low temperatures was confirmed. In contrast to C$_2$F$_2$, nematic phases have been observed in other spin-1/2 compounds with similar crystal structures, notably in the cuprate compound Ba$_2$CuSi$_2O$_6$ and the ferromagnetic compound Ba$_2$CuGe$_2$O$_6$. These findings suggest that the presence of nematic ordering in C$_2$F$_2$ is unlikely to occur, and that the spin-degenerate nature of the ground state contributes to its resilience against nematic instability. Furthermore, the experimental data are supported by large-scale density-matrix renormalization vector theory calculations.

In our study, we explored the confinement-deconfinement transition in $SU(3)$ Higgs theory on a 3D lattice with different temporal sites, denoted as $N_t$. We observed varying confinement properties, which were linked to the $0-2\pi$ periodicity of the Polyakov loop and the breaking of $Z_3$ symmetry. Notably, our results demonstrated that the phase transition curves and lattice spacing annotations diverged as $N_t$ decreased, particularly at high Higgs masses. This phenomenon was attributed to the differing complexity of $3D$ lattice configurations in the confining and Higgs phases. Furthermore, we found that the Higgs mixing boundary varied with $N_t$ in the $4D$ theory and that the $3D$ lattice could capture the $T_c$ anomaly in the $4D$ $SU(3)$ gauge theory without the need for Polyakov loop regularization.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits an antiferromagnetic arrangement similar to the Fe$_2$X type, with a N\'{e}el temperature identified through magnetometry as 100 K, and further validated by SHG and neutron diffraction experiments performed under cryogenic conditions. Magnetometry results on polycrystalline samples indicate a Curie temperature of 130 K. By employing phase-field simulations, researchers are able to model the 3D magnetic arrangement in the ground state and create a 2D magnetostatic pattern at 50 K, 5 K, and 150 K. However, due to the sample's orientation dependence in the laboratory setting, neutron diffraction experiments reveal orientation-dependent magnetization at the sample surface. The study also demonstrates that second-harmonic generation (SHG) can be employed as an in situ phase-sensitive measurement technique to detect magnetic phase transitions.

A new kinetic model is developed for simulating rarefied monatomic gas flows, specifically in the frame of reference of a typical molecule. By employing an expansion in terms of the average collision frequency, the model's kinetic equation is formulated, resulting in an expression that mirrors the Boltzmann equation. An intricate relationship between the model's equations and the conventional solution of the Boltzmann equation via the Chapman-Enskog expansion is established, with key factors including the ratio of specific heats, the Maxwell distribution, and an energy parameter. An adaptable procedure for calculating the model's collision integral is also presented.

Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa and Google Assistant, significantly benefit from advancements in semantic parsing, a core challenge in NLP. The latest state-of-the-art semantic parsers leverage sequence-to-sequence models, built upon advanced neural networks, to accurately capture the semantic meaning of spoken language. The N6 dataset, a comprehensive English dataset, has been instrumental in driving progress in semantic parsing, presenting a unique challenge due to its diverse and complex features. The paper presents a new state-of-the-art sequence-to-sequence model, incorporating a sophisticated graph attention mechanism to improve semantic parsing performance. The proposed approach achieves exceptional results on the N6 dataset, surpassing existing benchmarks with a 1.1% increase in exact match accuracy and establishing new standards for semantic parsing.

The Electron-Ion Collider's key objectives can be achieved through crucial measurements of heavy flavor hadron and jet production, which will help refine our understanding of the parton distribution functions and QCD dynamics at high energies and small scales. To attain this goal, identifying specific regions of the proton's parton distribution functions can be vital, particularly when studying chargedudderon production at an $e$+A collider. An initial assessment ofudderon production at an $e$-Au collider using next-to-leading-order theory reveals its potential as a viable probe for this research.

A new category of X-ray variability in black hole systems has been found, known as Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPEs). These unique outbursts exhibit short-lived episodes of intense flaring during the rising phase of an outburst, characterized by distinct, recurring patterns of bright and faint emission. While QPEs show similarities to Quasi-Periodic Oscillations (QPOs), they differ in their distinct characteristics. This study focuses on the analysis of two QPEs from the black hole system GX 339-4, which was previously thought to only exhibit QPOs. The detection of these QPEs in GX 339-4 challenges the existing notion that QPOs are primarily observed in low-mass black holes, raising questions about the fundamental source of their variability patterns.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has long sparked debate about their influence on the atmospheres of stars. Our research provides new evidence from spectropolarimetric analysis on how the strength of magnetic fields in early-type stars varies with height above the surface of the stars. Our findings reveal that magnetic fields in the outer layers of the atmospheres of these stars are significantly weaker than those closer to the core. The results of our study also indicate the presence of magnetic elements at all altitudes within the atmospheres of these stars, which the current theoretical models fail to explain. Our discovery raises intriguing possibilities, such as the magnetic fields in the outer layers of these stars potentially interacting with the surrounding interstellar medium, while also hinting at the existence of magnetic heating mechanisms similar to those found in magneticapsules in the atmospheres of white dwarfs.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative,
