exemplified through its equivalence to an operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

Using ALMA's high-resolution capabilities, researchers studied the H30$\alpha$ emission in a sample of nine nearby dwarf galaxies. This allowed them to measure how tightly the gas emission in these galaxies varies in intensity. To further understand the distribution of gas, they analyzed the smooth extent of the emissions. This analysis enabled them to quantify the mass of the gas within these galaxies, even in areas where individual gas clouds couldn't be distinguished. This approach helped reduce uncertainty in mass measurements due to spatial resolution limitations. By combining these methods, researchers were able to calculate a more reliable star formation rate for the galaxies in the sample, based on their $M_{\rm H_2}$ to stellar mass ratios. This rate was found to be 0.01--0.08 $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, indicating low star formation activity in these galaxies. This study also enabled researchers to calculate the star formation efficiency of the galaxies, which ranged from 0.03--0.40. These findings are important for understanding the star formation processes in dwarf galaxies, which are similar to dwarf galaxy candidates in the Milky Way's Local Group.
We demonstrate that two continuous minimal actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space can be orbit equivalent if and only if they are conjugate.

We explore the statistical approximations of the $L^2$-operator derived from a conditional expectation of a random variable. Utilizing a technique involving Hilbert-Schmidt operators, we establish a framework for discretizing this operator while ensuring its norm remains bounded, thus facilitating the proof of convergence of related processes. This approach is exemplified through the finite-sample analysis of a maximum likelihood estimator in the context of an ordered probability model.

Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and makes it difficult to establish linear relationships between system inputs, outputs, and state variables, particularly in cases where observation equations are undefined at zero. This study addresses these challenges by developing a novel backstepping-based state observer for nonlinear epidemiological models. Building on a dynamic system representation that incorporates an auxiliary variable to address observation equation issues at zero, we design an observer with a two-stage scheme. This scheme initially aligns the auxiliary variable with the correct value through a first-dynamic observer, followed by a second step that adjusts the state estimate. We demonstrate the convergence of both the state and auxiliary variable estimates to their respective true counterparts, supported by theoretical examples and simulations of a nonlinear SIR model.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings has been largely overlooked, despite its potential to enhance task performance. We demonstrate that incorporating temporal scopes of facts into these embeddings leads to improved results on downstream tasks. A novel temporal KGE framework is introduced, which captures the distinct temporal contexts of each fact and conditions the encoding of each token on its relevant temporal scope. This approach is evaluated on three tasks – link prediction, entity alignment, and entity ranking – and achieves significant gains in accuracy and recall, substantiating the importance of temporal context in KRE and highlighting its potential to elevate the performance of downstream applications.

Research driven by powerful ring resonators demands a more sophisticated approach to their analysis than traditional linear perturbation theory can provide.. By developing a nonlinear version of Rayleigh-Schrödinger perturbation theory, we are able to effectively separate the resonator's geometry and electromagnetic effects at various power levels.. This methodology enables us to accurately compute the modes of strongly coupled systems and their spatial modes, allowing for a deeper understanding of the resonator's behavior across multiple power thresholds.. Our analysis also uncovers new insights into threshold and mode switching phenomena, which are critical in the resonator's higher power regimes.

A widely discussed topic known as federated learning has garnered significant interest due to its ability to train non-publicized machine learning models while addressing data privacy concerns. Despite this, practical federated learning deployments are hindered by several challenges including non-IID data, variable client participation, and differing device capabilities. The application of federated learning in real-world scenarios requires substantial resources to be invested in both computing power and energy efficiency. The federated learning framework's high communication overhead in frequent model transmissions further exacerbates energy consumption and reduces system performance. To address these concerns, this paper proposes an adaptive learning rate algorithm utilizing stochastic gradient dynamics that can accommodate variable client participation and data heterogeneity. The proposed algorithm reduces communication overhead by introducing sparsification and quantization methods, ultimately achieving energy efficiency through the efficient utilization of edge computing resources. The proposed approach effectively addresses the challenges associated with practical federated learning deployments.

This research explores the utilization of a photonic crystal as a reflective coating to enhance thin-film silicon solar cells. The optical performance of these solar cells, each with different wavelengths in their photonic crystal, is evaluated under varying angles of incidence. The results are compared with a solar cell utilizing a traditional metal back reflector. The findings indicate that photonic crystals can be designed to optimize energy absorption within the solar cell. Specifically, by tailoring the photonic crystal's eigenfrequencies to match the solar cell's energy gap, maximum absorption is achieved. When applied to amorphous and polycrystalline thin-film silicon solar cells, significant improvements in energy conversion efficiency are observed. The use of a photonic crystal instead of a metal back reflector resulted in an enhanced efficiency of 0.52% for a-Si and 0.63% for p-Si, representing increases of 2.5 and 3.1 times, respectively.

We develop a set of holomorphic functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (z)$, that, when the absolute value of the variable $z$ approaches infinity, behave similarly to iterated exponentials. Our functions are effective in approximating the sine and cosine functions under certain conditions, leading to the establishment of new asymptotic formulas. By analytically continuing the hypergeometric series, we create functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (z)$, that exhibit series representations similar to Gelfand's hypergeometric series. Our functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (z)$, are defined for complex z and satisfy specific functional equations, particularly for odd values of $\lambda$. Our functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (z)$, can be seen as generalizations of the iterated exponential $e^{\mu z}$ and as solutions to certain differential equations. Our functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (z)$, are shown to be holomorphic in the right half-plane and to have specific series representations. Our functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (z)$, can be seen as generalizations of the iterated exponential when the variable $z$ approaches infinity, leading to the establishment of new asymptotic formulas for the sine and cosine functions.

We have developed a new method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces from a given topological structure. This method is similar to constructing expander graphs using coverings. Our group of researchers has established a clear relationship between the spectralogical properties of a cover and a dimensionally expanded object. Additionally, we have created a series of inductive tools that aid in constructing these dimensionally expanded objects. Our method also allows for the creation of constructions that are operable under a probabilistic framework with a low rate of failure.

To study the antiferromagnetic phase transitions in GdInO$_3$, a paramagnetic substance, we employed the finite-temperature linear spinwave analysis method within the mean-field framework of the spin-1 Blume-Capel Heisenberg model. This model effectively captures the underlying crystal structure and the non-uniform antiferromagnetic ordering in the system. Our calculations indicate that the model accurately predicts two successive antiferromagnetic phase transitions at $T=T_{AF1}$ and $T=T_{AF2}$ in the specified temperature range, with $T_{AF2}$ being approximately 80% of $T_{AF1}$. These findings align with experimental observations and show that the transition temperatures are largely influenced by the ratio of the quadrupolar to magnetic exchange interactions. Furthermore, the analysis of the direction of spontaneous magnetization reveals a unique characteristic of the specified system.

Real-world networks, such as social media platforms and transportation systems, are crucially important for various applications and have been extensively studied under the assumption of a static network structure. However, these structures often change dynamically due to the addition or removal of nodes and edges. To effectively manage and analyze such dynamic changes, it's essential to have a method for embedding nodes in a shared latent space across successive snapshots of a graph. Our novel approach, Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE), focuses on preserving high-level structural characteristics across separate instances of a graph, resulting in better performance than existing non-sparse methods on more than half of the tested benchmarks.

A low-cost water jet process is employed to create a $2.5\text{ mm}$ deep etch trench in a $3\text{ mm}$ thick glass atomic vapor cell. The success of this innovative deep etch achieves the maximum depth viable using the water jet process, making it the deepest etch carried out on this technology to date. The development of this technique employs a sophisticated control system to monitor the water jet pressure and movement in real-time, ensuring precise tracking of the etch probe along a complex path. The water jet laboratory was adapted to execute this complex maneuver by installing an APT Prover probe, coupled with a Sensofar focus sensor for precise vertical measurement of the etch probe. The probe is guided through a customized 3D printed track to facilitate accurate location and orientation. The track is fitted with three motors allowing for independent movement in all three axes, and features a camera providing real-time feedback and alignment with the etch path. The integration of this technology and precise tracking enables a level of precision previously unattainable with conventional water jet control systems, making it the most accurate deep etch achieved to date. The development of this technique has far-reaching implications for the water jet process, enabling more complex manufacturing projects to be executed with increased accuracy and depth.

We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB.

Preemptive wildfire detection is crucial for minimizing ecological damage, property loss, and human casualties. Acquiring early warnings through accurate fire identification also enables firefighters to target fires at their most combustible stage, maximizing containment possibilities.  With the integration of drones in wildfire monitoring, researchers are now focusing on developing drone-aided wildfire detection systems as a promising solution.  However, implementing these systems in diverse real-world settings poses challenges for algorithmic solutions.  This study tackles these practical issues by designing a novel detection algorithm for use in real-time drone-based systems.  The proposed approach involves fire detection using thermal imagery captured by drones in motion.  The algorithm incorporates robust estimation of local temperature maps, fire characterization, and fire identification.  The experimental results validate the efficacy of the designed system in detecting fires in real-time, even in the presence of shifting drone perspectives and motion.

Social media has become a significant platform for people's lives, with numerous users sharing personal experiences online. This wealth of data presents an opportunity to analyze individuals' mental health states. In our research, we focus on detecting early signs of depression in Norwegian social media postings, where we initially create a gold standard dataset categorizing depression into three stages: mild, moderate, and severe. Subsequently, we experiment with various machine learning models, incorporating different text reduction strategies. Ultimately, the best combination of algorithms and data processing methods yields an accuracy of 0.813, but more effective reduction techniques are needed to enhance the reliability of our findings.

The COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the Coronavirus, has become a major global concern since its discovery in December 2019. This infection is believed to follow a susceptible-infectious-susceptible dynamics, and by using a simplified model, it was demonstrated that the spread of the virus increased when lockdown measures were lifted in China. This was contrasted with the situation in Italy, where the spread was found to have slowed down. The model's predictions were verified by comparing the predicted dates of outbreak peaks with the actual dates reported in China and Italy. This verification process also allowed for the estimation of certain parameters in the model, such as the basic reproduction number. This number represents the average number of people that can be infected from one individual in a susceptible population.

A new method has been developed for analyzing nuclear density distributions using proton scattering cross sections and electromagnetic experiments. This method was tested successfully on three highly deformed isotopes of actinide nuclei. For the first time, density distributions were determined for the neutron-rich isotopes 228 and 230Np. The results for 230Np with a significant part-of-valence neutrons shell closure are particularly noteworthy. The application of the method to 230Np allows for constraints to be placed on the incompressibility modulus, supporting earlier findings that the bulk infinite nuclear matter value for the compressibility modulus is too low. Additionally, the method's results for 230Np provide valuable information on the neutron radius, thereby helping to resolve the long-standing issue of the Np valence neutrons shell closure.

A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near an equilibrium state, is confirmed through analytical means. Theoretical findings reveal that the system can only converge asymptotically, involving multiple sequences of stick-slip cycles, regardless of the starting conditions. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical models through diverse examples of convergence.

A novel reinforcement learning method based on the actor-critic type has been developed to tackle portfolio hedging challenges for a variety of financial securities and derivatives using historical data only. Key aspects of this approach involve leveraging derivatives like forwards and options to minimize risks, leveraging leverage to maximize returns, and leveraging market trends. This algorithm does not require market assumptions or linear relationships. Instead, it uses an algorithmic policy search to optimize risk management strategies. Through various tests using historical S&P 500 index data, we compared our approach with established research models, including a short-term arbitrage model and a portfolio diversification model, finding that it consistently outperformed these alternatives over the 10-year period studied.

In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential prediction models play a crucial role. These models depend on historical interaction data, both for training and making recommendations. As users increasingly engage with digital content, vast amounts of historical data are available, but real-time recommendations require only a limited look-ahead. A major challenge arises when a user arrives with no prior history, known as the new user (NU) problem, where recommendations must be provided immediately. A recent approach to addressing the NU problem involves storing full interaction sequences for all users, but this is impractical due to high storage demands. An alternative is to retain only a limited set of recent sequences for a subset of high-value users. A more recent solution proposes sampling a subset of users randomly. In this study, a new approach called Contextual High-Value Users (CHVU) is presented, aiming to efficiently address the NU problem. A key component of CHVU involves a contextual representation model, enabling contextual information to be extracted and matched with user profiles to identify high-value users worth retaining full interaction sequences for. CHVU also incorporates an efficient recommendation model, capable of making real-time recommendations using either historical or cached NU user sequences. Experimental results on a real-world dataset confirm the effectiveness of CHVU in reducing storage needs, particularly for large-scale recommender systems.

A specific reducible double confluent Heun equation, having certain prescribed singularities, can be precisely determined by a single parameter. It has a notable Fuchsian equation as a factor and can be derived from it. The focus lies on the solutions of these equations that exhibit certain symmetry behavior at the singularities, specifically at x=0 and x=1. As a result, these equations can be reduced to simpler forms, specifically limit cases of Heun equations, by making specific transformations. These simpler forms can then be compared to solutions of finite power series, providing explicit solutions to these equations, in turn facilitating the study of solutions to the original equations through their relationship with solutions to the simpler forms. The emphasis lies on solutions that are classified as admissible or inadmissible, depending on the power of the transforming function, in the context of the simpler forms. The article concludes with a presentation of the transformed equations, specifically limit cases of Heun equations, in a recognizable form, facilitating further research on solutions to these equations, in turn shedding light on the solutions to the original equations.

Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in various fields. Most existing methods, though effective for uniformly observed data with the same level of noise, are not suitable for scenarios where different data blocks are observed at varying noise levels. This limitation hampers their practical application in multi-source and diverse big data settings, which are increasingly common. To address this challenge, we develop a new robust low-rank matrix recovery method by leveraging the principle of maximum likelihood under a robust loss function. By maximizing a weighted sum of two terms that represent model fidelity and completion quality, our method can be efficiently computed via simple linear algebra. Theoretical convergence and accuracy guarantees for our method are derived, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments.

In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Absence of traditional symmetry in the model leads to topological equivalence with a spin-1 Chiral Dibron model. As a result, zero-energy edge modes appear at the 2nd order. Moreover, we identify an extra topological boundary mode at the middle of the band spectrum at 2nd order, originating from the merging of 0th order flat bands. The emergence of these boundary modes is facilitated by the presence of a level crossing, a phenomenon occurring before reaching the 2nd order exceptional point. A straightforward approach to realize these features involves using a string with two fixed ends.

We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio $R_\Sigma$ to verify electron-to-muon universality in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process at $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities. Our analysis suggests that a significant test of $R_\Sigma$ sensitivity at a future $e^+e^-$ collider is feasible, with results potentially limited by current data on electron universality in $e^+e^-$ collisions and the $\Upsilon(nS)$ resonance decays.

This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring agents to adjust their parameters. This promotes scalable design and flexible system configurations.

We propose an innovative COVID-19 diagnosis framework, which leverages CT image analysis in the lungs. Initially, we employ Bidirectional Attention Graph Convolutional Networks (BAGCN) to extract critical features from CT images. These features are then processed through a self-supervised Bag of Visual Words (BoVW) model, generating compact and unified features. Subsequently, a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier is trained on derived features to obtain robust diagnostic results. Our framework's effectiveness is demonstrated by achieving a high accuracy of 0.917, specifically in the form of a high Specificity rate of 0.943, along with a high F1 Score of 0.918 on the COVID CT challenge dataset.

Analysis of complex networks has become a crucial tool across various fields, including computer science, mathematics, physics, engineering, and others, as well as in medicine and biology. The broad appeal of network science stems from the natural occurrence of relational data everywhere. From social connections to molecular structures, networks effectively represent interactions. Due to their widespread occurrence, studying networks has become a vital activity in various fields. The breadth of network applications leads to a diverse range of problems that require tailored computational approaches. Despite the unique challenges, these problems share some common characteristics. One significant challenge is graph construction, which involves defining the nodes and edges of a network. Another crucial aspect is identifying patterns within a network, which can arise due to underlying structural features. We propose a set of best practices for network analysis, drawing from computational biology, that help overcome these challenges. We also provide accessible Python code for these methods to facilitate seamless network analysis.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is expanding beyond simple models to encompass more intricate representations of species interactions along with environmental factors and genetic diversity. To develop a framework for analyzing these complex systems, this research defines a set of fundamental principles that underlie and connect various eco-evolutionary models, making them suitable for coexistence in scenarios of global change. The identified principles include niche structure, resource competition, species interactions, and diversity, which can be applied to different levels of species diversity. By applying this framework, similar patterns of eco-evolutionary responses to global change can be observed in complex systems, even those exhibiting non-linear and unpredictable dynamics. The approach also highlights gaps in existing research and emphasizes the need for further empirical and theoretical exploration of eco-evolutionary dynamics, particularly in areas like symbiotic relationships and diverse species communities.

This study presents a new paradigm for self-supervised speech learning that outperforms previous methods by leveraging contrastive learning. It employs a contrastive learning model called x-vae+ in the supervised or semi-supervised domain, and when applied to the Speech Act Recognition task, improves accuracy and F1-score compared to the unsupervised supervisory signal. Our research demonstrates that the contrastive learning paradigm is effective for the Speech Act Recognition task and indicates that future research in this area could lead to significant improvements.

Our research delves into the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers, 
which enabled us to accurately forecast token price volatility and 
drum up theoretical and practical insights into their functioning. 
We discovered that maintaining a trade network is costly for Automated 
Market Makers, leading to the need to set minimum token transaction 
amounts to ensure sufficient liquidity. Our findings also imply the 
existence of a price range, known as the "orphaned zone," where prices 
no longer attract liquidity. By combining our results with real-world 
data, we verified the presence of the orphaned zone in Ethereum's 
ERC-20 tokens.

In the presence of missing outcome data, an important analytical approach is Sensitivity Analysis, which aims to assess how conclusions are affected by different assumptions regarding the missing data mechanism. A significant challenge in this area is the development of mathematical models that can accurately account for the impact of missing data. This paper proposes a new approach, using Bayesian techniques and hierarchical Markov models to perform sensitivity analysis for continuous outcomes. This method allows analysts to specify a prior distribution for the model parameters and makes flexible assumptions about how the missing data pattern varies over time. The approach can handle complex data structures and provides a thorough diagnostic for the assumption of a time-invariant missing data mechanism. The method's performance in real-world applications is demonstrated through an in-depth examination of a dataset from a large-scale randomized trial.

This paper develops a constructive method for identifying the generators of the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries associated with each vertex of the octahedral graph, utilizing the root vectors of the quantum algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ in relation to these generators. Furthermore, this paper reconfirms Lusanna's work on non-local observables through the context of root vectors. Additionally, it determines the commutator relationships of these generators with the Cartan generator $K_1$ and verifies that they constitute a complete set of generators for the octahedron $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-invariant observables under the condition of $q^2 = 1$.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Vehicles is beneficial, 
yet constrained by data privacy and security concerns due to security 
vulnerabilities. To address this limitation, a Federated Learning framework 
is proposed, enabling local data encryption and local model development, 
which can be securely combined at the edge under centralized management. 
Through experimental evaluation, the proposed framework has been demonstrated 
to safeguard user data and edge devices, effectively training robust models 
on large datasets, and showing promising capabilities in handling local 
distributions with varying feature importance, such as urban and highway 
scenarios, without experiencing model overfitting issues.

The ALICE experiment has recorded the $p_{\rm T}$ distribution of D mesons in $p$$+$$p$ collisions with a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV over an interval corresponding to 200 GeV/$c$ to 100 GeV/$c$ in the laboratory frame. The data, based on an integrated luminosity of 27 nb$^{-1}$ collected with the ALICE detector, represent the first detailed D-meson production cross-section measurements in the intermediate mass range. The data were analyzed from data samples of D-meson decays $(K\mu)$ and antiproton tracks in the ALICE detector, and cross-section values were calculated using two different methods, accounting for detector efficiency and acceptance. The results were compared with theoretical models such as NLO pQCD and were found to agree with data in two different $x_F$ regimes. The results were also compared with theoretical models at different $x_F$ regimes, and the results were expressed in terms of the radiation hemisphere variable $x_T$ and the Bjorken $x$ variable.

The escalating demand for large-scale cryogenic cooling systems in quantum computing is driving innovation in new cryogenic cooling platforms, capable of cooling multiple qubits to around 4 K.  A novel 16-road microchannel heat exchanger, approximately 10 cm in length and 2 cm in width, has been created to provide necessary coldness with the aid of a 4 K closed-loop cold head.  Experimental examinations were carried out on its cold transfer efficiency using a combination of thermometry, infrared imaging, and heat flux measurements and were compared against computational predictions based on numerical models.  Measurements revealed a 90% overall efficiency transfer of heat and a 94% local transfer of heat in regions not experiencing secondary fluid-related issues, both of which were close to the expected perfect transfer of heat values.  Furthermore, the heat exchanger's total surface area was found to be the main factor limiting its performance, with room for improvement in its design optimization.

To gauge the extent of secure coding practices, we evaluated the use of crypto APIs in Python projects on PyPI by manually reviewing 100 projects. Our study uncovered an alarming rate of insecure coding habits, with the majority of projects exhibiting at least one vulnerable practice. This paper documents our methodology, presents our findings, and offers recommendations for improving secure coding practices among PyPI project maintainers.

This paper introduces an enhanced method for locating fixed 3D objects within complex urban environments, where traditional localization techniques frequently experience difficulties due to obstacles and obstructions. The proposed approach combines multi-static ranging and dead reckoning to achieve accurate localization. Specifically, it utilizes data from various receivers to create a geometric location estimate, with an accompanying error analysis. When coupled with an autonomous agent equipped with dead reckoning capabilities, such as a wheeled robot, this method enables the establishment of a control loop that compensates for errors and adapts to changes in the environment. The proposed technique demonstrates effective and robust operation in the challenging environment of an indoor shopping mall.

In seismic reflection inversion, the process of deconvolving sparse signals is a critical initial step. A new method for sparse signal deconvolution has been proposed, based on a convolutional neural network. The proposed CNN model incorporates a sparse reguralization term and an adaptive learning rate. The method claims to outperform traditional deconvolution techniques, such as the common-echo gapped (CGC) method, in both effectiveness and simplicity. To validate the method's accuracy, tests were conducted using the BP data from the BP Cornell dataset. The results showed the new method's potential in improving the quality of sparse signal deconvolution.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao in 1992 and is characterized by functions f such that the integral of the absolute values of its Riemann-Morrey operators is bounded by a multiple of |1-z|^{1+rp} for 0<p<1 and 0<q<s+1. Our research reveals that a semigroup of composition operators on BMOA_p or VMOA_p is norm-closed, closed under taking limits, and forms a topological semigroup if and only if it is bounded. This generalizes prior findings on the boundedness of semigroups of composition operators on BMOA and its analogue VMOA.

Determining the precise values of operator product expansion coefficients in conformal field theory is a crucial step towards data-driven CFT characterization. We employ causality and the $adS_3$ unitarity constraints to derive an upper limit on the product of two coefficient values. Our findings align with an information-theoretic prediction that had been made concurrently. We also explore the scope of a linear relation that we identified between the central charge, OPE coefficient, and product of coefficients, and discuss its implications for bounds on the stress tensor two-point function coefficient and product of coefficients, both in primary operator product expansions and general conformal field theories.

Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed by machine learning methods. Although these methods rely on large, well-annotated datasets, such resources are scarce for historical languages due to limited texts available and lower transcription quality. This study proposes an innovative approach to POS tagging for languages with limited resources, leveraging the use of related, but larger datasets in a parallel fashion. By applying this method to the study of Old Turkish, this research demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy, achieving a higher Kruijff-Dijkstra score of 0.713 compared to 0.462 with monolingual supervision.

This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a utility function from a non-differentiable but locally Lipschitz candidate of a demand function. Using this method, two key criteria become clear: criteria that ensure a candidate represents a valid demand function and criteria that ensure a candidate is the lower boundary of an equally valid demand function. These findings are derived from an approach that utilizes a specific extension of the classical Dubovickii-Friedman theorem. This method also sheds light on the relationship between the necessary conditions for a valid demand function and the sufficient conditions for a valid demand function. Ultimately, two economic applications demonstrate the effectiveness of this new approach.

As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or they contain inaccuracies or ambiguities stemming from written English text. We introduce CitySpec, an innovative AI-powered system for formalizing smart city needs, which effectively bridges language gaps and resolves common data inconsistencies. The purpose of this research is to explain CitySpec's functionality by showcasing three practical applications: real-time requirements completion within CitySpec; a collaborative correction process when unexpected exceptions arise; and the adaptive learning mechanism of CitySpec.

Our research presents an error mitigation strategy that integrates hidden inverse algorithms directly into the quantum circuit design process. This is accomplished by placing the algorithm as a hidden layer within the circuit. Through numerical analysis, we demonstrate that incorporating this layer effectively compensates for systematic errors. Furthermore, we experimentally validate this mitigation strategy using the IBMQ cloud backend, specifically Qiskit's IBMQ Santiago chip, which is susceptible to calibration and noise issues due to its aging qubits. Our results reveal that our proposed approach outperforms existing mitigation methods in enhancing circuit fidelity, particularly in scenarios with limited experimental data for calibration.

In a general category $\mathbb E$, taking the direct image of a partial order under a surjective epimorphism may not yield a partial order. In the category of sets, the best partial order approximation of the image in such a case is obtained by forming the cofibered image of the original preorder above the epimorphism. In categories satisfying regularity conditions, the existence of such a cofibered image for partial orders corresponds to the existence of the least upper bound among all partial orders within the original domain. This work explores conditions ensuring the existence of these cofibered images, which can be used in two distinct areas of study: the context of topoi with suprema of subobject chains or the context of $n$-permutable categories.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the dependence between wind speed, wave height, and the probability of ship capsizing is investigated in the North East Atlantic between 50-70 degrees North and 5-25 degrees West. A non-parametric analysis revealed distinct patterns of extremal dependence between wind speed and wave height during storm events, which were found to weaken with increasing severity. A more detailed examination of dependence in high-severity storm periods was then carried out using a time series corresponding to a 30-year window. The results indicated negative dependence between wind speed and wave height during these periods, a finding supported by a geophysical model that simulates storm trajectories. Furthermore, a model based on the work of Schlather and Tawn was used to create a more fine-grained dependence model, which revealed a shift towards positive dependence under very severe conditions. A method for identifying and quantifying changes in extremal dependence over time was also employed, revealing significant variations at an annual and decadal scale.

Pre-trained models like CLIP offer high-quality image-text connections, yet they often hinder performance in downstream tasks. To strike a balance, this research introduces BARTCLIP, a flexible and efficient framework that unites CLIP with BART. Specifically, BARTCLIP integrates cross-modal alignment from CLIP and fine-tunes it with self-supervised vision-language tasks, such as image-text matching, visual-language modeling, and automatic image captioning. BARTCLIP achieves improved performance across diverse tasks like image captioning, visual question answering, and zero-shot classification, while also demonstrating enhanced interpretability on tasks like image captioning and sentiment analysis.

To enhance the accuracy of computational models, an error estimate based on a physical experiment or high-precision numerical result is necessary. This estimation method, known as model correction, involves calculating the difference between model solutions and an experiment-based reference solution. Historically, model correction has been limited to models based on linear algebra-based operators. This paper expands the model correction framework to a broader range, specifically nonsymmetric matrices, and extends the concept of 'operator shifting' to this expanded range. This revised framework utilizes the inherent characteristics of the expanded range to create a new class of correction methods. This paper also introduces corresponding algorithms and provides supporting numerical demonstrations.

We calculate the slices and the slice spectral sequence of the equivariant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, where the spectra of the form $H\mathbb{F}_p[X; \mathbb{Z}/p]$ are considered, with $X$ being a finite $G$-set, and $G$ being one of the form $\mathbb{Z}/n$. The calculations are performed under the $Q_8$-equivariance, which simplifies to using the $Q_8$-slices of the spectra and resulting spectra of the form $H\mathbb{F}_{4}[X_{Q_8}; \mathbb{Z}].$ The approach relies on applying the $Q_8$-slices method, $Q_8$-equivariant analysis, and further application of the $Q_8$-slices method to the spectra of the form $H\mathbb{F}_p[X; \mathbb{Z}/p]$. The resulting spectra of the form $H\mathbb{F}_p[X_{Q_8}; \mathbb{Z}]$ are then used to compute the $Q_8$-equivariant homotopy groups of highly connected examples of $Q_8$-equivariant exotica spectra, which are spectra that are not $Q_8$-free.

Let (A, \mathfrak{m}) be a Noetherian local ring with characteristics A being p for now, and let F be a continuous automorphism of the ring where the image of the maximal ideal is the maximal ideal.  We are looking to understand when the ring is said to be F-rational, which is based on the number of elements in the automorphism's invariant Hilbert-Samuel function.  We are investigating the properties of rings that are under a specific automorphism in this work and exploring how these properties relate to other mathematical concepts such as polarized endomorphisms, birational mappings, and rational singularities.  We are also examining the connection to other existing rings such as G-rationality and S-rationality, and we are using our results to derive test ideals for rational singularities under certain automorphisms.

The application of machine learning in medicine has grown significantly due to the availability of vast amounts of digital medical data in the ANSI/IEEE 1284-1995 format, also known as DICOM. The standardization of imaging data across various device types is crucial for data exchange, processing, and analysis. Additionally, DICOM includes metadata such as patient information, which is vital for machine learning. We provide an overview of incorporating machine learning into the DICOM standard, briefly outlining relevant components of the data format and popular machine learning tasks. Our goal is to highlight existing resources and challenges associated with combining machine learning and DICOM, thus facilitating future research in this area.

We're exploring the concept of entropy in a specific type of theory known as dRGT, which is based on an unconventional understanding of general relativity. By applying the concept of entropy to the gravitational system with a horizon, we find that the charge associated with the horizon, as calculated by the Black Hole Massless Dirichlet bracket, is directly related to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy but with a significantly reduced value. This reduction occurs due to constraints within the Dirichlet bracket. Consequently, entropies generated through the Bekenstein-Hawking method are insufficient to explain the entropies observed in stars and galaxies, which exhibit higher values than expected from classical physics alone.

A new method called DNA$^\Lambda$ is presented for creating a standardized, fixed-length code in an unsupervised manner for long and variable DNA sequences of any length. This method builds upon an existing model, AutoEncoder, by employing a Transformer architecture, specifically a Variational AutoEncoder (VAE) with a MaJorization-Minimization (MM) approach, to leverage the benefits of both models. DNA$^\Lambda$ uses a combination of a encoder and a decoder network, where the encoder reduces input data into a standardized, fixed-length code, and the decoder generates the original input sequence from this code. This code has optimal balance between minimizing representation size and preserving essential information about input sequences. DNA$^\Lambda$ optimizes its latent representation in an unsupervised manner on a given dataset, such as genomic sequences, like human chromosomes, and evaluates its effectiveness using relevant metrics, such as self-similarity, clustering, and regression tasks, like target sequence prediction and gene feature regression. DNA$^\Lambda$ is implemented in Python and made available on the public GitHub platform at the address https://github.com/krishanp/Park2022arXiv22071192T.

V$_2$O$_3$ is a well-known compound that exhibits a metal-insulator transition dependent on surface termination and thickness. By using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, the electronic structure of thin V$_2$O$_3$ films has been studied in detail. The measurements reveal a clear band gap in the (001) surface, but not in the (010) surface, indicating that the metal-insulator transition is controlled by surface reconstruction rather than a bulk property. The results also show that the (001) surface reconstruction leads to a midgap state due to charge transfer, while the (010) surface exhibits metallic behavior similar to the bulk. The findings are further supported by density functional theory calculations, which confirm the existence of midgap states in the (001) surface and show that the (010) surface has a similar electronic structure to the bulk.

A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been developed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems. The process involves calculating two momentum maps, one in the cotangent space and the other in the space itself, to subsequently apply a symplectic reduction. This results in a set of flows that are Hamiltonian in their original configuration and satisfy Hamiltonian conditions. Recent studies, including those on magnetohydrodynamics and fluid dynamics, have previously employed Clebsch canonization without fully considering its underlying mathematical structure. The current work provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for this method and offers insights into previously solved problems as well as identifying novel applications.

The team has completed a comprehensive analysis of microlensing planets identified by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder in 2018, resulting in 9 newly identified and 8 previously known planets in the sub-polar regions. Out of these 9 new planets, 6 were clearly shown to have a planetary nature, while 3 others due to lens position, could only be confirmed as being caused by a perturber rather than a star. Among these new discoveries, 4 planets have their mass relative to the mass of their central object established, representing a significant advancement in the field of microlensing planets. Notably, 3 of these new planets have central object masses derived from data, providing further insight into the relationship between the mass of the central object and its associated optical depth.

A standard model for examining optimal control problems involving hyperbolic conservation laws is the Euler equation for irrotational potential flow. We'll focus on the acoustic wave type equation, derive a Hamilton-Jacobi equation solution using a viscous resistance model as an example, and demonstrate the approach can be applied to the potential flow equation. The resistance model adds a dissipative term to the Euler equation, effectively making it a parabolic equation. By considering irrotational potential flow, the equation simplifies to the linear equation $u_t = u_{xx} - (u_x + \phi_x)_x$, where $u$ represents acoustic pressure and $\phi$ the external control function. Our goal is to find the optimal $\phi(x,t)$ that minimizes a given functional, where the optimality condition is defined by the Hamilton-Jacobi equation $\phi_t + \phi_{xx} = -u_t$. We'll demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of the optimal solution by assuming a small value for the resistance parameter.

Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a key factor for banks to mitigate credit risk and make informed lending decisions.
This process is typically grounded in thorough credit assessments and aligned with industry standards, drawing on the analysis of multiple borrowers to establish comparable benchmarks.
To address this challenge, we employ advanced machine learning techniques to evaluate the creditworthiness of clients from a leading African country, using data that encompasses 30 client variables and 3,678 observations.
Key findings from our analysis include the identification of key variables that most significantly influence non-performing loans, with insights suggesting that client variables are more crucial than business-related variables when assessing credit risk.
Furthermore, our results indicate that non-performing loans are more prevalent among younger applicants with shorter credit histories and lower credit limits, with correlations observed between non-performing loans and age, credit limit, and industry sector.
Through the application of machine learning models, including the decision tree, random forest, gradient boosting machine, and support vector machine, we derive the most important features for predicting non-performing loans.
Ultimately, the gradient boosting machine model emerges as the top performer, with the top three key variables that contribute to its success identified as loan amount, credit risk rating, and client industry sector.

The connections between the chromatic symmetric functions of specific Dyck paths, originally discovered by Stanley and later expanded on by Shareshian-Wachs in their $q$-analogs, are crucial in several areas of study. Recently, Garsia and Haggarty presented a general method for calculating the $q$-analogs of the chromatic functions for any Dyck paths using combinatorial techniques based on $q$-analogues of combinatorial objects. In this study, we establish analogues for the general method identified by Garsia and Haggarty, specifically for the case of non-attacking rooks on rectangular diagrams.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), excel at image recognition but often struggle when the image is not perfectly oriented for optimal recognition. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Orientation Convolution Network (OCN), an architecture that can normalize image orientations and be used as a pre-processing step for any DCNN. By combining OCNs with DCNNs, we call this hybrid model the OffCenter-Odin Network. Experimental results demonstrate that this integrated model surpasses traditional DCNNs and other image normalization methods, such as Cropping and Rotation Transformation (CRT), in terms of accuracy. Notably, the OffCenter-Odin network achieves higher accuracy than DCNNs with or without OCNs and also outperforms other models that utilize pre-processing to correct image orientations.

Using a novel relative trace formula, we investigate the linear periods on $GL_{2n}$ that are modulated by a character. The study involves the intersection theory of Hecke operators, which has also been applied to $Sp_{2n}$ cases. Consequently, the results establish the multiplicity bounds for the Fourier coefficients of certain automorphic forms on Chevalley groups, specifically for special affine and elliptic cases.

We employ systematic renormalization group methods in the $\overline{\rm MS}$ scheme to address the uncertainty in the pole mass of a heavy quark, specifically with flavor masses other than the top quark. Our calculation shows that mass splittings between quarks of lighter flavor can be resolved to a fraction of $m_q$ MeV, while those of similar flavor can be resolved to about $0.1\,\mu$m meter mass resolution. The methods developed here are crucial for understanding the top quark's mass and its decay width to the top quark and W boson, a process considered crucial for understanding the Higgs boson's interactions with the top quark.

Consider a graph $G$ and a subset $R$ of its vertices $G$, and a function $f$ that assigns colors to the vertices of $G$ incrementally from the vertices in $R$. This color assignment is called an $R$-sequential $t$-coloring if each vertex and its neighbors receive at most $t$ colors as the process progresses. We are studying a specific type of graph called circulant graphs and exploring the feasibility of $R$-sequential $t$-colorings for certain circulant graph configurations where $R$ consists of a single vertex. We are specifically focused on identifying the minimum number of colors required for these $R$-sequential $t$-colorings.

We establish a precise relationship between L^p to L^q contraction inequalities in weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, incorporating typical weight functions found in harmonic analysis. This outcome addresses an unresolved challenge in the research of Carleson-type theorems within Bergman spaces, specifically for the scenario where 2 < q < p ≤ 2 + 2. Furthermore, we explore consequences of our findings in the context of both Dirichlet series and multiple Fourier-Bergman transforms.

The global pandemic caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, known as COVID-19, has claimed numerous lives and severely impacted the world's economy, with the United States being one of the hardest hit countries. To diagnose COVID-19 quickly and efficiently, computed tomography (CT) scans have become a crucial diagnostic tool, available to patients in most hospitals across the US. However, obtaining standard dose CT scans can pose risks to patients, particularly those with pre-existing health conditions. To mitigate these risks, researchers have experimented with low-dose and ultra-low-dose CT scans while maintaining diagnostic accuracy. To achieve this goal, we have developed an advanced denoising technique utilizing deep learning and applied it to CT scans, resulting in noise-free images. Our study focuses on the effectiveness of our denoising method in producing high-quality images for both patients and the environment by utilizing the Noise2Noise method and assessing image quality metrics on ULDS data. Our results show that the N2N method produces denoised CT scans with enhanced image clarity, meeting the requirements for diagnostic purposes. Additionally, we have compared our method with other state-of-the-art techniques, such as Filter Denoising and Diffusion Convolution Recurrent Neural Network, and confirmed its superior performance through both visual inspections and metrics such as the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and the structural similarity index metric (SSIM).

Satellites in low-Earth orbit experiencing high collisions rates necessitate efficient space collision avoidance systems to ensure their operational safety. Effective space collision avoidance requires determining their space occupancy in three-dimensional space, which in turn demands an accurate prediction of their orbital trajectories. This research proposes an innovative space occupancy prediction method leveraging a Gaussian process-based model to forecast orbital trajectories. This approach utilizes past collision data, which is then utilized to calculate and predict the satellite's space occupancy at various points in time. By integrating the Gaussian process model with an occupancy generator, our method provides highly accurate and computationally efficient predictions. This research includes simulations of the TLE dataset to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in predicting space occupancy, particularly for satellites in low-Earth orbit.

To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models, we develop an efficient and flexible framework. A key element of this framework is an advanced Delaunay refinement method that utilizes customized cell indicators to identify and separate problematic tetrahedra. By strategically placing new vertices to fix these distorted tetrahedra, we can convert them into higher-quality quadrilateral elements. This approach allows for a high degree of control over mesh topology and geometry, enabling the seamless repair of underlying tetrahedral meshes. Additionally, our method leverages spatial partitioning techniques to significantly speed up computation even in complex scenarios with intricate CAD geometries and high mesh orders. Extensive numerical testing across various CAD models demonstrates the rapid and efficient construction of high-order quadrilateral meshes on up to non-Manifold data sets, showcasing its robustness and scalability.

Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed to evaluate the level of association between two variables. The scalar correlation coefficient receives the sole influence from the relative geometric relationships between pairs of points, thereby failing to capture potential geometric patterns among three or more variables. In contrast, circular correlation operates on the z-scored data and represents a measure of association between variables that considers all possible geometric relationships among points, thereby accounting for all possible rotations. The paper derives formulas for calculating circular correlations based on the minimum spanning tree and presents an algorithm specifically designed for this purpose. The study also demonstrates the relationship between minimum spanning tree and circular correlations, while providing an in-depth analysis of the underlying theory and discussing various applications and properties of circular correlations.

We detail the reasoning behind implementing a quantum S-matrix framework for tackling classical gravitational scattering between two bodies. Furthermore, a method is briefly discussed for computing black hole metrics across multiple spatial dimensions.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations' solvability in the $L^3(\mathbb{R}^3)$ space, a critical problem with implications for regularity theorems. In 2018, Bourgain and Li used an inverse Galerkin method to show the solvability of the Navier-Stokes equations in $L^3(\mathbb{R}^3)$, a result we build upon by removing certain growth restrictions in the equations. Furthermore, we establish the solvability of the Navier-Stokes equations in $L^3(\mathbb{R}^3)$ with non-zero initial conditions and provide a lower bound on the time to solvability.

Learning new words in a vocabulary can be facilitated through dictionaries, 
yet existing digital dictionaries often limit word learning by only offering 
definitions and not providing examples of how the words are used in context. 
A generative dictionary, as described in this research, can enhance vocabulary 
gain by allowing word encounters in various forms of input, such as text and 
audio, thereby increasing efficacy by up to five and seven times, as shown in 
our word recall and reading comprehension experiments, respectively. Additionally, 
our study indicates that the benefits of generative dictionaries are comparable to 
that of a comprehensive language training program when used in a controlled word 
learning environment.

The growing demand for transparent AI models has led to the emergence of explainable recommendation systems, focusing on providing understandable reasoning behind recommended items to end-users.  Human users' experience greatly rely on system transparency and trustworthiness, which can be established through clear and trustworthy explanations.  To address this need, researchers have made significant progress in developing XRS, although a comprehensive evaluation of existing XRS benchmarks is still pending.  This study aims to fill this gap by examining a novel benchmark suite for XRS, featuring both synthetic and real-world datasets.  A detailed analysis of the suite's performance on existing XRS methods will be presented, using multiple evaluation metrics, to better understand its performance in different user scenarios.  Our findings will be discussed in context, and the proposed benchmark suite will be made available to the public for further research purposes.

The electron mobility in InAs quantum wells, manufactured via molecular beam epitaxy with a 9 nm barrier height, has been examined using a magneto-transport technique. It has been found that surface morphology has a considerable influence on electron mobility. Devices with a smaller surface roughness, induced by a thin GaAs capping layer, exhibit a high electron mobility of approximately 104,000 cm^2/Vs/sec at a temperature of 1.5K. In contrast, a device with a surface roughness of about 1 nm, caused by omitting the capping layer, shows a lower electron mobility of approximately 76,000 cm^2/Vs/sec under the same temperature conditions.

Our research focuses on developing a resilient learning framework that can effectively use non-noisy local information to improve model accuracy in the face of adversarial attacks. We introduce a new concept, local membership queries (LMQs), which allows learners to obtain robust information from local data sources. We then propose the first robust learning model, Local Robust Learner (LRL), which is capable of learning complex classes from limited, adversarially altered data. We demonstrate the robustness of our model by testing it against the most up-to-date attack techniques and observe that it consistently outperforms traditional learners on various challenging datasets, including binary datasets in high-dimensional spaces and multi-class datasets in large datasets.

Our research focuses on a novel, underexplored matrix type, known as L/U-CoLT, characterized by having low rank plus structural zeros via upper triangular permutation. We propose an efficient, time-linear algorithm for performing basic matrix operations such as inversion, solving linear systems, calculating the determinant, and calculating the condition number without breaking down the matrix into its constituent parts. Unlike existing methods, our approach avoids costly factorization and instead leverages L/U-CoLT-specific properties to yield superior results. We validate our findings through several real-world data examples, demonstrating that L/U-CoLT matrices can arise naturally across multiple domains.

Young stars releasing energetic X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and atmospheric composition. We've simulated the effects of this radiation from multiple stellar sources, modeling the energy patterns using the THESPY code. Our model, which accounts for varying binary separation and age dependencies, creates realistic flux patterns across 0-500 Angstrom. By analyzing these patterns, we've found that most energy comes from the innermost star, and atmospheric escape rates remain similar for close and distant binary configurations. However, the energy from the outer stars can still significantly impact atmospheric composition after the disk dissipates, leading to the loss of volatile gases.

We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a medium with mechanical resistance. We introduce an effect where the medium is warped by the motion of charged particles, and the medium responds by generating an electric field due to inhomogeneities in its dielectric properties. For media without electric conduction, we find the general equation for the dielectric function and analyze various scenarios, such as the medium being overdense, underdense, and critical. We compare our results with existing research and apply our findings to real-world situations, such as the emission of light from fireflies and the interaction of antihydrogen with a target gas.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor method is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classifier, which accounts for uneven class distributions by incorporating a Poisson random projection as a pre-processing step. By analyzing this method, the classification error rate is shown to converge towards a population parameter that incorporates the influence of the uneven class distribution. A corresponding asymptotic confidence interval is developed and tested through a series of simulation studies. Additionally, the proposed method is successfully applied to a real-world dataset consisting of digital images from a telescopic search for radio-emitting quasars.

We employed photometric methods to discover 99 new quasars within a redshift range of $3.5<z<5.4$. These quasars were chosen based on data from the Panoramic Survey NYAIS project, and subsequent spectroscopic observations confirmed their identities. By utilizing our established photometric technique, we were able to refine the estimated number of quasars at higher redshifts using previously published data. Additionally, we derived the QSO luminosity function at high redshifts and compared our findings to prior studies. Notably, we observed an evolution in the QLF shape, specifically from a steep power-law at $z\approx5.3$ to a more complex distribution with two distinct power-law components separated by a "knee" at $z\approx4.3$. This structural shift indicates a potential change in QSO formation patterns. Extrapolating our data to $z\approx5.5$, we estimated the QLS volume density to be approximately $3.1$ times greater than at $z\approx4.8$.

We present an experiment where a semiconductor quantum dot near a superconducting island has the island attached to a critical current path in a Josephson ring modulator.  Conductance fluctuations within the quantum dot are analyzed as charge transfers through it via the lead it's connected to.  A distinctive pattern in these fluctuations emerges when a quantum dot charge state change is facilitated by a pair of Andreev particles, rather than a single electron.  This distinctive pattern is observed in our study, given that the quantum dot is part of a device where the superconducting island's critical current controls the critical current of a Josephson circuit, and a normal-superconducting transition is initiated when the island's charge is changed.  This experiment reveals that such a transition can occur through both electron tunneling and pair tunneling, producing two distinct phase space diagrams that influence the transition's probability.  A notable outcome of our study is that the latter typically involves larger probabilities than the former, especially at lower temperatures.  Furthermore, our study shows that the former's probability threshold is determined by the size of the superconducting gap, whereas the latter's threshold is largely independent of this parameter.  Lastly, our study shows that the former requires a relatively high bias voltage relative to the size of the superconducting gap, whereas the latter can facilitate a charge transfer at a lower voltage, even below the size of the superconducting gap, and may potentially facilitate such a transfer when coupled with a quantum dot

Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in systems of equations, particularly those that conserve quantities, given the presence of a convex "stability" function. To expand upon existing work, we introduce a new, simplified set of criteria that can be easily combined to yield a more comprehensive condition, thereby excluding unnecessary or overly restrictive assumptions. We demonstrate the validity of these conditions through two illustrative examples, and showcase the potential of our approach by applying it to a broad class of solutions to fluid dynamics equations, both with and without gravity, as well as in electromagnetic systems.

We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a given image -- through a new, promising approach. Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that synthesizes novel long-distance views by learning a plausible scene completion strategy. It relies on diffusion models combined with a simple, dynamic latent code movement mechanism. Our results show that image-conditioned models outperform previous solutions based on GANs. Additionally, we introduce a more realistic and detailed dataset, the 'Charm' dataset, which features more natural and challenging for model training compared to existing datasets. Our experiments confirm that the new approach outperforms previous methods and achieves more realistic and detailed results on this new dataset, both quantitatively and visually.

Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors, often governed by stochastic nonlinear dynamics. In such systems, statistical quantities like distribution profiles and correlation patterns are of great interest. Current theories typically rely on time-tested methods like Monte Carlo simulations, but these can be cumbersome and challenging to apply to large networks. To address this limitation, researchers have developed a new set of analytical tools to study complex stochastic dynamics, enabling the accurate prediction of emergent properties in large and complex networks. These tools involve a set of ordinary differential equations that describe how distribution profiles evolve over time, accompanied by a new method for approximating higher-order correlations. When applied to fundamental models of stochastic dynamics, like the stochastic birth-death process, these new tools demonstrate remarkable accuracy and efficiency, both within and outside the scope of Monte Carlo simulations.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that demonstrates the instability of a liquid film on a fiber due to perturbations that grow at a rate influenced by slip at the interface. What's more, in the case of a fiber with no slip, but whose center is expanded compared to a typical fiber, the model predicts a greater rate of growth for perturbations. This expansion leads to a greater rate of film thinning. This new understanding has been incorporated into a revised version of the Rayleigh-Plateau problem theory, which explains why films on expanded fibers tend to thin faster than those on standard fibers.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability of solutions to the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a continuous function. Our study builds upon previous work by Constantine and Khesin, which demonstrated the Lipschitz stability of smooth solutions. We expand upon their findings, showing that Lipschitz stability is maintained for solutions with mild singularities.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanner can automatically collect data at specific angles, streamlining the process. Although the robotic scanner's capabilities are uncertain in terms of measuring curvature severity, particularly at advanced stages. Researchers investigated whether robotic ultrasound can accurately and reliably assess scoliosis using the Cobb angle as a benchmark. The study found that robotic ultrasound yielded accurate results, with minor errors of 2.1 degrees when comparing the robotic scanner's measurements to those taken manually. The robotic scanner showed strong potential in scoliosis assessment, especially in obtaining necessary data at critical angles for accurate curvature severity evaluation.

This paper presents a new method for speech duration prediction that leverages a median-based approach to mitigate the influence of outliers. Traditional hidden Markov model-based duration models rely on mean estimation, which can lead to suboptimal performance due to the presence of durations far from the average. By utilizing median and interquartile range measures, this method is more resilient to duration anomalies. An ERM-based training framework enhances the model's robustness, which is evaluated on the speech synthesis quality of the corresponding speech. Acoustic and melodic quality assessments using the PESQ and FS score metrics reveal that this new model yields superior results compared to the baseline.

The internet is essentially a global hub of information, offering boundless knowledge and information to users. However, this platform's liberating potential is constantly undermined by the pervasive presence of offensive language. To preserve the integrity of online interactions, researchers have focused on pinpointing and categorizing harmful language, which has led to significant advancements in detecting and mitigating online abuse. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the prevailing types of offensive language, highlighting their distinct characteristics and societal implications. Furthermore, it seeks to identify and discuss critical gaps in current research and initiatives to tackle offensive language, ultimately serving as a foundation for future research directions and potential solutions.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by replicating the ensemble effect within a single network.  However, these networks have been found to be inefficient in terms of parameter usage and prone to overfitting.  This research presents an alternative approach, the split task network, which also combines multiple inputs to produce multiple outputs, but by dividing a standard fully connected layer into separate tasks, reducing the size of each task improves stability and reduces redundancy within the parameter set, ultimately leading to better results and more efficient models.  We test the split task method against MIMO and traditional ensemble baselines on both artificial and real world data sets, finding that split task networks consistently outperform MIMO networks while using significantly fewer parameters, and often rivaling ensemble performance.  We further examine the benefits of the split task method in terms of model interpretability, finding better separation of tasks and more consistent performance across each task, resulting in improved understanding of the model.

This study provides an overview of existing research on document image analysis, recapping key findings, tasks, datasets, applications, challenges, and important publications up to a recent cutoff date. A comprehensive, multi-task approach to document image analysis is outlined, contrasting prior studies that focused on individual tasks such as document categorization, automatic reading, and text or visual content extraction. A detailed, task-oriented overview of document image analysis is presented, covering visual content extraction, layout analysis, layout normalization, categorization, reading assistance, and active reading tasks. Additionally, key findings from applied fields such as automatic document identification, reading support, and active reading are discussed. A global summary of recent advancements in document image analysis is offered, along with identification of unresolved challenges and suggestions for future research directions.

This paper presents a novel real-time approach for rectifying kinematic errors in joinred machining robots through the implementation of an adaptive feedforward controller. A novel algorithm is proposed to identify and track the dynamic and static distortions affecting these robots. By integrating the findings of flexible body dynamics, external forces, and internal alignments, this algorithm effectively navigates the primary sources of error in industrial robots and machine tools. Utilizing hyper plane based recursive least squares methods, it is capable of rapidly and adaptively adjusting parameter updates in real-time. The proposed feedforward controller is then simulated and tested in different robotic scenarios, showcasing its ability to precisely counteract position errors resulting from distortions.

The study of how chronic diseases progress over an individual's lifetime has thus far been limited by a focus on either short-term or long-term perspectives, overlooking the impact of early life experiences and societal influences on future health outcomes. A proposed framework aims to address these limitations by being adaptable to various durations of follow-up, from a single health issue in early life to tracking multiple conditions throughout an entire lifetime. This framework emphasizes the importance of early life exposures as a foundation for future health trajectories and highlights the need for dynamic tracking of an individual's health path over time. A key challenge in implementing this approach lies in the incomplete information available on early life experiences and future health outcomes, which often relies on imputation and simulation techniques to fill in the gaps.

We have developed a comprehensive library called PyEC for computing various electronic integrals necessary for simulating chemical reactions on classical and quantum levels in polyatomic molecules. By utilizing PyEC, users can calculate electronic properties based on a molecular orbital model. The library leverages the capabilities of NumPy and Pytorch for efficient computations. It employs Becke's partitioning scheme to evaluate electronic integrals with high accuracy. The source code is freely available online.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding the smallest such subset is known as the metric dimension problem. This problem has been well-studied for nearly five decades, but its complexity remains largely understood only for certain special cases. This paper focuses on identifying the smallest resolving sets in graphs that are strongly regular. The paper also uses computer-assisted proofs to resolve the metric dimension problem for certain strong regular graphs and a case of weak regularity. Additionally, it presents a new, algorithmic method for finding small resolving sets in any given graph, potentially improving our understanding of the metric dimension problem's complexity.

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces of a domain) were initially defined for compact, ordered spaces by Martin and Reinhold in 2006.  Our work redefines these concepts for directed spaces, showing that powerdomains of a directed space exist uniquely up to domain-isomorphism, and that these powerdomains lie within the collection of all valued spaces topologically-isomorphic to directed spaces.  Further, our work establishes the existence of minimal powerdomain spaces for directed spaces, and provides a topological characterization of powerdomain spaces that hold minimal status.
